records.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents

source_hash_payload.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
source_hash_payload.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.

records.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution

source_hash_payload.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
source_hash_payload.abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

records.title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems

source_hash_payload.title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
source_hash_payload.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

records.title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance

source_hash_payload.title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance
source_hash_payload.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.

records.title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities

source_hash_payload.title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
source_hash_payload.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.

records.title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

source_hash_payload.title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
source_hash_payload.abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

records.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments

source_hash_payload.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
source_hash_payload.abstract: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. More broadly, our results show that how information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, making the environment worth optimizing in addition to the parameters and the harness.

records.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments

source_hash_payload.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
source_hash_payload.abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

source_hash_payload.title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
source_hash_payload.abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.

records.title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale

source_hash_payload.title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
source_hash_payload.abstract: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.

records.title: Agentic Behavior Engineering: A Design-by-Contract Methodology for Specifying, Verifying, and Governing Enterprise AI Agents

source_hash_payload.title: Agentic Behavior Engineering: A Design-by-Contract Methodology for Specifying, Verifying, and Governing Enterprise AI Agents
source_hash_payload.abstract: Enterprise teams that deploy large language model (LLM) agents inherit a maintenance problem that traditional testing does not address. The model is non-deterministic, but the larger risk is that most of what changes an agent's behavior (a retired model version, a revised policy, an upstream schema change, a prompt edit meant to fix one case) originates outside the owning team and is discovered as a production defect rather than caught as a regression. This paper presents Agentic Behavior Engineering (ABE), a platform-agnostic methodology that treats observable agent behavior, rather than the prompt or the model, as the version-controlled engineering artifact. ABE adapts Design by Contract to non-deterministic systems. A specification-only behavior contract with stable rule identifiers states what the agent must do, must not do, and when it must abstain for lack of evidence; a lightweight scenario library turns each rule into concrete situations; and every engineering artifact (tests, runtime policies, telemetry) references the contract in one direction only, so that specification and implementation can change independently without drifting apart. The method organizes the work into five responsibilities (Specify, Ground, Control, Verify, Observe), treats missing evidence and a verified negative as different things, enforces authority outside the model, gates releases on per-scenario pass^k reliability rather than aggregate accuracy, and classifies every production run against the contract so that each finding routes to the asset that must change. We illustrate the method with an executable capacity-allocation boundary suite and a constructed worked example of a product-review approval workflow.

records.title: ControlAnything: Generative UI and On-Demand Device Integration for Mixed-Reality Hand Interaction by a Coding Agent

source_hash_payload.title: ControlAnything: Generative UI and On-Demand Device Integration for Mixed-Reality Hand Interaction by a Coding Agent
source_hash_payload.abstract: Connecting hand input in mixed reality (MR) to a nearby physical device typically requires an integration written in advance for that device, its transport and the mapping. ControlAnything defers this integration to the moment of use and assigns it to a coding agent. On a Meta Quest 3, the wearer selects an object outlined by SAM 3.1 and states what their hands should control. An agent built on Meta's Muse Spark model then writes a connector program on the wearer's laptop, tests it against the live device through hand-written MIDI, Bluetooth and key-press transports, and returns augmented-reality (AR) controls, a per-frame hand program, or both. These outputs are a form of generative UI, interfaces created by an AI model; here, the agent also generates and tests the code that binds the interface to a physical device. In a single-session technical evaluation with the author as the only wearer, nine of ten requests addressing five targets reached a ready state, and the wearer stopped one. The median time to ready was 32.5 s (range 24.9-57.8 s, excluding speech transcription); sequential model calls accounted for a median of 89.9% of this time, and 91.7% of input tokens came from the prompt cache. The system's evidence of success extends to transport acknowledgements but not to physical effects. These findings point to connector reuse and the observation of effects through the headset's own sensors as next steps for on-demand device integration in MR. A user study with first-time wearers is planned.

records.title: Where Do Reported Long-Video QA Gains Come From? A Controlled Audit of Frame Selection, Evidence Injection, and Expert Routing

source_hash_payload.title: Where Do Reported Long-Video QA Gains Come From? A Controlled Audit of Frame Selection, Evidence Injection, and Expert Routing
source_hash_payload.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.

records.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions

source_hash_payload.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions
source_hash_payload.abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.

records.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

source_hash_payload.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
source_hash_payload.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

records.title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment

source_hash_payload.title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
source_hash_payload.abstract: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD.

records.title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?

source_hash_payload.title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
source_hash_payload.abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

source_hash_payload.title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
source_hash_payload.abstract: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.

source_hash_payload.title: ELLMO at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship, Reuse, and Taxonomy: Ontology Learning Across Contexts
source_hash_payload.abstract: Ontology learning aims to transform unstructured or semi-structured information into structured representations of domain knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for automating parts of this process, but their effectiveness depends on the type of information available, including source text, partial ontologies, and related ontologies from other domains. This paper presents our submission to the LLMs4OL Challenge 2026, where we address three ontology-learning tasks: the Flagship Task, focused on ontology construction from text; the Reuse Task, focused on extending a partial ontology using text and existing triples; and the Taxonomy Task, focused on identifying taxonomic relations in a target domain using ontologies from other domains. Across these tasks, we develop task-specific methods that combine LLM prompting, NLP-based extraction, ontology context, cross-domain classification, and embedding-based downselection. Our work explores how LLM-assisted ontology-learning workflows can be adapted to different forms of textual and structured input.

Title:Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities

Authors:Haoyang Zhang, Qumeng Sun, Xiao Zhang, Xiang Liu, Zhidong Fan, Junjie Wang
View a PDF of the paper titled Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities, by Haoyang Zhang and 5 other authors
View PDF HTML (experimental)
Abstract:Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.
Comments: 12 pages, 5 figures

Title:ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance

Authors:Hangyu Qin, Junbin Xiao, Angela Yao
View a PDF of the paper titled ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance, by Hangyu Qin and 2 other authors
View PDF HTML (experimental)
Abstract:Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.

Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution

Xiaobo Wang1,4,*    Zimu Wang2,*    Siyu Ye3,*    Jiaqi Li4,*    Min Tang1    Jun Bai4    Yuling Shi5    Ruobing Wang3    Jingjing Zhang2    Chaofan Wang5    Kai WU3    Mengnan Qi3    Kai Cai3    Xiaodong Gu5,†\dagger    Qi Liu1,†\dagger    Zilong Zheng4,†\dagger
Abstract

Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

Code: https://github.com/simple-agent-lab/RSIHub November 5, 2026

Correspondence: Siyu Ye at andyyesiyu@gmail.com, Xiaodong Gu at xiaodong.gu@sjtu.edu.cn, Jiaqi Li at lijiaqi@bigai.ai, Zilong Zheng at zlzheng@bigai.ai, Xiaobo Wang at xiaobow.0519@gmail.com.

1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) studies agents that iteratively revise their own designs based on experience (Zelikman et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). Agent harness evolution offers a concrete form of this idea for language-model agents: it keeps model weights fixed while persistently changing the surrounding system that shapes observations and turns model outputs into actions (Lin et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026c). Depending on the harness, these changes can target prompts, skills, tool interfaces, orchestration, or source code, going beyond static prompting and memory-based adaptation (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Recent frameworks close the loop between execution, diagnosis, mutation, and evaluation, reporting gains on standard benchmarks (Hu et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). These benchmark gains suggest that harness evolution is a promising avenue for pursuing RSI.

However, a higher overall benchmark score do not mean a more useful agent. It averages over tasks and trials, so newly solved tasks can conceal lost ones, while deployment cost and performance beyond the tasks that guided evolution remain unseen (Gao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Kapoor et al., 2025). Relying on that score alone can favor brittle or expensive agent versions and mistake adaptation to the tasks used during evolution for general improvement. Meaningful progress instead requires gains that are reliable across tasks, affordable to deploy, and effective on tasks that did not guide evolution. We aim to explain which persistent harness changes produce useful gains and how evolution generates and preserves them.

We organize our empirical investigation around three research questions:

  • •

    RQ1 (Phenomenology): Does agent evolution yield reliable and efficient improvements, or does it suffer from task-coverage trade-offs and hidden costs?

  • •

    RQ2 (Generalization): Do the gains achieved during evolving survive when the agent is deployed in novel environments or tasks?

  • •

    RQ3 (Mechanisms): How do specific evolutionary operators contribute to the generation and preservation of beneficial modifications?

We study AHE (Lin et al., 2026a), HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026c), A-Evolve (Lin et al., 2026b), and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) with MiniSWE (Yang et al., 2024) and Codex (OpenAI, 2026) on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking (Shi et al., 2026) for general tasks and Terminal-Bench 2 (Merrill et al., 2026) for coding tasks. Repeated evaluations compare evolved and initial agents in reliability, empirical coverage, regressions, and deployment cost. Split and cross-benchmark comparisons assess generalization, while controlled expansion of existing agents, change interventions, and admission replays trace how gains arise and persist.

Harness evolution redistributes task success, with new coverage accompanied by regressions across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms. The practical value of these gains depends on deployment cost and whether they persist beyond the tasks that guided evolution. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, yet combining them can alter their value. The strongest existing agent need not offer the greatest further improvement, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Useful improvement therefore requires productive starting points, compatible changes, and search decisions that preserve gains.

We connect these findings to operator redesign as a constructive follow-up. Analyses of Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms jointly guide revision hypotheses for select, analyze, mutate, and gate. Each hypothesis specifies its supporting evidence, expected effects, and applicability conditions. We combine these revisions into Audit-Guided Evolution (AGE) to test their practical value.

Our contributions can be summarized as:

  • •

    Revisiting Practical Improvement. We reveal a gap between benchmark gains and practical utility, showing that useful improvement in agent harness evolution requires preserving useful behavior, managing deployment cost, and sustaining gains beyond the tasks that guide evolution.

  • •

    Understanding the Fragility of Gains. We identify productive agent selection, change compatibility, and search retention as central challenges. Current performance can misrepresent further improvement potential, useful changes can interfere, and admission can discard stronger versions.

  • •

    Improving Evolution Through Analysis. We translate these findings into coordinated revisions of diagnosis, mutation, selection, and admission. The resulting AGE algorithm improves reliability and coverage over its reference method across both benchmarks and harnesses.

2 Related Work

Agent Optimization and Evolution. Agent improvement spans inference-time refinement, optimization of persistent artifacts, and open-ended self-modification. Reflexion retains linguistic feedback in episodic memory across trials, whereas Self-Refine iteratively revises the current output (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023). ReflectEvo trains small language models on self-generated reflections to improve introspection and reasoning (Li et al., 2025). RAM learns from communications to improve an external memory system (Li et al., 2024), and The AI Hippocampus surveys implicit, explicit, and agentic memory mechanisms (Jia et al., 2025). DSPy optimizes language-model programs, and TextGrad propagates textual feedback through computational graphs (Khattab et al., 2024; Yüksekgönül et al., 2025). Promptbreeder evolves both task and mutation prompts, ACE maintains evolving context playbooks, and CoEvoSkills co-evolves multi-file skill packages with a separate surrogate verifier (Fernando et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a). The four approaches examined here make different choices within this space. AHE exposes editable harness components and uses distilled execution evidence to guide revisions (Lin et al., 2026a). HyperAgents makes both the task agent and its modification procedure editable (Zhang et al., 2026c). A-Evolve frames deployment-time adaptation as goal-directed optimization over persistent system state (Lin et al., 2026b). GEPA combines trajectory reflection for prompt updates with Pareto selection of complementary candidates (Agrawal et al., 2026).

Harness and Program Evolution. Related approaches also optimize system structure and executable code. GPTSwarm optimizes prompt-bearing graph nodes and orchestration edges, while AgentSquare searches combinations of planning, reasoning, tool-use, and memory modules (Zhuge et al., 2024; Shang et al., 2025). ADAS uses a meta agent to generate agent programs (Hu et al., 2025). Self-modification extends to the improvement procedure itself: STOP revises optimizer scaffolding, and the Darwin Gödel Machine evolves its own coding agent (Zelikman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b). AlphaEvolve instead evolves target algorithm programs using executable evaluation feedback (Novikov et al., 2025). Recent work also explores optimizers that construct their own optimization pipelines (Xue and Yang, 2026). RSIHub composes evolution methods from reusable operators and provides shared evaluation and lineage tracking (Wang et al., 2026c). This distinction between improving task solutions, agent implementations, and optimization procedures motivates separating what changes from how those changes are generated and retained.

Capability Boundaries and Mechanisms. Empirical studies of reasoning distinguish improved small-kk success from expansion of large-kk task coverage (Yue et al., 2025). Token-level analyses identify concentrated learning signals at high-entropy decisions (Wang et al., 2025a), while studies of on-policy distillation examine behavioral compatibility and information novelty (Li et al., 2026). Related work also examines the feedback used for improvement. UAPO introduces uncertainty-aware utility anchors for preference optimization (Wang et al., 2025b), and SAVE uses value-anchored on-policy feedback to update reward models (Wang et al., 2026a). We apply a related analytical perspective to persistent agent-system changes rather than model-weight updates. Repeated evaluations distinguish reliability from empirical coverage, common-process Parent expansion tests improvement potential, Component interventions examine change compatibility, and frozen-pool admission replays assess retention.

Evaluation of Agent Systems. Agent evaluation must account for cost, reproducibility, and generalization beyond aggregate success (Kapoor et al., 2025). For harness evolution specifically, Wang et al. (2026b) find inconsistent advantages over test-time scaling under comparable feedback and inference budgets, together with limited held-out generalization. Performance also depends on interactions among the model, harness, task structure, and coordination overhead (Kim et al., 2025). The τ\tau-bench family emphasizes reliable tool-agent-user interaction, while Terminal-Bench 2 evaluates long-horizon execution in terminal environments (Yao et al., 2025; Merrill et al., 2026). We study general and coding tasks through these complementary settings, distinguish task exposure during evolution, and assess external transfer without further agent revision. These comparisons connect measured improvement to its deployment cost and scope of applicability.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Definitions

An agent A=(M,H)A=(M,H) consists of a frozen model MM and a harness HH. Following Lin et al. (2026a); Agrawal et al. (2026), an evolution algorithm EE starts from a Seed A0=(M,H0)A_{0}=(M,H_{0}) and runs for GG generations. At generation gg, a Parent is an eligible existing agent selected for modification, and 𝒞g\mathcal{C}_{g} contains the resulting proposed harnesses. Each H∈𝒞gH\in\mathcal{C}_{g} defines a Candidate agent (M,H)(M,H). The final Champion is A⋆=(M,H⋆)A_{\star}=(M,H_{\star}):

3.2 Experiment Setup

3.2.1 Evolution Process and Methods

Methods and Harnesses. We evaluate AHE (Lin et al., 2026a), HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026c), A-Evolve (Lin et al., 2026b), and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) using GPT-5.4. AHE and HyperAgents are implementation-centric recipes that emphasize agent engineering, whereas A-Evolve and GEPA are reflection-centric recipes that distill execution feedback into reusable changes. We run each recipe with two harnesses. MiniSWE 2.4.5 (Yang et al., 2024) is source-editable and permits inner-source changes. Codex 0.143.0 (OpenAI, 2026) is outer-layer-only and permits changes to prompts, skills, configuration, and external orchestration. These combinations let us examine different evolution designs under a common process. Appendix A details their implementations.

In this common process, each recipe specifies how seven operators are implemented: select chooses a Parent, rollout collects execution evidence, analyze diagnoses it, and mutate proposes a Candidate. The validate operator optionally checks the proposal, gate decides admission, and record archives outcomes. We focus the mechanism analysis on select, analyze, mutate, and gate because their decisions determine which Parents are used, how evidence guides changes, and which Candidates persist.

Figure 1 connects this operator process to the study’s empirical comparisons. The Phenomenology analysis characterizes gains and regressions through repeated task evaluations. The Generalization analysis examines how these gains vary across original splits and external benchmarks. The Mechanisms analysis examines Parent improvement potential under a common generation process, Component interactions, and admission decisions on frozen pools.

3.2.2 Benchmarks and Evaluation Metrics

Benchmarks. General tasks are represented by τ3\tau^{3}-Banking (Shi et al., 2026), with 97 tasks, and coding tasks by Terminal-Bench 2 (Merrill et al., 2026), with 89 tasks. Both are split into Train/Validation/Test. Evolution uses Train/Validation evidence for search and admission, while Test is reserved for Seed and Champion evaluation.

4 Phenomenology: Revisiting What Has Been Evolved

In this section, we compare each frozen Champion with its matching Seed in reliability, empirical coverage, task-level transitions, and deployment cost. Table 1 reports eight-pass aggregate results, Figure 2 shows paired task-level success counts, and Figure 3 relates Pass​@​k\mathrm{Pass}@k to Cdep​@​kC_{\mathrm{dep}}@k for k=1,2,4,8k=1,2,4,8 using the same canonical trials. Appendix B provides detailed comparisons and stability checks.

4.1 Overall Reliability and Empirical Task Coverage

Aggregate Improvement Is Not a Single Outcome. Table 1 shows reliability and coverage gains in eleven and ten of sixteen lineages, respectively. Four move the metrics in opposite directions across both harnesses, domains, and paradigms; another improves only reliability. Consistency and empirical reach are therefore distinct outcomes that aggregate improvement claims should separate.

4.2 Coverage Is a Flow

Evolution Redistributes Success. All sixteen Champions in Figure 2 gain and lose covered tasks, and increase repeated success on some tasks while decreasing it on others. This pattern spans both harnesses, domains, and paradigms: even when both aggregate metrics improve, coverage does not expand monotonically. Gains and losses should therefore be reported separately. Appendix B.2 gives further analysis.

Behavioral Changes Behind Task-Level Gains and Losses. We inspect contrasting traces for tasks with large success-count changes. Across the sampled harnesses, domains, and paradigms, recurring differences concern state preservation, precise grounding, and task completion. Successful traces preserve recovery files and respect action dependencies, while failures include incorrect arguments, premature termination, and solutions that work locally but fail in the required environment. These contrasts motivate preservation and end-to-end checks rather than equating every outcome flip with acquired or lost task knowledge. Table 2 summarizes the categories; Appendix B.3 gives case evidence.

4.3 Reliability and Deployment Efficiency

Per-Trial Cost and Deployment Efficiency Can Diverge. Eight of eleven reliability-improving Champions cost more per trial than Seed; the three lower-cost gains use the source-editable harness on coding tasks. Yet Figure 3 shows that higher per-trial cost can coexist with fewer attempts and lower cost to reach comparable coverage. MiniSWE with AHE on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking reaches 56.7% coverage in four passes, exceeding Seed’s 54.6% in eight at lower deployment cost. Practical efficiency therefore depends on both cost per attempt and the attempts needed to attain a given coverage level.

5 Generalization: Regularizing The Benefits Of Evolution Within A Controllable Boundary

Table 3 compares frozen Champions with matching Seeds across evolution splits and external transfer. Train, Validation, and Test report contributions to the full source-benchmark gain, summing to the overall change before rounding. Transfer reports gains measured on each external benchmark relative to its matching Seed. Appendix C gives protocols and interpretation.

5.1 Generalization Within the Same Benchmarks

Gains Often Survive Beyond Direct Feedback. Test reliability improves in ten of sixteen lineages, including seven of eight implementation-centric cases across both harness types and task domains. Reflection-centric gains are more harness-dependent: most source-editable cases improve, whereas all outer-layer-only cases decline. Improvement therefore frequently reaches feedback-excluded tasks, with systematic differences across harness–paradigm combinations.

5.2 Generalization Cross Benchmarks

We test general-task transfer from τ3\tau^{3}-Banking to the full τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al., 2026), and coding-task transfer from Terminal-Bench 2 to DeepSWE v1.1 (Huang et al., 2026). Table 3 gives Seed-relative gains and Appendix Table 14 gives absolute scores.

Transfer Selectively Preserves Gains. Coverage falls for seven of eight Champions on the general-task target but rises for seven of eight on the coding target, spanning both harness types and paradigms. Reliability can move in the opposite direction. All source-editable Champions improve general-task transfer reliability but lose coding-task transfer reliability, despite coverage gains in three coding cases. Transfer therefore changes the balance between reliability and coverage, so the persistence of improvement must be assessed separately for each outcome and target.

6 Mechanisms: Tracing How to Discover And Retain The Optimization Gains

6.1 Select: Choosing Which Agent to Improve

We test whether select identifies Parents with the greatest improvement potential. Each Champion produces three Candidates through the same A-Evolve analysis and mutation process.

Each benchmark and harness supplies one four-Parent pool, with one Train pass shared by each Parent’s three branches. The best Parent maximizes mean Candidate Test Avg​@​8\mathrm{Avg}@8 minus its own. Table 4 reports its selection probability. Original averages the native HyperAgents, A-Evolve, and GEPA rules using Train or Validation evidence; Random samples uniformly. Appendix D.1 gives the protocol.

Current Scores Do Not Consistently Identify Improvement Potential. Original falls below the 25% random baseline on general tasks but exceeds 55% on coding tasks, across both harnesses. This reversal shows that selection signals align with further improvement differently across domains. Evaluating select therefore requires measuring subsequent gains alongside current performance.

6.2 Analyze: Identifying What the Evidence Supports

Tables 5 and 7 inform analyze by comparing eight Champions’ Components, functionally related changes with their dependencies, against generic reminders such as checking tools and verifying results. Appendix D.5 defines each Component, and Appendix D.2 gives the protocol.

Specific Changes Outperform Generic Guidance. Fifteen of sixteen Components outperform their matching reminders in reliability, with at least one in every case across both harnesses and domains (Tables 5–7). This motivates trace-grounded diagnoses that identify what to change and preserve.

6.3 Mutate: Preserving Useful Behavior While Changing the Agent

Mutation Quality Depends on How Changes Combine. Six of eight Champions outperform either isolated Component in reliability, including all coding-task cases (Table 5). Two general-task cases, one per harness, favor a subset. In one coding case, only the combination improves over Seed. These patterns motivate mutate to preserve dependencies and check harmful interactions and useful complementarities in the complete Candidate. Appendix D.3 reports interaction estimates.

6.4 Gate: Deciding Which Changes to Retain

We compare original gate rules with a constraint requiring higher mean success and incumbent-relative mean regression ≤0.05\leq 0.05. A retained set ℛ\mathcal{R} scores 1/|ℛ|1/|\mathcal{R}| if it contains the reporting-panel best Candidate, and zero otherwise. Scores average four method-specific pools per harness; reporting outcomes remain hidden from decisions.

Admission Constraints Have Harness-Dependent Effects. Constrained admission reduces best-Candidate retention from fifteen to six pools. Yet its size-normalized score falls for the source-editable harness and rises for the outer-layer-only harness on both domains (Table 7). The increase reflects smaller sets retaining a best Seed alone. Admission quality therefore requires inspecting preservation, set size, and Candidate identity together. Appendix D.4 gives per-pool results.

7 Recipes: From Empirical Findings to Operator Design

Table 8 connects the findings to operator design.

7.1 From Synthesis to Operator Revisions

We propose EvoAudit, an agent-assisted workflow that runs diagnostics on archived artifacts and returns operator revisions with evidence and validation records (Figure 4).

Installing its four revisions in A-Evolve gives Audit-Guided Evolution (AGE). Other operators, model and evaluator contracts, and harness editing constraints remain fixed.

7.2 AGE Implementation

Recipe and Evidence Flow. AGE installs four fixed operator revisions in the A-Evolve recipe described in Appendix A, shared across both benchmarks and harnesses. Each generation selects a Parent, collects fresh Train trajectories, diagnoses behavior, and proposes one Candidate. Framework scope checks and canonical Validation evaluation precede admission and recording. The reference rollout and record implementations are unchanged, and the optional validate stage is disabled. MiniSWE permits changes to inner source and outer artifacts, whereas Codex permits only outer-artifact changes. The evaluator, task partitions, model settings, resource limits, and evolution operators remain fixed. Online decisions use Train and Validation evidence.

Run Configuration. Each run uses 20 generations, one proposed Candidate per generation, and search random seed 0. The target harnesses are MiniSWE 2.4.5 and Codex 0.143.0, both using GPT-5.4 with high reasoning effort. Diagnosis and mutation use Codex 0.146.0 with GPT-5.4 and xhigh effort through Harbor. Every rollout executes the 50 Train tasks afresh. Canonical scoring executes each Validation task once, using 20 tasks on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking and 19 on Terminal-Bench 2. Frozen Champions receive separate eight-pass reporting evaluations.

Select: Regression-Aware Tie-Breaking. AGE retains the highest-score objective and revises only exact ties. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the eligible Parents with finite recorded Validation scores s⁡(C)s(C), and let 𝒯=arg⁡maxC∈𝒫⁡s⁡(C)\mathcal{T}=\arg\max_{C\in\mathcal{P}}s(C). When comparable task-level evidence is available, selection minimizes Seed-relative regressions within 𝒯\mathcal{T}:

R(C)=∑t∈𝒟val𝕀[r¯t(C)<r¯t(A0)],P∼Uniform(argminC∈𝒯R(C)),R(C)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbb{I}[\bar{r}_{t}(C)<\bar{r}_{t}(A_{0})],\qquad P\sim\operatorname{Uniform}\!\left(\arg\min_{C\in\mathcal{T}}R(C)\right),

where 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}} is the Validation task set and r¯t\bar{r}_{t} is the mean recorded reward on task tt. Comparable evidence requires a unique eligible Seed evaluation, matching task-set hashes and task identities, equal per-task repetition counts, and completed trials with finite rewards for every tied Candidate and the Seed. Otherwise, the seeded generator samples uniformly from the original highest-score tie set. A unique maximizer is selected directly, and an empty eligible scored set stops selection. The rule reuses recorded outcomes and preserves the highest-score objective.

Analyze: Behavior-Grounded Diagnosis. The analyzer collects the current rollout and, when available, one preceding rollout along the selected lineage, retaining the last 30 records in their stored order. Each judge input contains chronological tool calls, successful and failed tool results, and the completion signal. Tool arguments and results are capped at 600 and 800 characters, respectively. Each rendered trajectory uses at most 12,000 characters, preserving approximately two-thirds from its beginning and one-third from its end when truncated. Interrupted executions can include a bounded termination message. The behavior bundle excludes benchmark rewards, verifier outputs, hidden tests, raw task text, and raw-case paths.

The judge returns score, category, outcome, and failure_reason. Scores 0–3 indicate visible breakdown, 4–6 indicate partial or ambiguous progress, and 7–10 indicate visible completion supported by an appropriate check or comparably decisive result. Verdicts distinguish Observed: behavior from Inference: explanations and ground completion judgments in trajectory evidence. These behavioral scores guide diagnosis, while benchmark scores drive select and gate. Each request permits one attempt with a 600-second timeout. Invalid or failed responses return an unknown verdict with sentinel score −1-1.

The analyzer exports trajectories, behavioral signals, and verdicts in a structured evidence bundle. The selected text view uses at most 30,000 characters for τ3\tau^{3}-Banking and 60,000 for Terminal-Bench 2, omitting trailing whole records beyond these budgets. Mutation consumes at most a 50,000-character prefix of this view. Both truncation steps add explicit omission markers.

Mutate: Mechanism-Linked, Dependency-Closed Changes. The mutation agent receives the selected behavior evidence, Parent workspace, prompt and skill inventory, and editing contract. Before choosing files, its instructions require the observed behavior, inferred mechanism, replacement behavior, activation conditions, and expected trade-off. A recurring concrete pattern or a single severe, visibly supported breakdown can motivate a change, while ambiguous evidence favors preserving current behavior. The agent must inspect affected interfaces and their producers and consumers, make one coherent intervention, preserve useful behavior in successful traces, and check for conflicting or duplicated guidance. Dependency-closed changes may span multiple files and layers.

The agent is instructed to edit the permitted target directly, inspect its final diff, run proportionate structural checks, and propose a validation case for the expected benefit. Outputs retain the patch, changed-file list, surface-check report, agent response, and usage record. Structural checks enforce editing surfaces and interfaces, while the mutation instructions specify evidence grounding, dependency closure, and behavior preservation. Execution errors stop the operator and are recorded with their diagnostic information.

Gate: Score-First, Cost-Aware Admission. AGE retains strict Parent-relative score improvement and adds a cost tie-break. For a Candidate CC and its matched Parent PP, with finite Validation scores, admission is

accept(C,P)=𝕀[s(C)>s(P)∨(s(C)=s(P)∧Q(C,P)∧c(C)<c(P))].\operatorname{accept}(C,P)=\mathbb{I}\!\left[s(C)>s(P)\;\lor\;\bigl(s(C)=s(P)\land Q(C,P)\land c(C)<c(P)\bigr)\right].

Here cc is the recorded USD cost of canonical Validation evaluation. The comparability predicate QQ requires matching task-set hashes, finite strictly positive costs, and a direct Parent evaluation. Equal-score admission requires a verified, comparable cost reduction. When cost comparability fails, only the score-improvement branch applies. A valid matched Parent and finite scores are required, and all other Candidates are rejected. The operator reuses canonical evaluations and preserves score improvement as its primary objective.

7.3 Human Evaluation of the Operator Revisions

Eight experts reviewed all four operator revisions. Each chose a direction before seeing the proposal, then judged its evidence, whether it addressed the stated problem, and whether it should enter validation. Table 9 reports the mean number of experts per revision. Overall, expert judgments broadly align with EvoAudit’s proposed directions and support validating the resulting revisions. Appendix E.2 details the protocol.

7.4 Comparison with Existing Evolution Methods

Table 10 compares AGE with the four methods across both benchmarks and harnesses.

Combined Revisions Improve Outcomes Across Settings. AGE improves reliability and coverage over A-Evolve in all four settings and loses fewer Seed-covered tasks in three, tying in the fourth. This consistency across domains and harnesses supports the practical value of evidence-guided revision.

8 Discussion

Feedback Can Be Narrower Than a Change’s Effects. Harness changes affect many behaviors, while evaluation samples finite executions and compresses their trade-offs. A prompt, skill, or execution routine can help the tasks that supply feedback while disrupting behavior elsewhere. This mismatch offers a common explanation for task regressions, context-dependent change interactions, and selective transfer. It suggests that practical evolution depends on how well feedback represents the consequences of a change, including the resources needed to deploy it.

Evidence Must Match the Decision. Current performance, improvement potential, change compatibility, and retention are distinct objectives. A high-scoring Parent need not yield the greatest subsequent gain, a useful Component can interfere with other changes, and a conservative gate can discard alternatives. Together, the diagnostics show why evidence supporting one decision need not support the next. Evaluation should test the desired consequence of each decision, rather than reuse the same aggregate score throughout evolution.

Toward Decision-Specific Feedback. Evaluate select through subsequent gains, ground analyze and mutate in traces and dependencies, and assess gate through both retained quality and preserved alternatives. Deployment cost and external evaluation then determine how broadly these benefits remain useful. EvoAudit and AGE illustrate how these complementary checks can guide a coordinated redesign while preserving the reference method’s execution and evaluation contracts.

9 Conclusion

Our study shows that harness evolution redistributes observed task success, bringing both gains and regressions. Across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms, practical improvement depends on productive Parents, compatible changes, preservation through search, and generalization at affordable cost. EvoAudit connects these findings to operator revisions, and AGE improves reliability and coverage over its reference method in all four settings. These results motivate evaluating evolution by the useful behavior it creates and sustains, beyond final benchmark scores.

Ethics Statement

Experiments run in isolated benchmark environments rather than live user-facing services. Evolving agent instructions and code can introduce regressions and unintended tool use. We retain fixed evaluation contracts and harness-specific editing permissions, and examine regressions and transfer alongside aggregate performance. Participants in the human evaluation provided informed consent. The expert-review protocol evaluates the evidence, reasoning, and proposed approaches for operator revisions, as described in Appendix E.2. Neither benchmark gains nor expert endorsement establishes safety for deployment.
