Appendix A Operator Implementations of the Compared Methods

We describe the implementations used in our experiments through the seven operator stages in Table 11. All four methods share fixed target-model and evaluator contracts. MiniSWE permits dependency-closed changes to inner source code as well as prompts, skills, configuration, and orchestration; Codex permits only changes outside its immutable executable and source. HyperAgents additionally permits changes to designated evolution operators.

Evolution Paradigms. Our design-based grouping distinguishes implementation-centric recipes, AHE and HyperAgents, from reflection-centric recipes, A-Evolve and GEPA. The former organize revision around engineering the agent implementation or improvement machinery; the latter organize it around distilling execution experience and feedback. Both use evidence and may modify code within the harness’s legal surface. The grouping follows recipe design, while the harness determines the permitted editing surface. Codex permits changes to external orchestration code while keeping its executable and inner source immutable.

Search scores use Train tasks for AHE and HyperAgents, and Validation tasks for A-Evolve and GEPA. The validate operator checks proposals, while the Validation split supplies evaluation tasks. Shared scope and evaluation-eligibility checks apply to all four methods, including those that omit the optional validate stage. Test outcomes remain excluded from search.

A.1 AHE

Selection and Diagnosis. AHE emphasizes observability-grounded revision (Lin et al., 2026a). Its select operator chooses the newest eligible Parent, not necessarily the highest-scoring one. The rollout operator reuses that Parent’s evaluation traces. The analyze operator produces task-level debugger reports: failure reports identify the failure point, possible cause, and corrective lesson, while successful traces expose reusable strategies and fragile behavior. Mixed outcomes on a task can therefore inform the diagnosis alongside outright failures. An overview links these reports to prior changes and their observed effects.

Revision and Admission. The mutation agent is instructed to make one coherent, testable change, supported by task evidence and an identified execution path. It considers whether to retain, revise, or roll back the preceding change and pursue a different explanation. A change manifest records the proposed mechanism, affected files, predicted fixes, and behaviors at risk. Debugger reports supply hypotheses for revision. There is no separate optional validate stage. The gate operator admits a completed, eligible evaluation without requiring a higher score, so the next Parent can come from a lower-scoring revision. The record operator preserves outcomes and change evidence. Admission and continuation are thus distinct from final Champion reporting.

A.2 HyperAgents

Selection and Evidence. HyperAgents permits revision of the improvement procedure as well as the target agent (Zhang et al., 2026c). Its initial select policy samples eligible Parents using a score-dependent weight and a penalty for having many children. Higher scores increase sampling weight, while the child-count penalty reduces repeated expansion of the same Parent. The rollout operator reuses Parent evaluation traces. The initial analyze operator supplies metrics and browsable raw traces, leaving their interpretation largely to the mutation agent rather than first producing AHE-style debugger reports.

Revision and Admission. Mutation may change the target and permitted operator implementations while leaving the evaluator and other fixed contracts unchanged. The mutation instructions favor substantive target changes but allow an operator-only revision when the evidence supports a process-level change. An operator revision takes effect at its next invocation, updating the initial policies in Table 11 for subsequent Generations. The initial validate stage checks Python syntax in target files and the mutation operator. The initial gate admits completed, eligible evaluations without a Parent-relative score threshold. The record operator stores lineage experience, including the Parent, outcome, and score. This editable search procedure distinguishes HyperAgents from target-only revision under fixed operators.

A.3 A-Evolve

Selection and Behavioral Feedback. Our A-Evolve implementation operationalizes experience-driven adaptation (Lin et al., 2026b). The select operator chooses the highest-scoring eligible Parent, and rollout collects fresh Train trajectories. The analyze operator compresses observable behavior, including tool use, repeated actions, errors, and completion signals, for a trajectory-only judge. This judge evaluates behavior without benchmark reward labels. Its proxy judgments provide feedback for revision, rather than replacing the benchmark score used for admission.

Revision and Admission. The mutate operator distills these observations into reusable task-solving guidance and executable target changes. Its instructions emphasize recurrent failure patterns, self-contained skills with their supporting dependencies, and preservation of unrelated behavior. Prompt and skill settings organize revision within the Harness’s legal editing boundary. The optional validate stage is disabled. After canonical evaluation, the strict gate admits a Candidate only if its Validation score exceeds that of the matched Parent. The record operator retains outcomes and the revision rationale. Unlike AHE and the initial HyperAgents policy, A-Evolve combines greedy Parent choice with score-improving admission.

A.4 GEPA

Selection and Reflection. GEPA combines trajectory-based reflection with per-task Pareto selection (Agrawal et al., 2026). The select operator identifies eligible Candidates attaining the best observed score on at least one task, prunes redundant coverage, and samples according to the remaining per-task memberships. This can preserve access to task specialists without selecting solely by aggregate score. The rollout operator collects fresh Train trajectories, and analyze assembles task examples, outputs, and feedback for focused reflection.

Revision Scope. The named reflection units differ by benchmark. On τ3\tau^{3}-Banking, MiniSWE focuses on its system-prompt configuration, while Codex alternates between its prompt and task-execution skill. On Terminal-Bench 2, both harnesses use the entire target as the reflection unit. These units guide evidence organization rather than impose text-only filesystem permissions. The frozen Champion from MiniSWE with GEPA on Terminal-Bench 2 retains inner-source changes to task-conditioned guidance and shell execution. Reflection-centric therefore describes the revision process, not the absence of code changes. These reflection units are distinct from the post-hoc Components isolated in our diagnostics.

Validation and Admission. The validate operator evaluates the proposal on the same Train task batch used for the Parent rollout and requires a complete, scorable comparison with strict improvement. This feedback-informed proposal filter precedes canonical Validation evaluation. The subsequent gate checks completion and eligibility without imposing a second Parent-relative improvement threshold. The record operator preserves reflection choices, proposals, and batch comparisons. Thus, GEPA’s improvement filter lies in validate, whereas A-Evolve’s lies in gate, and they use different task evidence.

Implications for the Analysis. These implementations differ in how they allocate search, summarize evidence, couple target and operator changes, and filter proposals. Similar final gains can therefore arise through different processes. These differences motivate diagnostics of selection, diagnosis, change compatibility, and admission.

Appendix B Phenomenology: Additional Protocols and Analyses

This appendix supplements the Phenomenology analysis in Section 4 with case-level comparisons, task-transition stability, deployment-cost accounting, and split-level heatmaps. Section B.4.1 provides the numerical cost table, and Section B.5 contains the split-level heatmaps.

B.1 Matched Outcome Comparisons

Evaluation and Interpretation. Every configuration in Table 1 uses the same benchmark tasks and eight complete passes. Each of the eight Champions per benchmark is paired with its harness Seed. The completed comparison contains 7,760 selected τ3\tau^{3}-Banking executions and 7,120 Terminal-Bench 2 executions, including the two Seeds once per benchmark. Each method–harness–benchmark combination contributes one canonical evolution lineage.

Metric Agreement and Disagreement. Across the sixteen Champions, eleven improve reliability and ten improve coverage. Eight improve both, four move the metrics in opposite directions, one improves reliability with unchanged coverage, and three reduce both. The opposite-sign cases occur in reflection-centric general-task evolution and implementation-centric coding-task evolution, each with both harness types. Thus, the distinction between consistency and reach is not confined to one harness type, task domain, or paradigm, even though agreement is more common than disagreement.

Interpreting Trends Across Dimensions. Reliability improves in all eight implementation-centric lineages across harness types and task domains. In the reflection-centric group, it improves in three of four source-editable cases but none of the four outer-layer-only cases. The paradigm-level pattern is therefore harness-dependent. Recipes also differ in feedback, search, and admission design, suggesting concrete mechanisms for further study.

B.2 Task-Level Turnover and Pass Stability

Transition Construction. Each 9×99\times 9 heatmap pairs a task’s Seed and Champion success counts from zero through eight, using complete 97×897\times 8 evaluations on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking or 89×889\times 8 evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2. Panels within each benchmark use the same task set and color scale. The split heatmaps retain the original Train, Validation, and Test task identities.

Coverage Turnover Across All Settings. All sixteen Champions both gain and lose covered tasks. Gains range from one to fifteen tasks and losses from two to ten, with both types present in every harness–task–paradigm combination. A positive net coverage delta therefore represents the balance of newly covered and lost tasks rather than preservation of the Seed’s solved set. This shared pattern motivates paired gain/loss accounting without requiring a specific method to have the largest net expansion.

Within-Task Reliability Also Redistributes. Every panel contains tasks on both sides of the success-count diagonal. Evolution can improve repeated success on already covered tasks, reduce it elsewhere, and change which tasks are covered at all. The shared combination of these movements explains why neither a net coverage gain nor a reliability gain summarizes preservation.

Pass-Half Stability. We compare passes 1–4 with passes 5–8 to assess the stability of aggregate trends and task transitions. Some aggregate directions differ between halves on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking, showing sensitivity to execution variability.

B.3 Behavioral Audit of Task-Level Transitions

Case Selection and Evidence. We identify the largest positive and negative changes in eight-pass success count within each lineage, breaking ties lexicographically by task identifier before trace inspection. The reported analysis contains 22 task–lineage comparisons with trace-linked behavioral evidence. For each increase, we inspect the first failed Seed execution and the first successful Champion execution in canonical pass order; for each decrease, we inspect the first successful Seed execution and the first failed Champion execution. The audit uses archived actions, observations, submitted artifacts, and verifier records.

Behavior Categories. We assign one primary category to each reference pair based on the concrete behavioral difference linked to its task outcome. The summary in Table 2 appears in the main text; Table 12 illustrates the underlying trace evidence. The agent-assisted audit examines execution behavior; the human evaluation reviews operator revisions.

What Changes Behind a Flip. Three themes recur across the selected cases with both harness types, task domains, and evolution paradigms. First, state and dependency management affects the complete workflow. Successful general-task executions order operations so that one preserves the conditions needed by another, while successful coding executions preserve source data before inspection and deliver self-contained artifacts. Second, exact grounding remains fragile after the main workflow succeeds: filed requests can contain an incorrect date, and reconstructed text can contain a single wrong character. Third, intermediate success can fall short of task completion. An agent can open one requested account and stop too early, announce a transfer without completing it, or pass its own program checks while leaving an unacceptable final artifact. These observations motivate checking preserved state, exact arguments, and the final execution boundary alongside the headline success rate. Tool recovery and implementation debugging provide complementary case evidence.

A Shared Execution Ledger. Each configuration has 776 selected logical trials on τ3\tau^{3}-Banking or 712 on Terminal-Bench 2. Coverage and cost use this ledger and the metrics in Section 3.2.2. Cost and Performance Need Joint Interpretation. All four outer-layer-only Champions on coding tasks cost more than Seed, although only two improve reliability. Coverage–cost curves relate empirical reach to deployment resources at each pass prefix. Evolution cost complements these curves by accounting for the resources used to obtain the evolved agent.

Full-Benchmark Evaluation. A Recurring Specificity Advantage. Fifteen of sixteen Component variants have higher reliability than their matching generic-reminder control, and every Champion case has at least one such Component. Case Composition. The eight Component cases cover both harness types and task domains. Seven are implementation-centric; the reflection-centric case uses the source-editable harness on coding tasks. Each case pairs concrete Champion changes with a generic-reminder intervention on the matching Seed.

Diagnosis Requirements. The specificity advantage motivates a diagnosis contract that links failure explanations to execution traces, identifies useful behavior to preserve, and states when the proposed correction applies. We assess this contract through the changes and outcomes it produces.

For method mm and gate gg, let 𝒫m\mathcal{P}_{m} be its four-Candidate input pool, ℛm,g\mathcal{R}_{m,g} the retained set including Seed, and ℬm=arg⁡maxc∈𝒫m​Avg​@​8​(c)\mathcal{B}_{m}=\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{P}_{m}}\mathrm{Avg}@8(c) on the reporting panel. The hit indicator is Hm,g=𝟏[ℛm,g∩ℬm≠∅]H_{m,g}=\mathbf{1}[\mathcal{R}_{m,g}\cap\mathcal{B}_{m}\neq\varnothing] and set size is Nm,g=|ℛm,g|N_{m,g}=|\mathcal{R}_{m,g}|. Retaining any tied maximizer counts as a hit. The size-normalized score is Hm,g/Nm,gH_{m,g}/N_{m,g}; Seed ensures a nonempty retained set. Each main-table cell reports 100​∑m(Hm,g/Nm,g)/4100\sum_{m}(H_{m,g}/N_{m,g})/4, separately for each benchmark and harness. This is the mean of per-pool ratios, not the ratio of mean hit to mean size. Values are rounded to one decimal place only after aggregation. All sixteen pools have a unique empirical best. The score therefore equals the chance of drawing that Candidate uniformly from the retained set; this interpretation does not prescribe the method’s actual select policy.

A Recurring Preservation Risk. The original policies retain the reporting-panel best in fifteen pools, compared with six under Constrained. The nine newly excluded best Candidates span both harness types, task domains, and paradigms. Size-normalized scores nevertheless improve in four pools, remain unchanged in three, and fall in nine. The improvements include two implementation-centric source-editable pools retaining the best among fewer alternatives, and two reflection-centric outer-layer-only pools retaining a best Seed alone. Pruning can therefore improve the diagnostic metric while excluding useful Candidates elsewhere. The two outer-layer-only averages increase even while evolved best Candidates are lost in other pools. Jointly reporting hit, set size, and Candidate identity distinguishes concentration on a strong fallback from preservation of evolved gains.

Replay Evidence and Design Implications. The replay applies original and constrained admission rules to the same frozen Candidate pools and measured scores. The constrained rule combines strict score improvement with a regression cap. Comparing retained-set quality, size, and membership motivates admission rules that balance improvement, preservation, and fallback retention.

D.5 Component Definitions and Representative Content

This subsection records the frozen Component definitions for the eight-case matrix of Table 5. All sixteen Component variants and eight Champion comparators have complete evaluations. A and B identify the two groups within each case. The definitions specify retained agent changes, implementation files, execution dependencies, and representative content. Prompt and code excerpts have line wrapping adjusted for display, and code excerpts reproduce the indicated implementation segment. MiniSWE paths are relative to src/minisweagent/; Codex paths are relative to the Candidate’s target directory. Each Component is evaluated as a complete agent intervention.

Construction and Comparison. Seed + A and Seed + B retain the matching Seed outside the specified Component and its execution dependencies. Components are separated by function: a configuration file can contain both interface settings and task-solving instructions, which we isolate by semantic key. Required compatibility adaptations are identified below. Codex Components remain outside its immutable executable and source. The Terminal-Bench 2 cases evaluate targeted Champion subsets. Interaction estimates use decompositions whose joint Components reproduce the compared Champion.

Case Selection. The matrix contains four Champion cases per benchmark, with two from each harness. Eligibility requires at least two functionally distinct groups of persistent changes that can be isolated with their execution dependencies on the matching Seed while keeping the model and evaluator fixed. The τ3\tau^{3}-Banking cases comprise Champions from AHE and HyperAgents in both harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 2, we retain the previously evaluated Champions from MiniSWE with AHE and Codex with HyperAgents, and add MiniSWE with GEPA and Codex with AHE after auditing all eight Champions. The additions prioritize clear functional boundaries and complementary mechanisms. Component boundaries were frozen before evaluation, and all completed outcomes are retained.

Selection History and Extension. The initial Terminal-Bench 2 sample selected the largest historical unrounded Avg​@​8\mathrm{Avg}@8 gain within each harness, yielding MiniSWE with AHE and Codex with HyperAgents. Case identities remain frozen, and source-faithful reevaluations replace the two superseded Codex Champion measurements. MiniSWE with GEPA separates task guidance from shell execution adaptation, complementing AHE’s broader validation and submission controls. Codex with AHE separates instruction content from persistent context and skill support, complementing HyperAgents’ dependency bootstrap. Functional clarity and mechanism complementarity determine the additions. Their identities and Component boundaries were frozen before evaluation, and all added outcomes are reported.

D.5.1 τ3\tau^{3}-Banking: MiniSWE with AHE (G2)

Component A: Interface. This Component changes how shell/tool output is presented to the model, while retaining the Seed’s task-solving instructions and bash action interface. It extracts readable text from structured tool-response envelopes, removes duplicate text blocks, and preserves salient information when an observation is long. Rather than retaining only its beginning and end, the observation also includes a bounded selection of middle content containing tool schemas, execution results, required fields, and conversation-control signals. The changed files are models/utils/actions_toolcall.py, models/utils/actions_toolcall_response.py, the added models/utils/observation_output.py, and the observation_template key in config/mini.yaml.

Observation-budget constants from the added helper:

DISPLAY_OUTPUT_LIMIT = 10000
DISPLAY_OUTPUT_HEAD_CHARS = 3000
DISPLAY_OUTPUT_TAIL_CHARS = 3000
SALIENT_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS = 2500

Component B: Strategy. This Component replaces the system prompt, task prompt, and format-error guidance in config/mini.yaml; observation processing stays at the Seed. The instructions distinguish the benchmark’s tool-driven general tasks from coding tasks, prioritize live state and tool schemas, require one focused action followed by inspection, prohibit invented arguments or case facts, and distinguish a stopped conversation from a successfully completed backend action. The format-error guidance also specifies concise recovery from token-limit truncation and a tool-only final submission.

Task-prompt excerpt: “Prefer live environment state, exact tool outputs, runtime status, and tool schemas over inference from general KB text.”

Completion-rule excerpt: “Only treat the task as complete when the required environment state or required action has actually been achieved.”

D.5.2 τ3\tau^{3}-Banking: MiniSWE with HyperAgents (G9)

Component A: Interface. This Component exposes structured benchmark tools in place of a bash-only interface when it detects tasks from the general-task benchmark. It adds tool schemas, argument parsing (including nested JSON-string normalization), dispatch to the benchmark environment, and a dedicated final-submission action. The dependency-closed implementation spans agents/interactive.py, environments/local.py, utils/tau3.py, both action/tool-response utilities, and seven adapters in models/: the chat and Responses implementations for LiteLLM, OpenRouter, and Portkey, plus Requesty. The thirteenth changed file, config/mini.yaml, adds neutral transport and format-error instructions so that the Seed prompt does not request an unavailable bash tool. This compatibility text describes how to call the exposed tools, without importing the Champion’s task-solving strategy.

Exposed tool names: tau3_call, tau3_list_tools, tau3_get_tool_schema, and submit_final_output.

Compatibility-note excerpt: “This note describes only the available transport; determine the task policy and actions from the task, tool schemas, and runtime responses.”

Component B: Strategy. This Component changes only the task-instance prompt in config/mini.yaml. It retains the Champion’s service workflow: start the conversation once, consult the latest user message and schema, perform one action at a time, separate user communication from domain-tool calls, respect stop/transfer signals, and ground advice in documented policy and hard user requirements. Because the Seed does not expose Component A’s structured tools, the workflow is expressed through the Seed’s tau3-mcp.py command-line interface. This is the evaluated CLI-translated strategy Component, not an unmodified copy of the native-tool prompt; the translation is an execution dependency, not an independent strategy finding.

Translated task-prompt excerpts: “Perform exactly one focused Tau3 CLI action per response and inspect its output before the next action.” “Do not recommend a product or action that misses a user-stated hard requirement.”

D.5.3 τ3\tau^{3}-Banking: Codex with AHE (G15)

Component A: Orchestration. The only changed file is the outer adapter agent.py. Before invoking Codex, it detects service-task markers in the instruction and appends a workflow-guidance block, unless that block is already present. The injected text emphasizes exact tool discovery, a per-entity worklist, assistant-side versus user-side actions, date and eligibility checks, canonical write arguments, and completing all requested items before ending. The Seed’s prompt and skill files are retained. Here, orchestration includes conditional instruction delivery; it does not mean that the Component contains no natural-language guidance.

Injected-guidance excerpt: “Keep a live per-entity worklist for the case. For each named transaction, card, account, product, referral, or other requested item, track the exact entity, the user-described problem, the currently grounded workflow or enum, any missing fields, and the next read or write needed.”

Component B: Prompt and Skills. This Component replaces prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md, and adds skills/tau3-service-workflows/SKILL.md, while retaining the Seed adapter. The prompt distinguishes coding work from the general-task benchmark’s workflows and directs the latter to the specialized skill. That skill specifies a six-part workflow: discover the live tool surface; ground on the exact entity; identify who must perform the next state change; construct exact writes; preserve the selected product or workflow branch; and finish all requested work. It includes explicit checks for relative dates, enums, optional fields, user-side follow-through, and multi-item completion.

Specialized-skill excerpt: “Once the user accepts a supported product or workflow branch, stop re-optimizing and execute that exact branch.”

Prompt excerpt: “If the task involves multiple requested actions or entities, keep a short checklist and do not finish while any requested item is unresolved.”

D.5.4 τ3\tau^{3}-Banking: Codex with HyperAgents (G18)

Component A: Orchestration. The outer agent.py detects the configured service server or service markers in the instruction, then prepends a guidance block unless its header is already present. The same server-detection helper is reused by the existing installation path. The injected guidance prioritizes live account investigation, eligible and actionable recommendations, exact knowledge-base procedures, discoverable-tool checks, literal argument formatting, and completion of accepted workflows. Prompt and skill files remain at the Seed, so the specialized-skill reference in this block does not itself install Component B.

Injected-guidance excerpt: “Do not substitute a neighboring tool or an incidental side effect for a separately documented step. If the KB names a dedicated replacement, approval, closure, report, or submission tool, use that exact tool instead of assuming another mutation already covered it.”

Component B: Skills. This Component changes skills/task-execution/SKILL.md to route tasks from the general-task benchmark to the added skills/tau3-banking-runtime/SKILL.md; the outer adapter and main prompt stay at the Seed. The specialized skill covers identity verification, account-specific lookups, recommendation eligibility, tool unlocking and execution checks, multi-step discrepancies, transfers, closures, and final-state verification. It also includes implementation-sensitive payload rules: preserve surfaced key order, whitespace, explicit null/false values, and numeric forms in nested argument strings. These are actual retained instructions, not a claim that equivalent JSON representations generally have different semantics.

Payload-formatting excerpt: “Serialize that inner JSON as a single-line object with double-quoted keys, the surfaced key order, and standard spaces after each comma and colon.”

Tool-check excerpt: “After unlock_discoverable_agent_tool, check that the returned tool name, description, and parameters match the tool you meant to unlock.”

D.5.5 Terminal-Bench 2: MiniSWE with AHE (G18)

Component A: Static Instructions. Only config/mini.yaml changes. The retained prompt additions call for early inspection of visible tests and checkers, exact deliverable paths and formats, fresh-shell verification, preservation of original inputs and consumers, and rechecking after any subsequent change. They reject proxy checks, fabricated substitutes, and unresolved failures as evidence of completion. These instructions do not add a programmatic submission guard.

Contract-first instruction: “Before long implementation, downloads, or external research, spend the first 1-2 commands locating the real acceptance path.”

Reverification instruction: “Any edit after a passing verification invalidates that verification. If you change the artifact, environment, dependency set, or generated output afterward, rerun the exact end-to-end check against the final state before submitting.”

Component B: Dynamic Guard. Files agents/default.py and environments/local.py implement the dynamic checks. The configuration file config/mini.yaml supplies their hooks and activation flags, without Component A’s static instructions. It discovers visible verifier files, derives deliverable-boundary hints from the task, supplies fresh-shell compatibility helpers, records test inspection and unresolved check failures, and inspects submission attempts. The guard can replace a completion signal with a warning about uninspected verifiers, unhealthy package state, unresolved failures, missing files, or deliverable-boundary violations. It warns once per warning fingerprint; repeating the same submission can proceed, so this is not an unconditional veto or a replacement for the benchmark evaluator.

Activated flags in the configuration:

pause_submit_for_uninspected_verifier: true
pause_submit_for_unhealthy_system_packages: true
pause_submit_for_unresolved_verifier_failures: true
pause_submit_for_deliverable_boundary_violations: true

D.5.6 Terminal-Bench 2: MiniSWE with GEPA (G20)

Component A: Task Guidance. This Component combines static instructions about exact deliverables and evidence preservation with task-conditioned reminders. In agents/default.py, _build_task_guardrails detects wording associated with exhaustive outputs or fragile evidence and generates the corresponding guidance. The template in config/mini.yaml consumes the generated task_guardrails value and includes the accompanying static instructions. The generator and template hook stay in the same Component because either alone disconnects the mechanism. The local command-execution implementation remains at the Seed.

Component B: Shell Execution Adaptation. Only environments/local.py changes. The helper _preferred_shell_executable resolves MSWEA_LOCAL_SHELL, defaulting to bash, and supplies the available executable to the subprocess launcher. It falls back to the platform default when the preferred shell cannot be resolved. This changes shell semantics at the command-execution boundary without importing Component A’s guidance or changing the model configuration.

D.5.7 Terminal-Bench 2: Codex with AHE (G20)

Component A: Prompt and Skills. This Component replaces the prompt and task-execution skill in prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md. The instructions prioritize the verifier-facing contract, a minimal coherent change on the active execution path, and checks of the final artifact at the consumer-visible boundary. Prompt and skill content form one guidance Component rather than separate Components based on file location. The adapter, compaction settings, model, reasoning effort, and Codex executable remain at the Seed.

Component B: Persistent Context and Skill Support. The outer agent.py moves temporary Codex state and skill-upload paths to a persistent Codex directory, while codex.toml enables prefix-preserving compaction with auto_compact_token_limit_scope set to body_after_prefix. These changes support instruction continuity without importing Component A’s prompt or skill contents. The evolved adapter changes are semantically applied to the exact evaluation Seed, preserving its authentication, provider routing, session handling, and cancellation cleanup. Codex’s executable and source, the model, and reasoning effort are unchanged.

D.5.8 Terminal-Bench 2: Codex with HyperAgents (G18)

Component A: Instructions. The prompt and task-execution skill are replaced in prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md; the outer adapter remains at the matching Seed. The prompt and skill instruct the agent to preserve authentic input artifacts, inspect visible verifiers, reconstruct missing checker dependencies, react to failed checks, match exact output paths and final-state requirements, remove probe-only artifacts, and run a final check from a fresh shell or process. They also ask the agent to diagnose silent long-running commands instead of repeatedly polling without new evidence.

Skill excerpt: “Recreate the verifier runtime before declaring the task unavailable.”

Failure-handling excerpt: “Clear red checks before closing. If any command, test, assertion, or custom validation failed after your last meaningful edit, rerun that same path cleanly or keep debugging.”

Component B: Orchestration and Bootstrap. Only the outer agent.py changes. The Champion’s bootstrap changes are merged onto the exact Seed adapter used in the matched evaluation, rather than replacing that adapter with a different baseline wrapper. During setup, the adapter installs or locates uv and uvx, creates a sourceable environment helper, and exposes stable executable entrypoints in standard locations for fresh-shell verifier commands. Installation first attempts the Python package route and then an installer fallback; setup reports a warning if the bootstrap remains unavailable. The Seed’s prompt and skills are retained. This Component prepares the execution environment; it does not alter the verifier’s scoring rules or Codex’s executable.

Bootstrap function’s documented purpose: “Install stable verifier entrypoints for uv-based test harnesses.”

Setup-hook excerpt:

try:
    await self.exec_as_root(environment,
        command=_verifier_bootstrap_command())
except RuntimeError:
    self.logger.warning(
        "Failed to bootstrap uv verifier entrypoints",
        exc_info=True)

Generic-Reminder Controls Are Separate. The reminders in Table 7 are not additional Champion Components. On τ3\tau^{3}-Banking, both harnesses receive: “This is an interactive tool-use task. Inspect the available runtime tool interface, use tools when needed, verify the resulting state, and complete every requested item before ending.” The Terminal-Bench 2 MiniSWE control adds: “Before final submission, inspect any available tests or check commands and run the closest exact end-to-end check on the final artifact. Do not submit while a relevant check is still failing or running.” These controls add general advice without the case-specific prompt bundle, interface implementation, or dynamic guard above.

Recovery of Interrupted Evaluations. Four τ3\tau^{3}-Banking Codex reminder evaluations were interrupted by API rate limits after their conversations had started. Under a documented recovery-policy amendment, we fixed these four task–pass identities and reran each once from its initial state with unchanged model, simulator, target, and evaluator settings. The other 772 numeric outcomes were retained, and all four replacement outcomes were accepted, including three zeros. Original attempts remain in the audit record; selected outcomes and their costs enter the reported metrics.

Appendix E Operator Redesign: Implementation and Evaluation

E.1 Evidence and Implementation Requirements

The analysis agent combines results from the Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms analyses with source traces and reference operators. It identifies recurring patterns across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms and links each finding to the relevant comparisons and observed behavior. The resulting evidence report supplies the rationale and applicability conditions for operator revision.

Each proposed revision specifies the original rule, observed problem, implementation change, expected effect, and validation checks. The implementation agent receives this specification together with the evidence report, reference code, input/output contract, and permitted editing surface. It returns versioned code or instructions, evidence links, applicability conditions, fallback behavior, and validation records. Interface checks preserve the reference rollout, validate, and record stages and each harness’s editing contract.

Diagnosis and Mutation Requirements. The analyze revision asks diagnoses to identify the observed failure and useful behavior to preserve. The mutate revision asks Candidate changes to implement that diagnosis coherently and retain the required dependencies. These complementary contracts connect execution evidence to the resulting intervention.

Revision Objectives. The four revisions in Table 8 target complementary decisions. Regression-aware select uses preservation evidence to resolve score ties, behavior-grounded analyze links diagnoses to execution traces, dependency-aware mutate organizes coherent changes, and cost-aware gate considers resource use at equal scores. These objectives guide implementation, expert review, and algorithm evaluation.

E.2 Human Review Materials and Reporting

Eight experts independently reviewed all four frozen operator revisions, with balanced case and direction-option orders. For each case, they inspected the original rule and evidence and submitted a direction before seeing EvoAudit’s proposal. They then reviewed its reasoning, implementation changes, applicability, and validation plan, judging evidence support, problem addressing, and approval to validate. Each question included an insufficient-evidence option and optional comments. Figures 8 and 9 show the direction-selection and proposal-review interfaces for the select revision.

Table 9 reports mean positive counts per revision out of eight experts. Direction agreement uses a frozen mapping between the initial choice and EvoAudit’s direction. Evidence support and problem addressing count fully positive responses, while endorsement counts approval to validate without further changes. Each measure sums positive counts across the four revisions and divides by four. Assignments, proposal versions, questions, and aggregation rules were frozen before formal review. All formal judgments are retained, and subsequent changes receive new proposal versions.

E.3 Comparison with Existing Evolution Methods

We compare archived 20-generation runs of AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve, and GEPA with separate 20-generation AGE runs on both primary benchmarks and harnesses. Each frozen Champion receives eight benchmark passes against its matching Seed. Table 10 reports reliability, coverage, task turnover, and deployment and evolution costs. Evidence-collection and analysis/design-agent costs are recorded separately from online evolution.

Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution Xiaobo Wang 1,4,* Zimu Wang 2,* Siyu Ye 3,* Jiaqi Li 4,* Min Tang 1 Jun Bai 4 Yuling Shi 5 Ruobing Wang 3 Jingjing Zhang 2 Chaofan Wang 5 Kai WU 3 Mengnan Qi 3 Kai Cai 3 Xiaodong Gu 5, † \dagger Qi Liu 1, † \dagger Zilong Zheng 4, † \dagger Abstract Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select , analyze , mutate , and gate , achieving the best performance. Code: https://github.com/simple-agent-lab/RSIHub November 5, 2026 Correspondence: Siyu Ye at andyyesiyu@gmail.com , Xiaodong Gu at xiaodong.gu@sjtu.edu.cn , Jiaqi Li at lijiaqi@bigai.ai , Zilong Zheng at zlzheng@bigai.ai , Xiaobo Wang at xiaobow.0519@gmail.com . 1 Introduction Recursive self-improvement (RSI) studies agents that iteratively revise their own designs based on experience ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Agent harness evolution offers a concrete form of this idea for language-model agents: it keeps model weights fixed while persistently changing the surrounding system that shapes observations and turns model outputs into actions ( Lin et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Depending on the harness, these changes can target prompts, skills, tool interfaces, orchestration, or source code, going beyond static prompting and memory-based adaptation ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Recent frameworks close the loop between execution, diagnosis, mutation, and evaluation, reporting gains on standard benchmarks ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Shang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . These benchmark gains suggest that harness evolution is a promising avenue for pursuing RSI. However, a higher overall benchmark score do not mean a more useful agent. It averages over tasks and trials, so newly solved tasks can conceal lost ones, while deployment cost and performance beyond the tasks that guided evolution remain unseen ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Kapoor et al., 2025 ) . Relying on that score alone can favor brittle or expensive agent versions and mistake adaptation to the tasks used during evolution for general improvement. Meaningful progress instead requires gains that are reliable across tasks, affordable to deploy, and effective on tasks that did not guide evolution. We aim to explain which persistent harness changes produce useful gains and how evolution generates and preserves them. We organize our empirical investigation around three research questions: • RQ1 (Phenomenology): Does agent evolution yield reliable and efficient improvements, or does it suffer from task-coverage trade-offs and hidden costs? • RQ2 (Generalization): Do the gains achieved during evolving survive when the agent is deployed in novel environments or tasks? • RQ3 (Mechanisms): How do specific evolutionary operators contribute to the generation and preservation of beneficial modifications? We study AHE ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , HyperAgents ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , A-Evolve ( Lin et al., 2026b ) , and GEPA ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) with MiniSWE ( Yang et al., 2024 ) and Codex ( OpenAI, 2026 ) on τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking ( Shi et al., 2026 ) for general tasks and Terminal-Bench 2 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) for coding tasks. Repeated evaluations compare evolved and initial agents in reliability, empirical coverage, regressions, and deployment cost. Split and cross-benchmark comparisons assess generalization, while controlled expansion of existing agents, change interventions, and admission replays trace how gains arise and persist. Figure 1 : The agent harness evolution procedure (left) and our analyses of Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms (right). Harness evolution redistributes task success, with new coverage accompanied by regressions across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms. The practical value of these gains depends on deployment cost and whether they persist beyond the tasks that guided evolution. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, yet combining them can alter their value. The strongest existing agent need not offer the greatest further improvement, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Useful improvement therefore requires productive starting points, compatible changes, and search decisions that preserve gains. We connect these findings to operator redesign as a constructive follow-up. Analyses of Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms jointly guide revision hypotheses for select , analyze , mutate , and gate . Each hypothesis specifies its supporting evidence, expected effects, and applicability conditions. We combine these revisions into Audit-Guided Evolution (AGE) to test their practical value. Our contributions can be summarized as: • Revisiting Practical Improvement. We reveal a gap between benchmark gains and practical utility, showing that useful improvement in agent harness evolution requires preserving useful behavior, managing deployment cost, and sustaining gains beyond the tasks that guide evolution. • Understanding the Fragility of Gains. We identify productive agent selection, change compatibility, and search retention as central challenges. Current performance can misrepresent further improvement potential, useful changes can interfere, and admission can discard stronger versions. • Improving Evolution Through Analysis. We translate these findings into coordinated revisions of diagnosis, mutation, selection, and admission. The resulting AGE algorithm improves reliability and coverage over its reference method across both benchmarks and harnesses. 2 Related Work Agent Optimization and Evolution. Agent improvement spans inference-time refinement, optimization of persistent artifacts, and open-ended self-modification. Reflexion retains linguistic feedback in episodic memory across trials, whereas Self-Refine iteratively revises the current output ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ) . ReflectEvo trains small language models on self-generated reflections to improve introspection and reasoning ( Li et al., 2025 ) . RAM learns from communications to improve an external memory system ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and The AI Hippocampus surveys implicit, explicit, and agentic memory mechanisms ( Jia et al., 2025 ) . DSPy optimizes language-model programs, and TextGrad propagates textual feedback through computational graphs ( Khattab et al., 2024 ; Yüksekgönül et al., 2025 ) . Promptbreeder evolves both task and mutation prompts, ACE maintains evolving context playbooks, and CoEvoSkills co-evolves multi-file skill packages with a separate surrogate verifier ( Fernando et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . The four approaches examined here make different choices within this space. AHE exposes editable harness components and uses distilled execution evidence to guide revisions ( Lin et al., 2026a ) . HyperAgents makes both the task agent and its modification procedure editable ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . A-Evolve frames deployment-time adaptation as goal-directed optimization over persistent system state ( Lin et al., 2026b ) . GEPA combines trajectory reflection for prompt updates with Pareto selection of complementary candidates ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . Harness and Program Evolution. Related approaches also optimize system structure and executable code. GPTSwarm optimizes prompt-bearing graph nodes and orchestration edges, while AgentSquare searches combinations of planning, reasoning, tool-use, and memory modules ( Zhuge et al., 2024 ; Shang et al., 2025 ) . ADAS uses a meta agent to generate agent programs ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . Self-modification extends to the improvement procedure itself: STOP revises optimizer scaffolding, and the Darwin Gödel Machine evolves its own coding agent ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . AlphaEvolve instead evolves target algorithm programs using executable evaluation feedback ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) . Recent work also explores optimizers that construct their own optimization pipelines ( Xue and Yang, 2026 ) . RSIHub composes evolution methods from reusable operators and provides shared evaluation and lineage tracking ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . This distinction between improving task solutions, agent implementations, and optimization procedures motivates separating what changes from how those changes are generated and retained. Capability Boundaries and Mechanisms. Empirical studies of reasoning distinguish improved small- k k success from expansion of large- k k task coverage ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . Token-level analyses identify concentrated learning signals at high-entropy decisions ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , while studies of on-policy distillation examine behavioral compatibility and information novelty ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Related work also examines the feedback used for improvement. UAPO introduces uncertainty-aware utility anchors for preference optimization ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and SAVE uses value-anchored on-policy feedback to update reward models ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . We apply a related analytical perspective to persistent agent-system changes rather than model-weight updates. Repeated evaluations distinguish reliability from empirical coverage, common-process Parent expansion tests improvement potential, Component interventions examine change compatibility, and frozen-pool admission replays assess retention. Evaluation of Agent Systems. Agent evaluation must account for cost, reproducibility, and generalization beyond aggregate success ( Kapoor et al., 2025 ) . For harness evolution specifically, Wang et al. (2026b) find inconsistent advantages over test-time scaling under comparable feedback and inference budgets, together with limited held-out generalization. Performance also depends on interactions among the model, harness, task structure, and coordination overhead ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . The τ \tau -bench family emphasizes reliable tool-agent-user interaction, while Terminal-Bench 2 evaluates long-horizon execution in terminal environments ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Merrill et al., 2026 ) . We study general and coding tasks through these complementary settings, distinguish task exposure during evolution, and assess external transfer without further agent revision. These comparisons connect measured improvement to its deployment cost and scope of applicability. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Definitions An agent A = ( M , H ) A=(M,H) consists of a frozen model M M and a harness H H . We evaluate AHE ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , HyperAgents ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , A-Evolve ( Lin et al., 2026b ) , and GEPA ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) using GPT-5.4 . AHE and HyperAgents are implementation-centric recipes that emphasize agent engineering, whereas A-Evolve and GEPA are reflection-centric recipes that distill execution feedback into reusable changes. We run each recipe with two harnesses. MiniSWE 2.4.5 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) is source-editable and permits inner-source changes. The validate operator optionally checks the proposal, gate decides admission, and record archives outcomes. We focus the mechanism analysis on select , analyze , mutate , and gate because their decisions determine which Parents are used, how evidence guides changes, and which Candidates persist. All sixteen Champions in Figure 2 gain and lose covered tasks, and increase repeated success on some tasks while decreasing it on others. The rule reuses recorded outcomes and preserves the highest-score objective. Analyze: Behavior-Grounded Diagnosis. The analyzer collects the current rollout and, when available, one preceding rollout along the selected lineage, retaining the last 30 records in their stored order. Each judge input contains chronological tool calls, successful and failed tool results, and the completion signal. Tool arguments and results are capped at 600 and 800 characters, respectively. Each rendered trajectory uses at most 12,000 characters, preserving approximately two-thirds from its beginning and one-third from its end when truncated. Interrupted executions can include a bounded termination message. The behavior bundle excludes benchmark rewards, verifier outputs, hidden tests, raw task text, and raw-case paths. The judge returns score , category , outcome , and failure_reason . Scores 0–3 indicate visible breakdown, 4–6 indicate partial or ambiguous progress, and 7–10 indicate visible completion supported by an appropriate check or comparably decisive result. Verdicts distinguish Observed: behavior from Inference: explanations and ground completion judgments in trajectory evidence. These behavioral scores guide diagnosis, while benchmark scores drive select and gate . Each request permits one attempt with a 600-second timeout. Invalid or failed responses return an unknown verdict with sentinel score − 1 -1 . The analyzer exports trajectories, behavioral signals, and verdicts in a structured evidence bundle. The selected text view uses at most 30,000 characters for τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking and 60,000 for Terminal-Bench 2, omitting trailing whole records beyond these budgets. Mutation consumes at most a 50,000-character prefix of this view. Both truncation steps add explicit omission markers. Mutate: Mechanism-Linked, Dependency-Closed Changes. The mutation agent receives the selected behavior evidence, Parent workspace, prompt and skill inventory, and editing contract. Before choosing files, its instructions require the observed behavior, inferred mechanism, replacement behavior, activation conditions, and expected trade-off. A recurring concrete pattern or a single severe, visibly supported breakdown can motivate a change, while ambiguous evidence favors preserving current behavior. The agent must inspect affected interfaces and their producers and consumers, make one coherent intervention, preserve useful behavior in successful traces, and check for conflicting or duplicated guidance. Dependency-closed changes may span multiple files and layers. The agent is instructed to edit the permitted target directly, inspect its final diff, run proportionate structural checks, and propose a validation case for the expected benefit. Outputs retain the patch, changed-file list, surface-check report, agent response, and usage record. Structural checks enforce editing surfaces and interfaces, while the mutation instructions specify evidence grounding, dependency closure, and behavior preservation. Execution errors stop the operator and are recorded with their diagnostic information. Gate: Score-First, Cost-Aware Admission. AGE retains strict Parent-relative score improvement and adds a cost tie-break. For a Candidate C C and its matched Parent P P , with finite Validation scores, admission is accept ( C , P ) = 𝕀 [ s ( C ) > s ( P ) ∨ ( s ( C ) = s ( P ) ∧ Q ( C , P ) ∧ c ( C ) < c ( P ) ) ] . \operatorname{accept}(C,P)=\mathbb{I}\!\left[s(C)>s(P)\;\lor\;\bigl(s(C)=s(P)\land Q(C,P)\land c(C)<c(P)\bigr)\right]. Here c c is the recorded USD cost of canonical Validation evaluation. The comparability predicate Q Q requires matching task-set hashes, finite strictly positive costs, and a direct Parent evaluation. Equal-score admission requires a verified, comparable cost reduction. When cost comparability fails, only the score-improvement branch applies. A valid matched Parent and finite scores are required, and all other Candidates are rejected. The operator reuses canonical evaluations and preserves score improvement as its primary objective. 7.3 Human Evaluation of the Operator Revisions Table 9 : Expert review of four revisions. Harness changes affect many behaviors, while evaluation samples finite executions and compresses their trade-offs. A prompt, skill, or execution routine can help the tasks that supply feedback while disrupting behavior elsewhere. This mismatch offers a common explanation for task regressions, context-dependent change interactions, and selective transfer. It suggests that practical evolution depends on how well feedback represents the consequences of a change, including the resources needed to deploy it. Evidence Must Match the Decision. Current performance, improvement potential, change compatibility, and retention are distinct objectives. A high-scoring Parent need not yield the greatest subsequent gain, a useful Component can interfere with other changes, and a conservative gate can discard alternatives. Together, the diagnostics show why evidence supporting one decision need not support the next. Evaluation should test the desired consequence of each decision, rather than reuse the same aggregate score throughout evolution. Toward Decision-Specific Feedback. Evaluate select through subsequent gains, ground analyze and mutate in traces and dependencies, and assess gate through both retained quality and preserved alternatives. Deployment cost and external evaluation then determine how broadly these benefits remain useful. EvoAudit and AGE illustrate how these complementary checks can guide a coordinated redesign while preserving the reference method’s execution and evaluation contracts. 9 Conclusion Our study shows that harness evolution redistributes observed task success, bringing both gains and regressions. Across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms, practical improvement depends on productive Parents, compatible changes, preservation through search, and generalization at affordable cost. EvoAudit connects these findings to operator revisions, and AGE improves reliability and coverage over its reference method in all four settings. These results motivate evaluating evolution by the useful behavior it creates and sustains, beyond final benchmark scores. Ethics Statement Experiments run in isolated benchmark environments rather than live user-facing services. Evolving agent instructions and code can introduce regressions and unintended tool use. We retain fixed evaluation contracts and harness-specific editing permissions, and examine regressions and transfer alongside aggregate performance. Participants in the human evaluation provided informed consent. The expert-review protocol evaluates the evidence, reasoning, and proposed approaches for operator revisions, as described in Appendix E.2 . Neither benchmark gains nor expert endorsement establishes safety for deployment. References Agrawal et al. (2026) L. A. Agrawal, S. Tan, D. Soylu, N. Ziems, R. Khare, K. Opsahl-Ong, A. Singhvi, H. External Links: Link Cited by: §2 . Appendix A Operator Implementations of the Compared Methods We describe the implementations used in our experiments through the seven operator stages in Table 11 . All four methods share fixed target-model and evaluator contracts. MiniSWE permits dependency-closed changes to inner source code as well as prompts, skills, configuration, and orchestration; Codex permits only changes outside its immutable executable and source. HyperAgents additionally permits changes to designated evolution operators. Evolution Paradigms. Our design-based grouping distinguishes implementation-centric recipes, AHE and HyperAgents, from reflection-centric recipes, A-Evolve and GEPA. The former organize revision around engineering the agent implementation or improvement machinery; the latter organize it around distilling execution experience and feedback. Both use evidence and may modify code within the harness’s legal surface. The grouping follows recipe design, while the harness determines the permitted editing surface. A.1 AHE Selection and Diagnosis. AHE emphasizes observability-grounded revision ( Lin et al., 2026a ) . Its select operator chooses the newest eligible Parent, not necessarily the highest-scoring one. The rollout operator reuses that Parent’s evaluation traces. The analyze operator produces task-level debugger reports: failure reports identify the failure point, possible cause, and corrective lesson, while successful traces expose reusable strategies and fragile behavior. Mixed outcomes on a task can therefore inform the diagnosis alongside outright failures. An overview links these reports to prior changes and their observed effects. Revision and Admission. The mutation agent is instructed to make one coherent, testable change, supported by task evidence and an identified execution path. It considers whether to retain, revise, or roll back the preceding change and pursue a different explanation. A change manifest records the proposed mechanism, affected files, predicted fixes, and behaviors at risk. Debugger reports supply hypotheses for revision. There is no separate optional validate stage. The gate operator admits a completed, eligible evaluation without requiring a higher score, so the next Parent can come from a lower-scoring revision. The record operator preserves outcomes and change evidence. Admission and continuation are thus distinct from final Champion reporting. A.2 HyperAgents Selection and Evidence. HyperAgents permits revision of the improvement procedure as well as the target agent ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Its initial select policy samples eligible Parents using a score-dependent weight and a penalty for having many children. Higher scores increase sampling weight, while the child-count penalty reduces repeated expansion of the same Parent. The rollout operator reuses Parent evaluation traces. The initial analyze operator supplies metrics and browsable raw traces, leaving their interpretation largely to the mutation agent rather than first producing AHE-style debugger reports. Revision and Admission. Mutation may change the target and permitted operator implementations while leaving the evaluator and other fixed contracts unchanged. The mutation instructions favor substantive target changes but allow an operator-only revision when the evidence supports a process-level change. An operator revision takes effect at its next invocation, updating the initial policies in Table 11 for subsequent Generations. The initial validate stage checks Python syntax in target files and the mutation operator. The initial gate admits completed, eligible evaluations without a Parent-relative score threshold. The record operator stores lineage experience, including the Parent, outcome, and score. This editable search procedure distinguishes HyperAgents from target-only revision under fixed operators. A.3 A-Evolve Selection and Behavioral Feedback. Our A-Evolve implementation operationalizes experience-driven adaptation ( Lin et al., 2026b ) . The select operator chooses the highest-scoring eligible Parent, and rollout collects fresh Train trajectories. The analyze operator compresses observable behavior, including tool use, repeated actions, errors, and completion signals, for a trajectory-only judge. This judge evaluates behavior without benchmark reward labels. Its proxy judgments provide feedback for revision, rather than replacing the benchmark score used for admission. Revision and Admission. The mutate operator distills these observations into reusable task-solving guidance and executable target changes. Its instructions emphasize recurrent failure patterns, self-contained skills with their supporting dependencies, and preservation of unrelated behavior. Prompt and skill settings organize revision within the Harness’s legal editing boundary. The optional validate stage is disabled. After canonical evaluation, the strict gate admits a Candidate only if its Validation score exceeds that of the matched Parent. The record operator retains outcomes and the revision rationale. Unlike AHE and the initial HyperAgents policy, A-Evolve combines greedy Parent choice with score-improving admission. A.4 GEPA Selection and Reflection. GEPA combines trajectory-based reflection with per-task Pareto selection ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . The select operator identifies eligible Candidates attaining the best observed score on at least one task, prunes redundant coverage, and samples according to the remaining per-task memberships. This can preserve access to task specialists without selecting solely by aggregate score. The rollout operator collects fresh Train trajectories, and analyze assembles task examples, outputs, and feedback for focused reflection. Revision Scope. The named reflection units differ by benchmark. On τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking, MiniSWE focuses on its system-prompt configuration, while Codex alternates between its prompt and task-execution skill. On Terminal-Bench 2, both harnesses use the entire target as the reflection unit. These units guide evidence organization rather than impose text-only filesystem permissions. The frozen Champion from MiniSWE with GEPA on Terminal-Bench 2 retains inner-source changes to task-conditioned guidance and shell execution. Reflection-centric therefore describes the revision process, not the absence of code changes. These reflection units are distinct from the post-hoc Components isolated in our diagnostics. Validation and Admission. The validate operator evaluates the proposal on the same Train task batch used for the Parent rollout and requires a complete, scorable comparison with strict improvement. This feedback-informed proposal filter precedes canonical Validation evaluation. The subsequent gate checks completion and eligibility without imposing a second Parent-relative improvement threshold. The record operator preserves reflection choices, proposals, and batch comparisons. Thus, GEPA’s improvement filter lies in validate , whereas A-Evolve’s lies in gate , and they use different task evidence. Implications for the Analysis. These implementations differ in how they allocate search, summarize evidence, couple target and operator changes, and filter proposals. Similar final gains can therefore arise through different processes. These differences motivate diagnostics of selection, diagnosis, change compatibility, and admission. Train trajectories supply evolution feedback, and Validation evidence can influence admission. Ten of sixteen Champions have positive Test reliability contributions.
