The Champions from HyperAgents have negative interactions for MiniSWE ( − 6.3 -6.3 ; [ − 11.7 , − 1.2 ] [-11.7,-1.2] ) and Codex ( − 6.6 -6.6 ; [ − 12.6 , − 0.6 ] [-12.6,-0.6] ). These cross-harness observations identify interference as a design risk in the sampled implementation-centric general-task cases. Compatibility Checks. Interaction estimates use the four verified τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking decompositions, while Terminal-Bench 2 provides targeted subset comparisons. Negative interactions motivate checking whether a Candidate diff follows its diagnosis, includes necessary dependencies, and preserves useful behavior. Coupled changes remain permissible when their dependencies and rationale are explicit. D.4 Gate: Size-Normalized Best-Candidate Retention Candidate Pools. For each benchmark, harness, and method, we freeze four distinct artifacts from the same evolution lineage: the Seed, historical Champion, last legal Candidate, and Candidate nearest 50% of cumulative recorded evolution cost. Predeclared 25% and 75% checkpoints resolve duplicates. This gives eight pools per benchmark. Each artifact has eight-pass measurements on separate decision and reporting panels of 20 and 27 tasks for τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking, or 19 and 20 for Terminal-Bench 2. These task panels follow the canonical diagnostic splits. Original Admission Policies. Original gate uses the initial implementations in Table 11 . AHE, HyperAgents, and GEPA accept all eligible Candidates with completed evaluations; A-Evolve requires strict mean improvement over its matched Parent. The comparison supplies four legal, fully evaluated Candidates to these fixed admission policies, with upstream proposal checks held outside the replay. Rules and Replay Contract. Each pool starts with Seed as incumbent and processes the historical Champion, last legal Candidate, and cost-indexed checkpoint in the frozen order. This is a diagnostic order, not the historical generation order. An accepted challenger becomes the incumbent for subsequent comparisons, while all previously retained Candidates remain in the set. The constrained rule is unchanged from the original replay: it requires strict mean improvement over the incumbent on the same purchased evidence, with ties rejected, and L = 1 | 𝒟 g | ​ ∑ x ∈ 𝒟 g max ⁡ { 0 , p ^ inc ​ ( x ) − p ^ cand ​ ( x ) } ≤ 0.05 , L=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{g}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{g}}\max\{0,\hat{p}_{\mathrm{inc}}(x)-\hat{p}_{\mathrm{cand}}(x)\}\leq 0.05, (6) where 𝒟 g \mathcal{D}_{g} contains 20 decision tasks on τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking or 19 on Terminal-Bench 2, and each success fraction uses passes 1–2. All policies receive the same 160 or 152 unique Candidate–task trials, respectively; eligibility-only gates need not use their numeric scores. For A-Evolve’s original gate, the matched parent is the current replay incumbent. A separate reporting panel of 27 or 20 tasks, respectively, uses eight passes to identify the empirical best and never supplies decision evidence. Both benchmarks use the same fixed order, strict-improvement rule, regression cap, and retained-set definition. Metric Definitions. For method m m and gate g g , let 𝒫 m \mathcal{P}_{m} be its four-Candidate input pool, ℛ m , g \mathcal{R}_{m,g} the retained set including Seed, and ℬ m = arg ⁡ max c ∈ 𝒫 m ​ Avg ​ @ ​ 8 ​ ( c ) \mathcal{B}_{m}=\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{P}_{m}}\mathrm{Avg}@8(c) on the reporting panel. The hit indicator is H m , g = 𝟏 [ ℛ m , g ∩ ℬ m ≠ ∅ ] H_{m,g}=\mathbf{1}[\mathcal{R}_{m,g}\cap\mathcal{B}_{m}\neq\varnothing] and set size is N m , g = | ℛ m , g | N_{m,g}=|\mathcal{R}_{m,g}| . Retaining any tied maximizer counts as a hit. The size-normalized score is H m , g / N m , g H_{m,g}/N_{m,g} ; Seed ensures a nonempty retained set. Each main-table cell reports 100 ​ ∑ m ( H m , g / N m , g ) / 4 100\sum_{m}(H_{m,g}/N_{m,g})/4 , separately for each benchmark and harness. This is the mean of per-pool ratios, not the ratio of mean hit to mean size. Values are rounded to one decimal place only after aggregation. All sixteen pools have a unique empirical best. The score therefore equals the chance of drawing that Candidate uniformly from the retained set; this interpretation does not prescribe the method’s actual select policy. Table 15 : Per-pool audit of size-normalized best-Candidate retention. Each policy cell gives H / N H/N , the binary best-retention indicator divided by set size, including Seed. The empirical best maximizes reporting-panel Avg ​ @ ​ 8 \mathrm{Avg}@8 ; Generation numbers identify the frozen artifacts. Benchmark Harness Method Empirical best Original gate Constrained H / N H/N H / N H/N τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking MiniSWE AHE Generation 9 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 HyperAgents Generation 3 1 / 4 1/4 1 / 2 1/2 A-Evolve Generation 1 1 / 2 1/2 1 / 2 1/2 GEPA Generation 9 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 Codex AHE Generation 10 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 2 0/2 HyperAgents Generation 11 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 2 0/2 A-Evolve Generation 20 0 / 2 0/2 0 / 2 0/2 GEPA Seed 1 / 4 1/4 1 / 1 1/1 Terminal-Bench 2 MiniSWE AHE Generation 18 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 HyperAgents Generation 10 1 / 4 1/4 1 / 2 1/2 A-Evolve Generation 4 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 GEPA Generation 20 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 2 0/2 Codex AHE Generation 20 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 HyperAgents Generation 18 1 / 4 1/4 0 / 1 0/1 A-Evolve Seed 1 / 1 1/1 1 / 1 1/1 GEPA Seed 1 / 4 1/4 1 / 1 1/1 A Recurring Preservation Risk. The original policies retain the reporting-panel best in fifteen pools, compared with six under Constrained. The nine newly excluded best Candidates span both harness types, task domains, and paradigms. Size-normalized scores nevertheless improve in four pools, remain unchanged in three, and fall in nine. The improvements include two implementation-centric source-editable pools retaining the best among fewer alternatives, and two reflection-centric outer-layer-only pools retaining a best Seed alone. Pruning can therefore improve the diagnostic metric while excluding useful Candidates elsewhere. The two outer-layer-only averages increase even while evolved best Candidates are lost in other pools. Jointly reporting hit, set size, and Candidate identity distinguishes concentration on a strong fallback from preservation of evolved gains. Replay Evidence and Design Implications. The replay applies original and constrained admission rules to the same frozen Candidate pools and measured scores. The constrained rule combines strict score improvement with a regression cap. Comparing retained-set quality, size, and membership motivates admission rules that balance improvement, preservation, and fallback retention. D.5 Component Definitions and Representative Content This subsection records the frozen Component definitions for the eight-case matrix of Table 5 . All sixteen Component variants and eight Champion comparators have complete evaluations. A and B identify the two groups within each case. The definitions specify retained agent changes, implementation files, execution dependencies, and representative content. Prompt and code excerpts have line wrapping adjusted for display, and code excerpts reproduce the indicated implementation segment. MiniSWE paths are relative to src/minisweagent/ ; Codex paths are relative to the Candidate’s target directory. Each Component is evaluated as a complete agent intervention. Construction and Comparison. Seed + A and Seed + B retain the matching Seed outside the specified Component and its execution dependencies. Components are separated by function: a configuration file can contain both interface settings and task-solving instructions, which we isolate by semantic key. Required compatibility adaptations are identified below. Codex Components remain outside its immutable executable and source. The Terminal-Bench 2 cases evaluate targeted Champion subsets. Interaction estimates use decompositions whose joint Components reproduce the compared Champion. Case Selection. The matrix contains four Champion cases per benchmark, with two from each harness. Eligibility requires at least two functionally distinct groups of persistent changes that can be isolated with their execution dependencies on the matching Seed while keeping the model and evaluator fixed. The τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking cases comprise Champions from AHE and HyperAgents in both harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 2, we retain the previously evaluated Champions from MiniSWE with AHE and Codex with HyperAgents, and add MiniSWE with GEPA and Codex with AHE after auditing all eight Champions. The additions prioritize clear functional boundaries and complementary mechanisms. Component boundaries were frozen before evaluation, and all completed outcomes are retained. Selection History and Extension. The initial Terminal-Bench 2 sample selected the largest historical unrounded Avg ​ @ ​ 8 \mathrm{Avg}@8 gain within each harness, yielding MiniSWE with AHE and Codex with HyperAgents. Case identities remain frozen, and source-faithful reevaluations replace the two superseded Codex Champion measurements. MiniSWE with GEPA separates task guidance from shell execution adaptation, complementing AHE’s broader validation and submission controls. Codex with AHE separates instruction content from persistent context and skill support, complementing HyperAgents’ dependency bootstrap. Functional clarity and mechanism complementarity determine the additions. Their identities and Component boundaries were frozen before evaluation, and all added outcomes are reported. D.5.1 τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking: MiniSWE with AHE (G2) Component A: Interface. This Component changes how shell/tool output is presented to the model, while retaining the Seed’s task-solving instructions and bash action interface. It extracts readable text from structured tool-response envelopes, removes duplicate text blocks, and preserves salient information when an observation is long. Rather than retaining only its beginning and end, the observation also includes a bounded selection of middle content containing tool schemas, execution results, required fields, and conversation-control signals. The changed files are models/utils/actions_toolcall.py , models/utils/actions_toolcall_response.py , the added models/utils/observation_output.py , and the observation_template key in config/mini.yaml . Observation-budget constants from the added helper: DISPLAY_OUTPUT_LIMIT = 10000 DISPLAY_OUTPUT_HEAD_CHARS = 3000 DISPLAY_OUTPUT_TAIL_CHARS = 3000 SALIENT_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS = 2500 Component B: Strategy. This Component replaces the system prompt, task prompt, and format-error guidance in config/mini.yaml ; observation processing stays at the Seed. The instructions distinguish the benchmark’s tool-driven general tasks from coding tasks, prioritize live state and tool schemas, require one focused action followed by inspection, prohibit invented arguments or case facts, and distinguish a stopped conversation from a successfully completed backend action. The format-error guidance also specifies concise recovery from token-limit truncation and a tool-only final submission. Task-prompt excerpt: “Prefer live environment state, exact tool outputs, runtime status, and tool schemas over inference from general KB text.” Completion-rule excerpt: “Only treat the task as complete when the required environment state or required action has actually been achieved.” D.5.2 τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking: MiniSWE with HyperAgents (G9) Component A: Interface. This Component exposes structured benchmark tools in place of a bash-only interface when it detects tasks from the general-task benchmark. It adds tool schemas, argument parsing (including nested JSON-string normalization), dispatch to the benchmark environment, and a dedicated final-submission action. The dependency-closed implementation spans agents/interactive.py , environments/local.py , utils/tau3.py , both action/tool-response utilities, and seven adapters in models/ : the chat and Responses implementations for LiteLLM, OpenRouter, and Portkey, plus Requesty. The thirteenth changed file, config/mini.yaml , adds neutral transport and format-error instructions so that the Seed prompt does not request an unavailable bash tool. This compatibility text describes how to call the exposed tools, without importing the Champion’s task-solving strategy. Exposed tool names: tau3_call , tau3_list_tools , tau3_get_tool_schema , and submit_final_output . Compatibility-note excerpt: “This note describes only the available transport; determine the task policy and actions from the task, tool schemas, and runtime responses.” Component B: Strategy. This Component changes only the task-instance prompt in config/mini.yaml . It retains the Champion’s service workflow: start the conversation once, consult the latest user message and schema, perform one action at a time, separate user communication from domain-tool calls, respect stop/transfer signals, and ground advice in documented policy and hard user requirements. Because the Seed does not expose Component A’s structured tools, the workflow is expressed through the Seed’s tau3-mcp.py command-line interface. This is the evaluated CLI-translated strategy Component, not an unmodified copy of the native-tool prompt; the translation is an execution dependency, not an independent strategy finding. Translated task-prompt excerpts: “Perform exactly one focused Tau3 CLI action per response and inspect its output before the next action.” “Do not recommend a product or action that misses a user-stated hard requirement.” D.5.3 τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking: Codex with AHE (G15) Component A: Orchestration. The only changed file is the outer adapter agent.py . Before invoking Codex, it detects service-task markers in the instruction and appends a workflow-guidance block, unless that block is already present. The injected text emphasizes exact tool discovery, a per-entity worklist, assistant-side versus user-side actions, date and eligibility checks, canonical write arguments, and completing all requested items before ending. The Seed’s prompt and skill files are retained. Here, orchestration includes conditional instruction delivery; it does not mean that the Component contains no natural-language guidance. Injected-guidance excerpt: “Keep a live per-entity worklist for the case. For each named transaction, card, account, product, referral, or other requested item, track the exact entity, the user-described problem, the currently grounded workflow or enum, any missing fields, and the next read or write needed.” Component B: Prompt and Skills. This Component replaces prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md , and adds skills/tau3-service-workflows/SKILL.md , while retaining the Seed adapter. The prompt distinguishes coding work from the general-task benchmark’s workflows and directs the latter to the specialized skill. That skill specifies a six-part workflow: discover the live tool surface; ground on the exact entity; identify who must perform the next state change; construct exact writes; preserve the selected product or workflow branch; and finish all requested work. It includes explicit checks for relative dates, enums, optional fields, user-side follow-through, and multi-item completion. Specialized-skill excerpt: “Once the user accepts a supported product or workflow branch, stop re-optimizing and execute that exact branch.” Prompt excerpt: “If the task involves multiple requested actions or entities, keep a short checklist and do not finish while any requested item is unresolved.” D.5.4 τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking: Codex with HyperAgents (G18) Component A: Orchestration. The outer agent.py detects the configured service server or service markers in the instruction, then prepends a guidance block unless its header is already present. The same server-detection helper is reused by the existing installation path. The injected guidance prioritizes live account investigation, eligible and actionable recommendations, exact knowledge-base procedures, discoverable-tool checks, literal argument formatting, and completion of accepted workflows. Prompt and skill files remain at the Seed, so the specialized-skill reference in this block does not itself install Component B. Injected-guidance excerpt: “Do not substitute a neighboring tool or an incidental side effect for a separately documented step. If the KB names a dedicated replacement, approval, closure, report, or submission tool, use that exact tool instead of assuming another mutation already covered it.” Component B: Skills. This Component changes skills/task-execution/SKILL.md to route tasks from the general-task benchmark to the added skills/tau3-banking-runtime/SKILL.md ; the outer adapter and main prompt stay at the Seed. The specialized skill covers identity verification, account-specific lookups, recommendation eligibility, tool unlocking and execution checks, multi-step discrepancies, transfers, closures, and final-state verification. It also includes implementation-sensitive payload rules: preserve surfaced key order, whitespace, explicit null/false values, and numeric forms in nested argument strings. These are actual retained instructions, not a claim that equivalent JSON representations generally have different semantics. Payload-formatting excerpt: “Serialize that inner JSON as a single-line object with double-quoted keys, the surfaced key order, and standard spaces after each comma and colon.” Tool-check excerpt: “After unlock_discoverable_agent_tool , check that the returned tool name, description, and parameters match the tool you meant to unlock.” D.5.5 Terminal-Bench 2: MiniSWE with AHE (G18) Component A: Static Instructions. Only config/mini.yaml changes. The retained prompt additions call for early inspection of visible tests and checkers, exact deliverable paths and formats, fresh-shell verification, preservation of original inputs and consumers, and rechecking after any subsequent change. They reject proxy checks, fabricated substitutes, and unresolved failures as evidence of completion. These instructions do not add a programmatic submission guard. Contract-first instruction: “Before long implementation, downloads, or external research, spend the first 1-2 commands locating the real acceptance path.” Reverification instruction: “Any edit after a passing verification invalidates that verification. If you change the artifact, environment, dependency set, or generated output afterward, rerun the exact end-to-end check against the final state before submitting.” Component B: Dynamic Guard. Files agents/default.py and environments/local.py implement the dynamic checks. The configuration file config/mini.yaml supplies their hooks and activation flags, without Component A’s static instructions. It discovers visible verifier files, derives deliverable-boundary hints from the task, supplies fresh-shell compatibility helpers, records test inspection and unresolved check failures, and inspects submission attempts. The guard can replace a completion signal with a warning about uninspected verifiers, unhealthy package state, unresolved failures, missing files, or deliverable-boundary violations. It warns once per warning fingerprint; repeating the same submission can proceed, so this is not an unconditional veto or a replacement for the benchmark evaluator. Activated flags in the configuration: pause_submit_for_uninspected_verifier: true pause_submit_for_unhealthy_system_packages: true pause_submit_for_unresolved_verifier_failures: true pause_submit_for_deliverable_boundary_violations: true D.5.6 Terminal-Bench 2: MiniSWE with GEPA (G20) Component A: Task Guidance. This Component combines static instructions about exact deliverables and evidence preservation with task-conditioned reminders. In agents/default.py , _build_task_guardrails detects wording associated with exhaustive outputs or fragile evidence and generates the corresponding guidance. The template in config/mini.yaml consumes the generated task_guardrails value and includes the accompanying static instructions. The generator and template hook stay in the same Component because either alone disconnects the mechanism. The local command-execution implementation remains at the Seed. Component B: Shell Execution Adaptation. Only environments/local.py changes. The helper _preferred_shell_executable resolves MSWEA_LOCAL_SHELL , defaulting to bash , and supplies the available executable to the subprocess launcher. It falls back to the platform default when the preferred shell cannot be resolved. This changes shell semantics at the command-execution boundary without importing Component A’s guidance or changing the model configuration. D.5.7 Terminal-Bench 2: Codex with AHE (G20) Component A: Prompt and Skills. This Component replaces the prompt and task-execution skill in prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md . The instructions prioritize the verifier-facing contract, a minimal coherent change on the active execution path, and checks of the final artifact at the consumer-visible boundary. Prompt and skill content form one guidance Component rather than separate Components based on file location. The adapter, compaction settings, model, reasoning effort, and Codex executable remain at the Seed. Component B: Persistent Context and Skill Support. The outer agent.py moves temporary Codex state and skill-upload paths to a persistent Codex directory, while codex.toml enables prefix-preserving compaction with auto_compact_token_limit_scope set to body_after_prefix . These changes support instruction continuity without importing Component A’s prompt or skill contents. The evolved adapter changes are semantically applied to the exact evaluation Seed, preserving its authentication, provider routing, session handling, and cancellation cleanup. Codex’s executable and source, the model, and reasoning effort are unchanged. D.5.8 Terminal-Bench 2: Codex with HyperAgents (G18) Component A: Instructions. The prompt and task-execution skill are replaced in prompt.md and skills/task-execution/SKILL.md ; the outer adapter remains at the matching Seed. The prompt and skill instruct the agent to preserve authentic input artifacts, inspect visible verifiers, reconstruct missing checker dependencies, react to failed checks, match exact output paths and final-state requirements, remove probe-only artifacts, and run a final check from a fresh shell or process. They also ask the agent to diagnose silent long-running commands instead of repeatedly polling without new evidence. Skill excerpt: “Recreate the verifier runtime before declaring the task unavailable.” Failure-handling excerpt: “Clear red checks before closing. If any command, test, assertion, or custom validation failed after your last meaningful edit, rerun that same path cleanly or keep debugging.” Component B: Orchestration and Bootstrap. Only the outer agent.py changes. The Champion’s bootstrap changes are merged onto the exact Seed adapter used in the matched evaluation, rather than replacing that adapter with a different baseline wrapper. During setup, the adapter installs or locates uv and uvx , creates a sourceable environment helper, and exposes stable executable entrypoints in standard locations for fresh-shell verifier commands. Installation first attempts the Python package route and then an installer fallback; setup reports a warning if the bootstrap remains unavailable. The Seed’s prompt and skills are retained. This Component prepares the execution environment; it does not alter the verifier’s scoring rules or Codex’s executable. Bootstrap function’s documented purpose: “Install stable verifier entrypoints for uv-based test harnesses.” Setup-hook excerpt: try: await self.exec_as_root(environment, command=_verifier_bootstrap_command()) except RuntimeError: self.logger.warning( "Failed to bootstrap uv verifier entrypoints", exc_info=True) Generic-Reminder Controls Are Separate. The reminders in Table 7 are not additional Champion Components. On τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking, both harnesses receive: “This is an interactive tool-use task. Inspect the available runtime tool interface, use tools when needed, verify the resulting state, and complete every requested item before ending.” The Terminal-Bench 2 MiniSWE control adds: “Before final submission, inspect any available tests or check commands and run the closest exact end-to-end check on the final artifact. Do not submit while a relevant check is still failing or running.” These controls add general advice without the case-specific prompt bundle, interface implementation, or dynamic guard above. Recovery of Interrupted Evaluations. Four τ 3 \tau^{3} -Banking Codex reminder evaluations were interrupted by API rate limits after their conversations had started. Under a documented recovery-policy amendment, we fixed these four task–pass identities and reran each once from its initial state with unchanged model, simulator, target, and evaluator settings. The other 772 numeric outcomes were retained, and all four replacement outcomes were accepted, including three zeros. Original attempts remain in the audit record; selected outcomes and their costs enter the reported metrics. Appendix E Operator Redesign: Implementation and Evaluation E.1 Evidence and Implementation Requirements The analysis agent combines results from the Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms analyses with source traces and reference operators. It identifies recurring patterns across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms and links each finding to the relevant comparisons and observed behavior. The resulting evidence report supplies the rationale and applicability conditions for operator revision. Each proposed revision specifies the original rule, observed problem, implementation change, expected effect, and validation checks. The implementation agent receives this specification together with the evidence report, reference code, input/output contract, and permitted editing surface. It returns versioned code or instructions, evidence links, applicability conditions, fallback behavior, and validation records. Interface checks preserve the reference rollout , validate , and record stages and each harness’s editing contract. Diagnosis and Mutation Requirements. The analyze revision asks diagnoses to identify the observed failure and useful behavior to preserve. The mutate revision asks Candidate changes to implement that diagnosis coherently and retain the required dependencies. These complementary contracts connect execution evidence to the resulting intervention. Revision Objectives. The four revisions in Table 8 target complementary decisions. Regression-aware select uses preservation evidence to resolve score ties, behavior-grounded analyze links diagnoses to execution traces, dependency-aware mutate organizes coherent changes, and cost-aware gate considers resource use at equal scores. These objectives guide implementation, expert review, and algorithm evaluation. E.2 Human Review Materials and Reporting Eight experts independently reviewed all four frozen operator revisions, with balanced case and direction-option orders. For each case, they inspected the original rule and evidence and submitted a direction before seeing EvoAudit’s proposal. They then reviewed its reasoning, implementation changes, applicability, and validation plan, judging evidence support, problem addressing, and approval to validate. Each question included an insufficient-evidence option and optional comments. Figures 8 and 9 show the direction-selection and proposal-review interfaces for the select revision. Table 9 reports mean positive counts per revision out of eight experts. Direction agreement uses a frozen mapping between the initial choice and EvoAudit’s direction. Evidence support and problem addressing count fully positive responses, while endorsement counts approval to validate without further changes. Each measure sums positive counts across the four revisions and divides by four. Assignments, proposal versions, questions, and aggregation rules were frozen before formal review. All formal judgments are retained, and subsequent changes receive new proposal versions. Figure 8 : Human review of select before proposal disclosure. Experts inspect the original rule and evidence, then submit their preferred revision direction. Figure 9 : Human review of select after proposal disclosure. Experts inspect the revision and its reasoning, then assess evidence support, problem addressing, and endorsement for validation. E.3 Comparison with Existing Evolution Methods We compare archived 20-generation runs of AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve, and GEPA with separate 20-generation AGE runs on both primary benchmarks and harnesses. Each frozen Champion receives eight benchmark passes against its matching Seed. Table 10 reports reliability, coverage, task turnover, and deployment and evolution costs. Evidence-collection and analysis/design-agent costs are recorded separately from online evolution. Appendix F Evolution Trees The following figures show all sixteen archived evolution runs, each comprising the Seed and 20 generation attempts. Unsuccessful attempts are retained. Arrows follow the recorded parent-to-child relationships, not chronological adjacency; layout positions and node colors do not indicate performance or acceptance decisions. Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities

Haoyang Zhang22 2 Corresponding Author. 17@evomap.ai   Qumeng Sun   Xiao Zhang   Xiang Liu
Zhidong Fan    Junjie Wang

Infinite Evolution Lab, EvoMap

https://github.com/EvoMap/evolver
Abstract

Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents have progressed from language generation to multi-step problem solving through tool use and environmental interaction, with growing applications in software engineering and other complex tasks [1, 2]. Executing these tasks often requires extensive environment exploration, tool invocation, failure recovery, and outcome verification, incurring substantial computational and interaction costs. Yet the procedural knowledge acquired through these interactions is often confined to individual executions, leaving subsequent tasks to rediscover useful strategies and repeat similar exploratory efforts. This raises a fundamental question: How can the computational effort invested in past exploration be transformed into reusable experience that continuously improves future agent capabilities?

Recent coding agents, such as Codex [3] and Claude Code [4], have demonstrated the growing potential of autonomous software development. Meanwhile, Skill-based approaches enable agents to reuse packaged instructions, workflows, and domain-specific resources [5], while other methods leverage historical trajectories, execution feedback, and evolving contexts to improve agent behavior without updating model parameters [6, 7, 8]. More recently, research on strategy genes has shown that compact, control-oriented Gene representations can provide more effective experience reuse and iterative refinement than documentation-oriented Skill representations in controlled scientific coding settings [9]. Despite these advances, a central systems challenge remains: how to transform task-specific exploration into persistent, reusable strategy assets that can be integrated with existing agents and progressively refined through execution feedback. Moreover, accumulating experience does not necessarily improve performance, as irrelevant or outdated strategies may introduce redundant computation or interfere with otherwise successful executions.

To address this challenge, we introduce Evolver, an experience-driven agent evolution system built around the principle of Exploration-to-Evolution: transforming knowledge acquired through task execution into persistent strategy assets that can guide subsequent decisions and support iterative adaptation. Building on the Gene representation, Evolver encodes reusable procedures and their applicability conditions as structured Gene objects, associates them with concrete execution cases through Capsules, and maintains event, provenance, and review records to support experience management. Through integration with existing agent harnesses, Evolver makes historical experience available during subsequent task execution without modifying the underlying model parameters. Rather than treating execution histories as passive records, Evolver organizes procedural knowledge into reusable assets that can be selected, applied, and maintained in response to new execution feedback. This design establishes a mechanism through which previously invested exploration can contribute to future agent behavior, providing a foundation for experience-driven capability evolution.

We evaluate Evolver across two agent harnesses, Claude Code [4] and Codex [3], two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1 [10], SWE-bench Multilingual [11], SWE-rebench [12], and GAIA [13]. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Gene augmentation improves the overall task success rate from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points), with gains observed under both Claude Code (+2.50 points) and Codex (+6.25 points). These improvements vary across models and benchmarks, with nine of the 16 evaluated configurations exhibiting higher task success. Beyond task effectiveness, Evolver reduces recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24% overall. Notably, among 265 pairs that succeed both with and without Evolver, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, indicating that historical experience can improve execution efficiency even when task success is already achieved. Representative cases in terminal operations and software repair further illustrate these efficiency gains through fewer model invocations and lower token usage without compromising task success. Together, these findings highlight the complementary benefits of reusable procedural experience for task effectiveness and execution efficiency, positioning Evolver as a practical systems approach to transforming agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters.

2 Related Work

2.1 Procedural Experience Representation and Reuse

Agent interactions generate procedural knowledge through exploration, tool use, and execution feedback, motivating approaches that reuse historical experience without updating model parameters. Early methods extract reusable insights from successful and failed trajectories [6, 14], while subsequent studies organize such knowledge into workflows, adaptive memory, and procedural guidance [15, 16, 17, 18]. Complementary approaches package reusable procedures as executable skills or structured instructions [19, 20, 21], whereas Agentic Plan Caching [22] reuses adaptable planning templates to reduce repeated computation. Recent studies further highlight that experience utility depends on representation quality and contextual applicability, as inappropriate skills may increase execution costs or degrade performance [23, 24].

More closely related, the study [9] demonstrates the advantages of compact, control-oriented Gene representations over documentation-oriented Skill packages for experience reuse and iterative refinement. Building on this representational foundation, Evolver operationalizes procedural knowledge as persistent strategy assets associated with execution cases, provenance, and lifecycle states, enabling experience reuse within existing agent systems.

2.2 Experience-Driven Agent Adaptation and Evolution

Beyond experience reuse, recent research investigates how execution feedback can progressively improve agent behavior. GEPA [7] and Agentic Context Engineering [8] evolve prompts and contextual guidance through reflection and feedback, while EvolveR [25] combines experience-derived principles with reinforcement learning. Other approaches support continual adaptation through procedural memory refinement, skill evolution, and experience governance [26, 27, 28, 29]. At the implementation level, Godel Agent [30] and Darwin Godel Machine [31] pursue self-improvement through modifications to agent code.

These studies demonstrate complementary pathways for agent evolution, spanning prompts, memory, skills, model policies, and executable programs. In contrast, Evolver focuses on evolving external procedural experience while preserving the underlying foundation model and existing agent harnesses. Its Exploration-to-Evolution design connects experience acquisition, structured strategy reuse, and feedback-supported lifecycle management, allowing historical exploration to inform subsequent execution. We examine the conditional benefits and computational trade-offs of experience reuse, recognizing that accumulated experience does not necessarily yield consistent improvements.

3 Evolver: From Exploration to Evolution

3.1 Design Principles and System Overview

Problem Formulation. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote a fixed foundation-model policy, hh an existing agent harness, and xtx_{t} the task encountered at step tt. Without updating model parameters, Evolver maintains an external experience state ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} to inform subsequent execution. The interaction is formulated as

gt\displaystyle g_{t} =ℛh​(xt,ℰt),\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{h}(x_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t}), (1)
τt\displaystyle\tau_{t} =Execπθ,h⁡(xt;gt),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Exec}_{\pi_{\theta},h}(x_{t};g_{t}),
ℰt+1\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t+1} =𝒰⁡(ℰt,τt,ft),\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{E}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}),

where ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h} retrieves applicable experience, τt\tau_{t} denotes the resulting execution trajectory, and ftf_{t} represents available execution feedback. The update operator 𝒰\mathcal{U} abstracts experience acquisition and lifecycle operations, which depend on the enabled system components.

Design Principles. Evolver follows the Exploration-to-Evolution principle, which transforms knowledge acquired through agent exploration into persistent strategy assets that can support future adaptation. This principle is realized through three complementary designs. First, Experience Externalization separates reusable procedural knowledge from individual execution trajectories, enabling its persistent representation and management. Second, Experience-Conditioned Execution makes relevant strategies available to existing agents without modifying their underlying model parameters or replacing their execution harnesses. Third, Feedback-Guided Evolution supports the assessment and maintenance of accumulated experience through execution feedback and lifecycle operations. Together, these designs establish a pathway for preserving the knowledge value of historical exploration and making it available to subsequent agent executions.

System Architecture. As illustrated in Figure 1, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, persistent asset management, retrieval, and feedback-supported evolution into a unified system. Historical agent interactions provide execution traces from which reusable strategies are extracted through signal analysis, automatic drafting, or optional model-based distillation. The resulting experience is organized into structured Gene objects, associated Capsule records, and supporting event, provenance, and review information. During subsequent tasks, relevant experience is retrieved and delivered through hooks, MCP interfaces, or host-specific integrations to condition agent behavior. Evolver further connects to EvoMap 11 1 https://evomap.ai/ for network-based experience publishing, discovery, and retrieval. Provenance tracking, review mechanisms, and execution safeguards provide operational controls whose enforcement depends on the integration pathway and deployment environment. The following sections detail these components and their roles in transforming historical exploration into reusable and evolving agent capabilities.

3.2 Experience Representation and Asset Management

Structured Strategy Representation. To preserve the knowledge acquired through historical exploration, Evolver represents reusable procedural knowledge as structured strategy assets rather than retaining complete execution trajectories as the primary unit of reuse. Building on the strategy-gene representation [9], each Gene gig_{i} is characterized by

gi=(si,𝒮i,𝒫i,ℳi,𝒱i),g_{i}=(s_{i},\mathcal{S}_{i},\mathcal{P}_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i},\mathcal{V}_{i}), (2)

where sis_{i} summarizes the experience, 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} specifies procedural steps, 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} describes applicability conditions, ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} provides task-matching signals, and 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} contains optional validation plans. This representation separates reusable operational guidance from task-specific execution details, allowing historical strategies to be retrieved and adapted to subsequent tasks. Importantly, applicability conditions and validation plans provide guidance rather than enforceable execution constraints or guarantees of prior verification.

Complementary Experience Assets. Beyond Gene objects, Evolver maintains complementary assets that preserve execution context and support experience management. A Capsule associates a strategy with a concrete execution case, providing contextual examples that can accompany retrieved strategies. An AntiGene captures negative procedural guidance, identifying actions or practices to avoid in subsequent executions. Meanwhile, Event records capture asset-related operations, while separate provenance and review records track experience origins, trust status, and approval decisions. Together, these components constitute the persistent experience state ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}, separating reusable strategies, supporting execution cases, and operational metadata.

Persistent Asset Management. Evolver maintains experience assets through content-addressed, append-only storage, preserving asset identity independently of subsequent lifecycle decisions. Review and provenance states are maintained in separate records, supporting experience quarantine, approval, rejection, and revocation without overwriting the underlying assets. This separation enables persistent procedural knowledge to coexist with evolving eligibility and trust states, providing a foundation for feedback-driven experience management. The enforcement of these states depends on the corresponding acquisition and retrieval pathways, as detailed in Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5.

3.3 Experience Acquisition and Consolidation

Experience Sources. Evolver treats historical agent interactions as a source of reusable procedural knowledge, capturing not only task outcomes but also the exploration and feedback that precede them. When session ingestion is enabled, runtime adapters collect records from supported agent harnesses, including task context, tool interactions, execution errors, and available outcomes. These records are normalized into bounded experience materials with heuristic sensitive-information redaction. Additional experience can be acquired through explicit asset submissions and external experience repositories, providing complementary sources beyond automatically collected sessions.

Experience Extraction. Given collected experience materials, Evolver identifies lightweight signals associated with successful execution, failures, and task difficulty to construct candidate Gene objects. The default automated drafting pathway extracts concise procedural hints from assistant utterances and marks them as unproven, rather than assuming that the resulting strategies have been validated. When enabled, LLM-based distillation further supports structured experience extraction from execution records, including reusable strategies, associated cases, and negative procedural guidance. These complementary pathways separate low-cost experience collection from more structured synthesis, while leaving the effectiveness of generated strategies subject to subsequent evaluation.

Experience Consolidation. Extracted experience is consolidated into persistent, content-addressed assets, with supporting execution cases retained when available. Automatically drafted and model-distilled candidates are placed under review, whereas certain explicit submission pathways can persist assets directly. Review and provenance records maintain experience eligibility and source information separately from the underlying strategy content, although admission and trust enforcement depend on the acquisition and retrieval pathways. By preserving candidate knowledge independently of its current lifecycle state, Evolver establishes a reusable experience base that supports subsequent retrieval and feedback-guided evolution, as detailed in Sections 3.4 and 3.5.

3.4 Experience Retrieval and Agent Integration

Task-Conditioned Experience Retrieval. To reuse historical knowledge, Evolver provides multiple retrieval pathways that select experience according to task context and integration requirements. Session-start hooks supply a bounded set of locally eligible Gene objects, while optional prompt-time recall matches task descriptions against stored experience signals. MCP interfaces additionally support on-demand experience retrieval, whereas autonomous execution employs a separate heuristic selection mechanism incorporating task relevance, experience quality, and historical reuse feedback. These pathways differ in their ranking strategies, context budgets, and eligibility checks, allowing experience delivery to accommodate different execution settings.

Experience-Conditioned Execution. Retrieved Gene objects, together with associated Capsule examples when available, are delivered through session hooks, prompt-time injection, MCP tools, or host-specific integrations. Rather than modifying foundation model parameters or replacing agent execution policies, Evolver introduces procedural guidance into the existing interaction context, enabling the host agent to interpret and apply historical strategies. This separation between experience management and task execution allows Evolver to augment existing agent harnesses while preserving their native reasoning, tool-use, and verification capabilities. Consequently, historical exploration can inform subsequent decisions without requiring additional model training or modifications to the underlying agent architecture.

Networked Experience through EvoMap. Beyond local experience reuse, Evolver integrates with EvoMap to support the publication, discovery, and retrieval of experience assets across connected agents. This interface extends the available knowledge beyond individual execution histories, allowing agents to access strategies contributed by other nodes. External assets can be associated with provenance and trust metadata, although direct retrieval and locally imported assets follow different admission and review pathways. Together, local and network-based experience access provides a foundation for broader experience reuse.

3.5 Feedback-Guided Experience Evolution

Execution Feedback. Beyond preserving and reusing historical knowledge, Evolver supports experience evolution through feedback collected from subsequent executions. Depending on the execution pathway, feedback includes task outcomes, validation results, reuse events, and interaction signals from agent hosts. Autonomous execution evaluates task outcomes using execution status and available verification procedures, while host integrations can report observed checks and reuse-related signals. These observations provide a basis for experience assessment.

Experience Lifecycle. Rather than treating accumulated experience as permanently applicable, Evolver maintains lifecycle states that govern how strategies are retained and reused. Automatically drafted and model-distilled Gene candidates initially enter quarantine and can subsequently be approved or rejected through review. An optional probation mechanism further supports promotion based on recorded successes and failures, while autonomous execution incorporates historical reuse signals and failure-based restrictions into candidate selection. Rejection and provenance revocation are recorded separately from the underlying content-addressed assets, preserving their identity while modifying their subsequent eligibility. These mechanisms instantiate the lifecycle operations underlying 𝒰\mathcal{U} in Equation 1, allowing experience states to evolve without modifying foundation model parameters.

Trust-Aware Evolution. Because experience may originate from local execution or external contributors, Evolver associates assets with provenance and review information to support source-aware management. Imported EvoMap assets can be marked as untrusted until explicitly promoted, while supported execution pathways apply additional validation and operational safeguards. However, admission checks and trust enforcement are pathway-dependent, and some direct retrieval interfaces do not apply the same restrictions. Together, these mechanisms provide a foundation for feedback-guided experience adaptation, distinguishing the evolution of reusable strategy states from an assumption of uniformly improving agent performance.

4 Experimental Evaluation and Analysis

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and Agent Configurations. We evaluate Evolver on four benchmarks covering diverse agent capabilities: Terminal-Bench 2.1 [10], SWE-bench Multilingual [11], SWE-rebench [12], and GAIA [13]. Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluates terminal-based engineering tasks, SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-rebench assess software issue resolution, and GAIA examines multi-step information seeking and reasoning. We consider two agent harnesses, Claude Code and Codex, each paired with two foundation model configurations, deepseek-v4.1-flash [32] and gpt-5.6-sol [33]. For each benchmark, we prioritize the first 20 tasks in their original order. Tasks yielding empty responses due to malformed outputs, timeouts, or execution failures are replaced sequentially with subsequent tasks. We ensure that all harness–model configurations are evaluated on the same 20 tasks per benchmark, yielding 16 configurations in total. All experiments use Evolver v2.0.33.

Experience Construction and Paired Evaluation. We adopt a three-stage Baseline–Extraction–Gene (B–E–G) protocol to examine the effects of historical experience reuse. In the Baseline Execution (B) stage, each agent executes the original task using its native tools and built-in skills without additional Gene injection. In the Experience Extraction (E) stage, reusable strategies are distilled from valid baseline trajectories, including both successful and unsuccessful executions, using a model configuration matched to the corresponding evaluation setting. Experience pools are isolated by evaluation batch, benchmark, harness, and model, and candidate assets are frozen before augmented execution. In the Gene-Augmented Execution (G) stage, the agent receives the original task together with selected Gene guidance in a fresh session with the task environment restored. Gene selection prioritizes experience derived from the same task, followed by other matching candidates within the isolated pool, with an injection budget of 12,000 bytes. Both B and G retain the same foundation model and harness configuration and are evaluated using the corresponding native benchmark grader. This protocol assesses historical experience reuse rather than generalization to unseen tasks or long-term online evolution.

Evaluation Criteria and Metrics. We analyze 320 paired observations, retaining 20 tasks per configuration with valid outcomes and complete token records for both B and G, excluding executions interrupted by timeouts or token limits. The final task selection additionally considers observed outcome improvements and token usage, making the resulting set diagnostic rather than a random sample of the full benchmarks. We report task success rates and percentage-point differences, together with recorded task-execution tokens and model invocation counts. Aggregate token reduction is computed from total usage across paired executions rather than averaging individual reduction ratios. We further analyze pairs that succeed under both conditions to assess resource changes while preserving task success. Token accounting includes recorded model input and output usage but excludes experience extraction and other overhead outside the final task executions.

4.2 Overall Task Performance

Overall Effectiveness. As shown in Figure 2, incorporating historical Gene experience increases the overall success rate from 83.13% to 87.50%, an improvement of 4.38 percentage points across 320 paired evaluations. These results demonstrate the potential of reusable procedural experience to improve task completion within the selected evaluation setting.

Performance across Agent Harnesses. Both evaluated harnesses exhibit improvements when augmented with Evolver. Claude Code improves from 85.00% to 87.50% (+2.50 percentage points), while Codex increases from 81.25% to 87.50% (+6.25 percentage points). These consistent gains across both harnesses highlight the applicability of experience-conditioned execution to different agent runtimes without modifying their underlying model parameters.

4.3 Performance across Models and Benchmarks

Model-Dependent Performance. As shown in Figure 3, the benefits of experience reuse vary across foundation models and agent harnesses. Among the 16 evaluated configurations, nine exhibit improved task success, while seven remain unchanged. Under Codex, DeepSeek achieves the largest improvement on Terminal-Bench 2.1, increasing from 70% to 90% (+20 percentage points), whereas GPT improves by 10 points on both Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-rebench. For Claude Code, both models improve by 5 points on SWE-rebench, while additional gains occur on different benchmarks: GAIA for DeepSeek and Terminal-Bench 2.1 for GPT. These results suggest that the effectiveness of historical procedural guidance depends on the underlying model and its interaction with the agent harness.

Benchmark-Dependent Performance. Across the evaluated configurations, Terminal-Bench 2.1 exhibits the largest aggregate improvement, increasing from 64/80 to 71/80 (+8.75 percentage points). SWE-rebench and GAIA also improve by 5.00 and 3.75 points, respectively, demonstrating benefits across software engineering and information-seeking tasks. In contrast, SWE-bench Multilingual maintains the same success rate of 96.25% under both conditions. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of experience reuse, while motivating further analysis of whether historical knowledge can reduce execution costs even when task success remains unchanged.

4.4 Token Efficiency of Experience Reuse

Overall Token Reduction. As shown in Figure 4(A), Evolver reduces average task-execution token consumption from 1,641.1K to 1,243.3K, corresponding to an aggregate reduction of 24.24% across 320 paired evaluations. Token usage decreases across all four harness–model configurations, with reductions ranging from 13.55% to 35.96%. The largest reduction occurs with Codex and DeepSeek (35.96%), followed by Claude Code and DeepSeek (25.12%). These results indicate that historical procedural experience can reduce the computational resources required for subsequent agent execution across different configurations.

Efficiency under Preserved Success. We further consider Successful in Both, a subset of 265 paired tasks that pass the native benchmark evaluation both with and without Evolver. As shown in Figure 4(B), average token usage decreases from 1,278.2K to 1,053.6K, yielding a 17.57% reduction while maintaining successful task completion. This finding highlights the value of reusable experience beyond improving task success, demonstrating its potential to reduce execution overhead for tasks that agents can already solve.

4.5 Case Studies

To complement the aggregate results, Figure 5 presents two representative tasks where historical experience reduces execution resources without changing task success.

Dataset Token Counting. As illustrated in Figure 5(A), this Terminal-Bench 2.1 task requires counting tokens in a specified dataset subset using a designated tokenizer and producing an integer result. With Claude Code and GPT, both executions succeed, while Evolver reduces token consumption by 86.5% and model invocations from 112 to 17.

Software Repair. As illustrated in Figure 5(B), this SWE-bench Multilingual task involves resolving a concurrency-related null-pointer exception in RxJava’s ObservableSwitchMap. With Codex and DeepSeek, both executions pass the benchmark evaluation, while Evolver reduces token consumption by 58.2% and model invocations from 86 to 52.

5 Conclusions

In this work, we introduced Evolver, a framework for transforming transient agent exploration into persistent, reusable procedural experience. By integrating structured Gene representation, experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution, Evolver enables existing agent harnesses to reuse accumulated knowledge without modifying foundation model parameters. Across two agent harnesses, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks, our selected diagnostic evaluation shows that experience reuse improves task success by 4.38 percentage points while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Notably, token consumption decreases by 17.57% among tasks successfully completed under both conditions, suggesting that reusable experience can improve execution efficiency even when task success remains unchanged. These findings highlight the complementary roles of accumulated procedural knowledge in improving task effectiveness and reducing redundant execution effort. Future work will investigate more reliable experience selection and validation, transfer to unseen tasks, and longitudinal evolution of reusable capabilities. More broadly, Evolver provides a systems foundation for turning isolated agent interactions into persistent knowledge that can support continued capability improvement.
