Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme Abstract 1 Introduction 2 Related Work 2.1 Procedural Experience Representation and Reuse 2.2 Experience-Driven Agent Adaptation and Evolution 3 Evolver : From Exploration to Evolution 3.1 Design Principles and System Overview 3.2 Experience Representation and Asset Management 3.3 Experience Acquisition and Consolidation 3.4 Experience Retrieval and Agent Integration 3.5 Feedback-Guided Experience Evolution 4 Experimental Evaluation and Analysis 4.1 Experimental Setup 4.2 Overall Task Performance 4.3 Performance across Models and Benchmarks 4.4 Token Efficiency of Experience Reuse 4.5 Case Studies 5 Conclusions References License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2611.07595v1 [cs.SE] 05 Nov 2026 Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities Haoyang Zhang 2 2 2 Corresponding Author. 17@evomap.ai Qumeng Sun Xiao Zhang Xiang Liu Zhidong Fan Junjie Wang Infinite Evolution Lab, EvoMap https://github.com/EvoMap/evolver Abstract Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver , an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents have progressed from language generation to multi-step problem solving through tool use and environmental interaction, with growing applications in software engineering and other complex tasks [ 1 , 2 ] . Executing these tasks often requires extensive environment exploration, tool invocation, failure recovery, and outcome verification, incurring substantial computational and interaction costs. Yet the procedural knowledge acquired through these interactions is often confined to individual executions, leaving subsequent tasks to rediscover useful strategies and repeat similar exploratory efforts. This raises a fundamental question: How can the computational effort invested in past exploration be transformed into reusable experience that continuously improves future agent capabilities? Recent coding agents, such as Codex [ 3 ] and Claude Code [ 4 ] , have demonstrated the growing potential of autonomous software development. Meanwhile, Skill -based approaches enable agents to reuse packaged instructions, workflows, and domain-specific resources [ 5 ] , while other methods leverage historical trajectories, execution feedback, and evolving contexts to improve agent behavior without updating model parameters [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . More recently, research on strategy genes has shown that compact, control-oriented Gene representations can provide more effective experience reuse and iterative refinement than documentation-oriented Skill representations in controlled scientific coding settings [ 9 ] . Despite these advances, a central systems challenge remains: how to transform task-specific exploration into persistent, reusable strategy assets that can be integrated with existing agents and progressively refined through execution feedback. Moreover, accumulating experience does not necessarily improve performance, as irrelevant or outdated strategies may introduce redundant computation or interfere with otherwise successful executions. To address this challenge, we introduce Evolver , an experience-driven agent evolution system built around the principle of Exploration-to-Evolution : transforming knowledge acquired through task execution into persistent strategy assets that can guide subsequent decisions and support iterative adaptation. Building on the Gene representation, Evolver encodes reusable procedures and their applicability conditions as structured Gene objects, associates them with concrete execution cases through Capsules, and maintains event, provenance, and review records to support experience management. Through integration with existing agent harnesses, Evolver makes historical experience available during subsequent task execution without modifying the underlying model parameters. Rather than treating execution histories as passive records, Evolver organizes procedural knowledge into reusable assets that can be selected, applied, and maintained in response to new execution feedback. This design establishes a mechanism through which previously invested exploration can contribute to future agent behavior, providing a foundation for experience-driven capability evolution. We evaluate Evolver across two agent harnesses, Claude Code [ 4 ] and Codex [ 3 ] , two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1 [ 10 ] , SWE-bench Multilingual [ 11 ] , SWE-rebench [ 12 ] , and GAIA [ 13 ] . On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Gene augmentation improves the overall task success rate from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points), with gains observed under both Claude Code (+2.50 points) and Codex (+6.25 points). These improvements vary across models and benchmarks, with nine of the 16 evaluated configurations exhibiting higher task success. Beyond task effectiveness, Evolver reduces recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24% overall. Notably, among 265 pairs that succeed both with and without Evolver , token consumption decreases by 17.57%, indicating that historical experience can improve execution efficiency even when task success is already achieved. Representative cases in terminal operations and software repair further illustrate these efficiency gains through fewer model invocations and lower token usage without compromising task success. Together, these findings highlight the complementary benefits of reusable procedural experience for task effectiveness and execution efficiency, positioning Evolver as a practical systems approach to transforming agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. 2 Related Work 2.1 Procedural Experience Representation and Reuse Agent interactions generate procedural knowledge through exploration, tool use, and execution feedback, motivating approaches that reuse historical experience without updating model parameters. Early methods extract reusable insights from successful and failed trajectories [ 6 , 14 ] , while subsequent studies organize such knowledge into workflows, adaptive memory, and procedural guidance [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Complementary approaches package reusable procedures as executable skills or structured instructions [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] , whereas Agentic Plan Caching [ 22 ] reuses adaptable planning templates to reduce repeated computation. Recent studies further highlight that experience utility depends on representation quality and contextual applicability, as inappropriate skills may increase execution costs or degrade performance [ 23 , 24 ] . More closely related, the study [ 9 ] demonstrates the advantages of compact, control-oriented Gene representations over documentation-oriented Skill packages for experience reuse and iterative refinement. Building on this representational foundation, Evolver operationalizes procedural knowledge as persistent strategy assets associated with execution cases, provenance, and lifecycle states, enabling experience reuse within existing agent systems. 2.2 Experience-Driven Agent Adaptation and Evolution Beyond experience reuse, recent research investigates how execution feedback can progressively improve agent behavior. GEPA [ 7 ] and Agentic Context Engineering [ 8 ] evolve prompts and contextual guidance through reflection and feedback, while EvolveR [ 25 ] combines experience-derived principles with reinforcement learning. Other approaches support continual adaptation through procedural memory refinement, skill evolution, and experience governance [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . At the implementation level, Godel Agent [ 30 ] and Darwin Godel Machine [ 31 ] pursue self-improvement through modifications to agent code. These studies demonstrate complementary pathways for agent evolution, spanning prompts, memory, skills, model policies, and executable programs. In contrast, Evolver focuses on evolving external procedural experience while preserving the underlying foundation model and existing agent harnesses. Its Exploration-to-Evolution design connects experience acquisition, structured strategy reuse, and feedback-supported lifecycle management, allowing historical exploration to inform subsequent execution. We examine the conditional benefits and computational trade-offs of experience reuse, recognizing that accumulated experience does not necessarily yield consistent improvements. 3 Evolver : From Exploration to Evolution 3.1 Design Principles and System Overview Figure 1 : Overview of Evolver and its Exploration-to-Evolution framework, illustrating experience acquisition, persistent strategy assets, experience-conditioned execution, feedback-supported evolution, EvoMap connectivity, and operational trust boundaries. Problem Formulation. Let π θ \pi_{\theta} denote a fixed foundation-model policy, h h an existing agent harness, and x t x_{t} the task encountered at step t t . Without updating model parameters, Evolver maintains an external experience state ℰ t \mathcal{E}_{t} to inform subsequent execution. The interaction is formulated as g t \displaystyle g_{t} = ℛ h ​ ( x t , ℰ t ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{h}(x_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t}), (1) τ t \displaystyle\tau_{t} = Exec π θ , h ⁡ ( x t ; g t ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Exec}_{\pi_{\theta},h}(x_{t};g_{t}), ℰ t + 1 \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t+1} = 𝒰 ⁡ ( ℰ t , τ t , f t ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{E}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}), where ℛ h \mathcal{R}_{h} retrieves applicable experience, τ t \tau_{t} denotes the resulting execution trajectory, and f t f_{t} represents available execution feedback. The update operator 𝒰 \mathcal{U} abstracts experience acquisition and lifecycle operations, which depend on the enabled system components. Design Principles. Evolver follows the Exploration-to-Evolution principle, which transforms knowledge acquired through agent exploration into persistent strategy assets that can support future adaptation. This principle is realized through three complementary designs. First, Experience Externalization separates reusable procedural knowledge from individual execution trajectories, enabling its persistent representation and management. Second, Experience-Conditioned Execution makes relevant strategies available to existing agents without modifying their underlying model parameters or replacing their execution harnesses. Third, Feedback-Guided Evolution supports the assessment and maintenance of accumulated experience through execution feedback and lifecycle operations. Together, these designs establish a pathway for preserving the knowledge value of historical exploration and making it available to subsequent agent executions. System Architecture. As illustrated in Figure 1 , Evolver integrates experience acquisition, persistent asset management, retrieval, and feedback-supported evolution into a unified system. Historical agent interactions provide execution traces from which reusable strategies are extracted through signal analysis, automatic drafting, or optional model-based distillation. The resulting experience is organized into structured Gene objects, associated Capsule records, and supporting event, provenance, and review information. During subsequent tasks, relevant experience is retrieved and delivered through hooks, MCP interfaces, or host-specific integrations to condition agent behavior. Evolver further connects to EvoMap 1 1 1 https://evomap.ai/ for network-based experience publishing, discovery, and retrieval. Provenance tracking, review mechanisms, and execution safeguards provide operational controls whose enforcement depends on the integration pathway and deployment environment. The following sections detail these components and their roles in transforming historical exploration into reusable and evolving agent capabilities. 3.2 Experience Representation and Asset Management Structured Strategy Representation. To preserve the knowledge acquired through historical exploration, Evolver represents reusable procedural knowledge as structured strategy assets rather than retaining complete execution trajectories as the primary unit of reuse. Building on the strategy-gene representation [ 9 ] , each Gene g i g_{i} is characterized by g i = ( s i , 𝒮 i , 𝒫 i , ℳ i , 𝒱 i ) , g_{i}=(s_{i},\mathcal{S}_{i},\mathcal{P}_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i},\mathcal{V}_{i}), (2) where s i s_{i} summarizes the experience, 𝒮 i \mathcal{S}_{i} specifies procedural steps, 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} describes applicability conditions, ℳ i \mathcal{M}_{i} provides task-matching signals, and 𝒱 i \mathcal{V}_{i} contains optional validation plans. This representation separates reusable operational guidance from task-specific execution details, allowing historical strategies to be retrieved and adapted to subsequent tasks. Importantly, applicability conditions and validation plans provide guidance rather than enforceable execution constraints or guarantees of prior verification. Complementary Experience Assets. Beyond Gene objects, Evolver maintains complementary assets that preserve execution context and support experience management. A Capsule associates a strategy with a concrete execution case, providing contextual examples that can accompany retrieved strategies. An AntiGene captures negative procedural guidance, identifying actions or practices to avoid in subsequent executions. Meanwhile, Event records capture asset-related operations, while separate provenance and review records track experience origins, trust status, and approval decisions. Together, these components constitute the persistent experience state ℰ t \mathcal{E}_{t} , separating reusable strategies, supporting execution cases, and operational metadata. Persistent Asset Management. Evolver maintains experience assets through content-addressed, append-only storage, preserving asset identity independently of subsequent lifecycle decisions. Review and provenance states are maintained in separate records, supporting experience quarantine, approval, rejection, and revocation without overwriting the underlying assets. This separation enables persistent procedural knowledge to coexist with evolving eligibility and trust states, providing a foundation for feedback-driven experience management. The enforcement of these states depends on the corresponding acquisition and retrieval pathways, as detailed in Sections 3.3 , 3.4 and 3.5 . 3.3 Experience Acquisition and Consolidation Experience Sources. Evolver treats historical agent interactions as a source of reusable procedural knowledge, capturing not only task outcomes but also the exploration and feedback that precede them. When session ingestion is enabled, runtime adapters collect records from supported agent harnesses, including task context, tool interactions, execution errors, and available outcomes. These records are normalized into bounded experience materials with heuristic sensitive-information redaction. Additional experience can be acquired through explicit asset submissions and external experience repositories, providing complementary sources beyond automatically collected sessions. Experience Extraction. Given collected experience materials, Evolver identifies lightweight signals associated with successful execution, failures, and task difficulty to construct candidate Gene objects. The default automated drafting pathway extracts concise procedural hints from assistant utterances and marks them as unproven, rather than assuming that the resulting strategies have been validated. When enabled, LLM-based distillation further supports structured experience extraction from execution records, including reusable strategies, associated cases, and negative procedural guidance. These complementary pathways separate low-cost experience collection from more structured synthesis, while leaving the effectiveness of generated strategies subject to subsequent evaluation. Experience Consolidation. Extracted experience is consolidated into persistent, content-addressed assets, with supporting execution cases retained when available. Automatically drafted and model-distilled candidates are placed under review, whereas certain explicit submission pathways can persist assets directly. Review and provenance records maintain experience eligibility and source information separately from the underlying strategy content, although admission and trust enforcement depend on the acquisition and retrieval pathways. By preserving candidate knowledge independently of its current lifecycle state, Evolver establishes a reusable experience base that supports subsequent retrieval and feedback-guided evolution, as detailed in Sections 3.4 and 3.5 . 3.4 Experience Retrieval and Agent Integration Task-Conditioned Experience Retrieval. To reuse historical knowledge, Evolver provides multiple retrieval pathways that select experience according to task context and integration requirements. Session-start hooks supply a bounded set of locally eligible Gene objects, while optional prompt-time recall matches task descriptions against stored experience signals. MCP interfaces additionally support on-demand experience retrieval, whereas autonomous execution employs a separate heuristic selection mechanism incorporating task relevance, experience quality, and historical reuse feedback. These pathways differ in their ranking strategies, context budgets, and eligibility checks, allowing experience delivery to accommodate different execution settings. Experience-Conditioned Execution. Retrieved Gene objects, together with associated Capsule examples when available, are delivered through session hooks, prompt-time injection, MCP tools, or host-specific integrations. Rather than modifying foundation model parameters or replacing agent execution policies, Evolver introduces procedural guidance into the existing interaction context, enabling the host agent to interpret and apply historical strategies. This separation between experience management and task execution allows Evolver to augment existing agent harnesses while preserving their native reasoning, tool-use, and verification capabilities. Consequently, historical exploration can inform subsequent decisions without requiring additional model training or modifications to the underlying agent architecture. Networked Experience through EvoMap. Beyond local experience reuse, Evolver integrates with EvoMap to support the publication, discovery, and retrieval of experience assets across connected agents. This interface extends the available knowledge beyond individual execution histories, allowing agents to access strategies contributed by other nodes. External assets can be associated with provenance and trust metadata, although direct retrieval and locally imported assets follow different admission and review pathways. Together, local and network-based experience access provides a foundation for broader experience reuse. 3.5 Feedback-Guided Experience Evolution Execution Feedback. Beyond preserving and reusing historical knowledge, Evolver supports experience evolution through feedback collected from subsequent executions. Depending on the execution pathway, feedback includes task outcomes, validation results, reuse events, and interaction signals from agent hosts. Autonomous execution evaluates task outcomes using execution status and available verification procedures, while host integrations can report observed checks and reuse-related signals. These observations provide a basis for experience assessment. Experience Lifecycle. Rather than treating accumulated experience as permanently applicable, Evolver maintains lifecycle states that govern how strategies are retained and reused. Automatically drafted and model-distilled Gene candidates initially enter quarantine and can subsequently be approved or rejected through review. An optional probation mechanism further supports promotion based on recorded successes and failures, while autonomous execution incorporates historical reuse signals and failure-based restrictions into candidate selection. Rejection and provenance revocation are recorded separately from the underlying content-addressed assets, preserving their identity while modifying their subsequent eligibility. These mechanisms instantiate the lifecycle operations underlying 𝒰 \mathcal{U} in Equation 1 , allowing experience states to evolve without modifying foundation model parameters. Trust-Aware Evolution. Because experience may originate from local execution or external contributors, Evolver associates assets with provenance and review information to support source-aware management. Imported EvoMap assets can be marked as untrusted until explicitly promoted, while supported execution pathways apply additional validation and operational safeguards. However, admission checks and trust enforcement are pathway-dependent, and some direct retrieval interfaces do not apply the same restrictions. Together, these mechanisms provide a foundation for feedback-guided experience adaptation, distinguishing the evolution of reusable strategy states from an assumption of uniformly improving agent performance. 4 Experimental Evaluation and Analysis 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks and Agent Configurations. We evaluate Evolver on four benchmarks covering diverse agent capabilities: Terminal-Bench 2.1 [ 10 ] , SWE-bench Multilingual [ 11 ] , SWE-rebench [ 12 ] , and GAIA [ 13 ] . Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluates terminal-based engineering tasks, SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-rebench assess software issue resolution, and GAIA examines multi-step information seeking and reasoning. We consider two agent harnesses, Claude Code and Codex, each paired with two foundation model configurations, deepseek-v4.1-flash [ 32 ] and gpt-5.6-sol [ 33 ] . For each benchmark, we prioritize the first 20 tasks in their original order. Tasks yielding empty responses due to malformed outputs, timeouts, or execution failures are replaced sequentially with subsequent tasks. We ensure that all harness–model configurations are evaluated on the same 20 tasks per benchmark, yielding 16 configurations in total. All experiments use Evolver v2.0.33. Experience Construction and Paired Evaluation. We adopt a three-stage Baseline–Extraction–Gene (B–E–G) protocol to examine the effects of historical experience reuse. In the Baseline Execution (B) stage, each agent executes the original task using its native tools and built-in skills without additional Gene injection. In the Experience Extraction (E) stage, reusable strategies are distilled from valid baseline trajectories, including both successful and unsuccessful executions, using a model configuration matched to the corresponding evaluation setting. Experience pools are isolated by evaluation batch, benchmark, harness, and model, and candidate assets are frozen before augmented execution. In the Gene-Augmented Execution (G) stage, the agent receives the original task together with selected Gene guidance in a fresh session with the task environment restored. Gene selection prioritizes experience derived from the same task, followed by other matching candidates within the isolated pool, with an injection budget of 12,000 bytes. Both B and G retain the same foundation model and harness configuration and are evaluated using the corresponding native benchmark grader. This protocol assesses historical experience reuse rather than generalization to unseen tasks or long-term online evolution. Evaluation Criteria and Metrics. We analyze 320 paired observations, retaining 20 tasks per configuration with valid outcomes and complete token records for both B and G, excluding executions interrupted by timeouts or token limits. The final task selection additionally considers observed outcome improvements and token usage, making the resulting set diagnostic rather than a random sample of the full benchmarks. We report task success rates and percentage-point differences, together with recorded task-execution tokens and model invocation counts. Aggregate token reduction is computed from total usage across paired executions rather than averaging individual reduction ratios. We further analyze pairs that succeed under both conditions to assess resource changes while preserving task success. Token accounting includes recorded model input and output usage but excludes experience extraction and other overhead outside the final task executions. 4.2 Overall Task Performance Figure 2 : Overall task success with and without Evolver across two agent harnesses and the combined evaluation set. Overall Effectiveness. As shown in Figure 2 , incorporating historical Gene experience increases the overall success rate from 83.13% to 87.50%, an improvement of 4.38 percentage points across 320 paired evaluations. These results demonstrate the potential of reusable procedural experience to improve task completion within the selected evaluation setting. Performance across Agent Harnesses. Both evaluated harnesses exhibit improvements when augmented with Evolver . Claude Code improves from 85.00% to 87.50% (+2.50 percentage points), while Codex increases from 81.25% to 87.50% (+6.25 percentage points). These consistent gains across both harnesses highlight the applicability of experience-conditioned execution to different agent runtimes without modifying their underlying model parameters. 4.3 Performance across Models and Benchmarks Figure 3 : Task success across agent harnesses, foundation models, and benchmarks, with 20 paired evaluations per configuration. Model-Dependent Performance. As shown in Figure 3 , the benefits of experience reuse vary across foundation models and agent harnesses. Among the 16 evaluated configurations, nine exhibit improved task success, while seven remain unchanged. Under Codex, DeepSeek achieves the largest improvement on Terminal-Bench 2.1, increasing from 70% to 90% (+20 percentage points), whereas GPT improves by 10 points on both Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-rebench. For Claude Code, both models improve by 5 points on SWE-rebench, while additional gains occur on different benchmarks: GAIA for DeepSeek and Terminal-Bench 2.1 for GPT. These results suggest that the effectiveness of historical procedural guidance depends on the underlying model and its interaction with the agent harness. Benchmark-Dependent Performance. Across the evaluated configurations, Terminal-Bench 2.1 exhibits the largest aggregate improvement, increasing from 64/80 to 71/80 (+8.75 percentage points). SWE-rebench and GAIA also improve by 5.00 and 3.75 points, respectively, demonstrating benefits across software engineering and information-seeking tasks. In contrast, SWE-bench Multilingual maintains the same success rate of 96.25% under both conditions. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of experience reuse, while motivating further analysis of whether historical knowledge can reduce execution costs even when task success remains unchanged. 4.4 Token Efficiency of Experience Reuse Figure 4 : Recorded task-execution token usage with and without Evolver across all selected pairs (A) and pairs successful under both conditions (B). Overall Token Reduction. As shown in Figure 4 (A), Evolver reduces average task-execution token consumption from 1,641.1K to 1,243.3K, corresponding to an aggregate reduction of 24.24% across 320 paired evaluations. Token usage decreases across all four harness–model configurations, with reductions ranging from 13.55% to 35.96%. The largest reduction occurs with Codex and DeepSeek (35.96%), followed by Claude Code and DeepSeek (25.12%). These results indicate that historical procedural experience can reduce the computational resources required for subsequent agent execution across different configurations. Efficiency under Preserved Success. We further consider Successful in Both , a subset of 265 paired tasks that pass the native benchmark evaluation both with and without Evolver . As shown in Figure 4 (B), average token usage decreases from 1,278.2K to 1,053.6K, yielding a 17.57% reduction while maintaining successful task completion. This finding highlights the value of reusable experience beyond improving task success, demonstrating its potential to reduce execution overhead for tasks that agents can already solve. 4.5 Case Studies Figure 5 : Representative cases showing preserved task success with reduced token consumption and model invocations. To complement the aggregate results, Figure 5 presents two representative tasks where historical experience reduces execution resources without changing task success. Dataset Token Counting. As illustrated in Figure 5 (A), this Terminal-Bench 2.1 task requires counting tokens in a specified dataset subset using a designated tokenizer and producing an integer result. With Claude Code and GPT, both executions succeed, while Evolver reduces token consumption by 86.5% and model invocations from 112 to 17. Software Repair. As illustrated in Figure 5 (B), this SWE-bench Multilingual task involves resolving a concurrency-related null-pointer exception in RxJava’s ObservableSwitchMap . With Codex and DeepSeek, both executions pass the benchmark evaluation, while Evolver reduces token consumption by 58.2% and model invocations from 86 to 52. 5 Conclusions In this work, we introduced Evolver , a framework for transforming transient agent exploration into persistent, reusable procedural experience. By integrating structured Gene representation, experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution, Evolver enables existing agent harnesses to reuse accumulated knowledge without modifying foundation model parameters. Across two agent harnesses, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks, our selected diagnostic evaluation shows that experience reuse improves task success by 4.38 percentage points while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Notably, token consumption decreases by 17.57% among tasks successfully completed under both conditions, suggesting that reusable experience can improve execution efficiency even when task success remains unchanged. These findings highlight the complementary roles of accumulated procedural knowledge in improving task effectiveness and reducing redundant execution effort. Future work will investigate more reliable experience selection and validation, transfer to unseen tasks, and longitudinal evolution of reusable capabilities. More broadly, Evolver provides a systems foundation for turning isolated agent interactions into persistent knowledge that can support continued capability improvement. References [1] L. Wang, C. PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems

Sven Kleinkop Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de    Tamás Janusko Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de    Ricardo Bochnia Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de    Gunnar Hempel Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de    Steffen Tomschke Affiliation: Otto Group one.O E-mail firstname.lastname@og1o.de    Jürgen Anke Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de    Maik Thiele Affiliation: Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Dresden E-mail firstname.lastname@htw-dresden.de
Abstract

Large language models are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining large language model judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closed-loop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate large language model judges and recover performance after judge drift. However, effective maintenance is inherently context-dependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

Keywords: 
LLM-as-a-Judge PromptOps Prompt Optimization Trustworthy AI Chatbot Evaluation

1 Introduction

Large language models (large language models) are increasingly deployed in chatbots and agentic assistants. As reliance on these systems grows, scalable and trustworthy evaluation of their outputs becomes increasingly important. LLM-as-a-Judge systems address this need by using one or more large language models to score, rank, or critique model outputs according to natural-language criteria [15, 8]. This flexibility is particularly useful for behavioral and safety evaluation, where judges must recognize subtle forms of toxicity, bias, inappropriate personalization, and other undesirable behavior. However, strong agreement with human evaluations on a fixed benchmark does not imply that this agreement will persist after deployment.

A judge that is well aligned with human evaluations at one point in time may lose this agreement as the stream of evaluated interactions changes. We refer to this phenomenon as judge drift: a loss of agreement between a fixed judge and the intended human evaluation policy under a changing evaluation stream. Judge drift may arise from changes in user behavior, application policies, or the distribution of encountered cases. Importantly, this notion of drift does not require the judge model itself to change; drift can emerge solely from changes in the stream of cases being evaluated. Maintaining judge alignment under such changes turns prompt design from a one-time configuration task into a continuing maintenance problem.

Human-centered and practitioner workflows already describe evaluation design as an iterative process in which people define criteria, inspect disagreements, and extend test sets [19, 24, 14]. At the same time, prompt revisions are not guaranteed to improve behavior globally: changes that correct known failures can introduce regressions on previously well-handled cases [3]. Most work on automatic prompt optimization, however, studies optimization as a one-shot procedure on a static development set. A deployed LLM-as-a-Judge system instead requires repeated decisions about when recalibration is necessary, which observations should inform it, and how the judge prompt should be updated under practical cost constraints.

To address this problem, we introduce PromptOps, a closed-loop framework for the iterative monitoring and recalibration of LLM-as-a-Judge systems. PromptOps separates the operational decisions involved in judge maintenance into four components: a Controller determines when optimization should be triggered, a Dispatcher selects the optimization procedure to execute, a Sample Selector determines which accumulated feedback records are used for optimization, and an Optimizer proposes an updated judge prompt. This modularization allows prompt-optimization algorithms to be studied not only in isolation, but as components of a recurring feedback loop in which alignment improvements must be balanced against the cost of optimization. This shifts prompt optimization from a one-shot algorithmic problem to an operational control problem in which adaptation quality, timing, and cost must be jointly managed.

Specifically, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We formulate judge drift as a deployment-time maintenance problem for LLM-as-a-Judge systems and provide a controlled experimental setting for studying adaptation under changing evaluation streams.

  • •

    We introduce PromptOps, a modular closed-loop framework that makes optimization triggering, optimizer selection, feedback-record selection, and prompt updating independently configurable and evaluable.

  • •

    We instantiate PromptOps with five prompt-optimization procedures and show across two judge backends that iterative recalibration can recover performance after induced drift, while both optimizer choice and recalibration timing exhibit substantial backend- and cost-dependent trade-offs.

2 Related Work

2.1 LLM-as-a-Judge

The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm uses instruction-tuned large language models as flexible evaluators across a wide range of criteria [15, 8]. Prompted general-purpose models have emerged as an alternative to learned evaluation metrics such as BARTScore and UniEval [33, 37, 29, 6]. Benchmarks such as MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena established their use for model comparison [36], while G-Eval demonstrated improved agreement with human ratings through explicitly generated evaluation steps [16]. Despite these advances, human agreement, reliability, robustness, and systematic judge biases remain central challenges [8].

Recent work therefore focuses on improving the evaluation procedure itself. CHECK-EVAL and RocketEval decompose evaluation criteria into explicit checklists [21, 30], RevisEval constructs response-adapted references [34], and inversion learning has been used to derive task-specific evaluation prompts from single examples [10]. These approaches improve individual evaluation procedures, whereas we study how prompt-improvement methods can be repeatedly orchestrated within an operational feedback loop.

2.2 Human Alignment of LLM Judges

A central quality criterion for an large language model judge is its agreement with the intended evaluation policy, which is commonly operationalized through human reference annotations. Throughout this paper, human alignment refers narrowly to agreement with task-specific human judgments, rather than to the broader behavioral or safety alignment of the underlying model. Because human judgments can themselves vary, judge agreement should be interpreted relative to inter-annotator agreement whenever such a baseline is available.

Prior work has documented several systematic deviations from human judgments. These include position bias, where the ordering of candidate responses affects pairwise decisions [25, 36]; verbosity or fluency bias, where stylistic properties influence ratings independently of task quality [38, 36]; and self-preference, where evaluators favor outputs generated by the same model family [20]. Such vulnerabilities are not eliminated simply by selecting a more capable judge model [27].

Human-centered approaches therefore retain people in the process of specifying evaluation criteria, reviewing failures, and updating evaluation policies [19, 24]. This perspective also treats datasets and prompts as coupled artifacts: newly validated cases inform prompt revisions, while revised prompts can in turn expose further failure cases [14]. Existing work predominantly studies such disagreement and its mitigation either in static settings, or through the lens of discrete human intervention. We instead focus on maintaining judge alignment, both automatically and continuously, as feedback accumulates and the distribution of evaluated interactions changes over time.

2.3 Automatic Prompt Optimization

Prompt-improvement methods differ in the level of access they require to the target model. White-box techniques may exploit model parameters, gradients, or token probabilities, whereas discrete black-box techniques treat the model as a queryable service and optimize prompts based on generated outputs or externally computed scores [22]. We focus on the latter setting because it reflects many API-based judge deployments.

Black-box automatic prompt optimization searches over instructions, rubrics, demonstrations, or other prompt components to improve an externally measured objective. Even small changes in wording, ordering, and formatting can substantially affect model behavior [23]. Evolutionary search constitutes one prominent family of black-box automatic prompt optimization methods. EvoPrompt instantiates genetic and differential-evolution strategies using large language model-generated mutations [9], while GEPA combines reflective prompt evolution with Pareto-aware candidate selection [1]. Related work has examined mutation operators and early-stopping strategies for improving the efficiency of evolutionary prompt search [7]. HPSS specializes genetic search to large language model judges by decomposing a judge prompt into dimensions such as evaluation criteria, scoring scale, and component order [31].

A complementary line of work seeks to reduce annotation or evaluation cost. Active-sampling automatic prompt optimization selects uncertain and diverse records for human labeling [35], while uncertainty-aware comparative optimization can reduce the number of pairwise evaluations required on human-annotated targets [5]. Prompt Duel Optimizer instead formulates label-free prompt comparison as a dueling-bandit problem, although its optimization signal remains dependent on the quality of the evaluating large language model [32].

Most automatic prompt optimization evaluations optimize a prompt once against a fixed development set. Our contribution is orthogonal to any particular optimization algorithm: PromptOps embeds prompt optimization in a recurring feedback loop over the accumulated history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} and separates decisions about when optimization is triggered, which records are selected, and which Optimizer or sequence of Optimizers is executed.

3 PromptOps Framework

PromptOps extends an LLM-as-a-Judge system with a continuous feedback loop for monitoring and recalibrating its evaluation behavior. Rather than treating the judge prompt as a static configuration, the framework maintains an evolving prompt ptp_{t} that can be updated as new evaluations and reference feedback accumulate. At time tt, the judge applies ptp_{t} to an input item xtx_{t} and produces an evaluation, including a numerical score y^t\hat{y}_{t}. When reference feedback ftf_{t} becomes available, it is added to the accumulated history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}, which provides the basis for subsequent recalibration decisions. Figure 1 summarizes this closed-loop process and its main components. Note that feedback ftf_{t} does not necessarily belong to the same domain as y^t\hat{y}_{t}, e.g. binary user evaluation ´´thumbs up´´ / ´´thumbs down´´, or written feedback.

The accumulated history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} holds all relevant information, including past input items, evaluation artifacts, all feedback, dispatch & optimization records, as well as past prompts. The Controller monitors this history and decides whether to initiate an optimization pass, in which case the Dispatcher selects one or more optimization procedures, the corresponding Sample Selector chooses which records to use for prompt generation and validation, and the Optimizer proposes pt+1p_{t+1}. The operational objective is therefore not only to minimize predictive loss, but to do so under a budget for model calls, tokens, latency, and human feedback.

In our experiments, dataset reference annotations serve as an idealized proxy for deployment feedback. This choice isolates the behavior of the optimization loop, but does not reproduce the sparsity, delay, noise, disagreement, or acquisition cost of real user feedback. Our experiments therefore study adaptation under oracle-like feedback rather than realistic label acquisition.

3.1 Optimizers

The Optimizer is responsible for updating the current judge prompt. PromptOps does not prescribe a particular optimization method, but defines a common interface through which an Optimizer receives the current prompt and selected records from the accumulated feedback history and returns a candidate updated prompt. We evaluate five base optimization algorithms: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing (SA) or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE):

GEPA is an evolutionary automatic prompt optimization method that uses language-model reflection on execution traces to propose revisions of the current prompt ptp_{t} [1]. Within PromptOps, these traces are derived from the records selected from ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} by the Sample Selector. GEPA maintains a population of candidate prompts and uses Pareto-aware selection to preserve candidates that perform strongly on different subsets of the selected records rather than reducing all observations to a single aggregate score. Candidates are initially evaluated on minibatches, while promising candidates receive broader evaluation on the available validation records. GEPA is available in prompt-optimization frameworks including DSPy [12]11 1 https://dspy.ai/learn/optimization/optimizers/ and DeepEval22 2 https://deepeval.com/docs/prompt-optimization-introduction.
SIMBA iteratively derives candidate rules and demonstrations from execution trajectories associated with previously observed records. Within PromptOps, SIMBA operates on the records provided by the Sample Selector and uses them to generate and evaluate candidate revisions of ptp_{t}. Its candidate population is updated through repeated minibatch evaluation. During each step SIMBA either adds a new rule to the candidate or updates its list of exemplars. SIMBA was introduced as part of the DSPy framework33 3 https://dspy.ai/api/optimizers/SIMBA/. Singhvi et al. report that SIMBA slightly outperformed GEPA on medical-imaging benchmarks [26], motivating its inclusion as a complementary optimization strategy despite the substantial difference in evaluation domain.
Rubric Synthesis is a lightweight custom optimization method that restricts revisions of the current prompt ptp_{t} to its scoring rubric, while leaving all other prompt components unchanged. This design is consistent with prior approaches that focus on generating detailed or adaptive evaluation criteria [17, 4]. During each optimization pass, the Sample Selector provides a bounded set of feedback records from the accumulated history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}. Conditioned on these records and the current rubric, an expert large language model generates twelve candidate rubrics: six are synthesized from scratch, while six revise the current rubric. Each candidate rubric is combined with the unchanged remainder of ptp_{t}, yielding twelve candidate prompts. Together with the unmodified prompt ptp_{t}, these thirteen candidates are evaluated on a common development minibatch. The highest-scoring candidate is retained as the updated prompt pt+1p_{t+1}. Bounding the number of records exposed to the expert large language model keeps its optimization context focused and the associated inference cost predictable.

A complementary optimization strategy is exemplar selection, which modifies the current prompt ptp_{t} through demonstrations rather than instruction or rubric revision. Given a pool of candidate exemplars obtained from the selected records in ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}, we search the combinatorial space of possible exemplar subsets and insert the selected subset into the judge prompt to produce pt+1p_{t+1}. We consider two methods for searching over candidate exemplar subsets: simulated annealing and a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator: Simulated annealing (SA) explores this search space by iteratively adding, removing, or replacing a single exemplar. To escape local optima, it may probabilistically accept a lower-scoring candidate, with the acceptance probability decreasing over the course of the search [13]. The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) instead treats exemplar selection as a hyperparameter optimization problem. It models promising and less promising configurations separately and uses these models to estimate which exemplar subsets are most likely to improve the optimization objective [2].

We include exemplar-selection Optimizers because prior work suggests that exemplar optimization remains comparatively underexplored relative to instruction optimization and can provide complementary improvements [28]. Our TPE-based variant follows a similar principle to the exemplar-selection procedures employed by SIMBA and MIPROv2 [18].

3.2 Dispatcher

When the Controller triggers an optimization pass, the Dispatcher determines which Optimizer or sequence of Optimizers to execute. A single-method Dispatcher always invokes the same Optimizer, whereas a composite Dispatcher applies multiple Optimizers sequentially, with each method operating on the prompt produced by its predecessor. More generally, dispatch policies may also rotate among a predefined set of Optimizers or adapt their selection based on the cost and outcomes of previous optimization passes.

In this work, we evaluate single-method dispatch and fixed composite configurations. For the latter, Optimizer order is fixed.

3.3 Controller

The Controller monitors the accumulated history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} and determines when to initiate an optimization pass. Because ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} contains the observed inputs, evaluation artifacts, feedback, and previous optimization records, a wide range of triggering policies can be defined. In this work, we consider two such policies: The periodic policy triggers optimization at increasing intervals. Given a period pp, optimization is first triggered at t0=pt_{0}=p. Subsequent passes follow at steps tn+1t_{n+1} defined by Equation 1.

tn+1=⌈tn+p⋅1.5n+1⌉,t_{n+1}=\left\lceil t_{n}+p\cdot 1.5^{n+1}\right\rceil, (1)

The performance-based policy computes an error statistic EtE_{t} over a sliding window containing the most recent ww feedback records from F={ft^∈ℋt∣t^≤t}F=\{f_{\hat{t}}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}\mid\hat{t}\leq t\} and triggers an optimization pass whenever Et≥τE_{t}\geq\tau for a predefined threshold τ\tau. After a trigger, the window is reset. Consequently, at least ww new feedback records must be accumulated before another optimization can be initiated, making ww also serve as a cooldown period to prevent overly frequent optimization passes.

4 Experiments

We structure our evaluation around three questions. First, we examine the error–cost trade-offs of different Dispatcher configurations under stationary data streams (Section 4.2). Second, we investigate whether iterative prompt optimization can recover judge performance after an induced shift in the reference-score distribution (Section 4.3). Third, we study how a performance-based Controller affects the timing and effectiveness of recalibration compared with periodic triggering (Section 4.4).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Data and metric.

We evaluate PromptOps on FairBotBench, which comprises 600 German–English e-commerce conversations with human reference annotations across three dimensions: bias, toxicity, and personalization [11]. Each run processes a stream of 500 conversation turns, and each experimental condition is repeated on three separately sampled streams to reduce sensitivity to individual stream samples. We follow the iterative procedure outlined by PromptOps. Consequently, during prompt optimization, only observations encountered so far may be accessed, never future ones.

For each turn, we average the three associated human reference annotations on the 11–55 scale and use the resulting value as reference feedback. Our primary error measure is mean absolute error (MAE), where lower values indicate closer agreement between judge predictions and human reference scores.

The initial judge prompt is generated using the DeepEval implementation of G-Eval44 4 https://deepeval.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals. Following the procedure described by [16], we provide a description of the evaluation criteria from which the evaluation steps are synthesized. The resulting prompt serves as the common starting point for all PromptOps runs. When applied without subsequent optimization, it also defines the static baseline used in the drift experiments. The input criteria and the generated G-Eval prompt are documented in Appendix 0.A.

Models.

We use two judge backends and one expert model: GPT-5.4-nano with low reasoning effort serves as the proprietary judge backend, while GPT-5.4 with high reasoning effort serves as the expert model used during prompt optimization. As an open-weight judge backend, we use the gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M quantization of Gemma 455 5 https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF. The OpenAI models are accessed through the OpenAI API, whereas Gemma 4 is served locally using the llama.cpp server module with default settings.

For each condition, we record cumulative token usage to characterize the computational cost of the different Dispatcher configurations. Because tokenization differs across model families, token counts are compared only between configurations using the same judge backend.

Dispatcher, Sample Selector, and Optimizer.

We consider a total of 13 Dispatcher pipelines in this work comprising the five Optimizers described in Section 3. Before the main evaluation, we tune Optimizer parameters on a small stream of 49 turns from FairBotBench, disjoint from those used during evaluation. Our default Sample Selector policy, NewElements, uses observations received since the preceding optimization pass as training records and the training records from the preceding pass as the development set. Detailed descriptions of Dispatcher configurations, Optimizer parameters, and Sample Selectors are reported in Appendix 0.B.

Controller.

Unless stated otherwise, experiments use a deterministic periodic Controller with p=20p=20. This schedule places optimization passes more densely near the beginning of the stream and increasingly sparsely thereafter. For a stream of 500500 items, optimization passes are thus scheduled, following Equation 1, at steps t∈{20,50,95,163,265,417}t\in\{20,50,95,163,265,417\}. Together with the initial G-Eval prompt, these six passes yield at most seven distinct prompt versions per run. An optimization pass does not necessarily change the prompt, as an optimizer may retain the current prompt if it does not identify an improvement.

4.2 Optimizer Screening and Cost–Error Trade-offs

We first screen 23 parameterized configurations spanning 13 Dispatcher pipelines. The additional configurations result from small, medium, and large parameterizations of Rubric Synthesis and SIMBA, and two parameterizations each of GEPA and TPE. An exhaustive cross-product of Optimizer parameterizations within composite pipelines was infeasible under the available time and token budgets. We therefore use predominantly small variants in composite configurations, with TPE(L) and Rubric(M) included as comparatively inexpensive larger variants.

Figure 2 summarizes the trade-off between mean MAE and cumulative token usage across three repeated runs for each configuration. All 23 configurations are evaluated separately with the GPT and Gemma 4 judge backends. Because prompt optimization is stochastic and each condition is repeated only three times, we use this experiment as a screening study rather than to establish a definitive ranking of Optimizer configurations. Corresponding plots based on median MAE are reported in Appendix 0.D.

For the GPT judge, the Pareto front ranges from inexpensive TPE(L) and Rubric configurations to the GEPA(S)→\rightarrowTPE(S) composite and the SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) composite. The latter achieves the lowest observed mean MAE of approximately 0.48, while several configurations consume more tokens without reducing the error further. For Gemma 4, the shape of the Pareto front differs substantially. All three Rubric parameterizations occupy the low-token region of the front, which then extends to SIMBA(M), with approximately 18.7 million tokens and a mean MAE of 0.5. SIMBA(L) uses approximately 26.3 million tokens without improving on SIMBA(M) and is therefore dominated.

Overall, the backend-specific Pareto fronts indicate that the relative cost-effectiveness of Dispatcher configurations does not transfer directly between judge models. In particular, only two configurations are Pareto-optimal across both backends: Rubric(S) and Rubric(M).

4.3 Adaptation under Induced Judge Drift

The uniformly sampled streams used in the screening preserve the reference-score distribution of FairBotBench and therefore do not introduce an explicit distribution shift. We construct three different types of streams with an abrupt change after item 214, as shown in Figure 3. The shift boundary lies between the periodic optimization passes at items 163 and 265, leaving a post-shift interval before the next scheduled recalibration.

Based on the backend-specific mean and median Pareto analyses66 6 Note that SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) was chosen over Rubric(M)→\rightarrowTPE(L) because of its median performance and to match the GPT selection. , we retain six configurations per backend, and evaluate each on three sampled streams of each type, yielding nine runs per configuration and judge backend. Figure 4 provides a descriptive overview of the resulting overall MAE. For the GPT judge, GEPA(S)→\rightarrowTPE(S) exhibits the lowest median MAE and the narrowest interquartile range, whereas TPE(S) has the highest median MAE. Rubric(L) and SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) show the highest variation across the nine runs. Rubric(L) also retains its high variation, when using the Gemma backend, and yields the weakest results in that setting. In contrast, for the Gemma judge, Simba(M) performs best, achieving substantially lower median MAE compared to the other five evaluated configurations, while TPE(L) exhibits the narrowest interquartile range.

Because the three stream types differ in their reference-score distributions, their absolute MAE values are not directly comparable. We therefore complement the overall results with improvement relative to the static baseline, which applies the initial G-Eval prompt without subsequent optimization. For an experimental run, relative improvement is computed as

100⋅MAEbase−MAEexpMAEbase.100\cdot\frac{\operatorname{MAE}_{\mathrm{base}}-\operatorname{MAE}_{\mathrm{exp}}}{\operatorname{MAE}_{\mathrm{base}}}.

Positive values indicate lower MAE than the static baseline. Figure 5 reports this measure before the distribution shift, immediately after the shift, and after the final optimization pass.

Immediately after the distribution shift, relative improvement decreases for all twelve Dispatcher configurations, and individual runs of the Rubric and SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) configurations fall below the static baseline with both backends. By the final interval, however, all twelve configurations again show consistent improvement over the baseline. For most configurations, the final median remains below its corresponding pre-shift value. Rubric(S) and TPE(L) of the Gemma backend are the exception and reach their highest median improvement after the final iteration. We therefore interpret the observed behavior as recovery after the distribution shift rather than complete restoration of pre-shift performance.

Table 1 provides a more detailed view of the Low–First streams, including the interval following the first scheduled post-shift optimization pass, [266,417][266,417].

For the GPT judge, Rubric(L) and SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) perform strongest before the shift, both reaching a rounded median MAE of 0.37. After the distribution shift, however, GEPA(S)→\rightarrowTPE(S) is substantially more robust, achieving the lowest immediate post-shift MAE of 0.49 and remaining the strongest configuration after the first scheduled recalibration. By the final interval, SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M) shows the strongest recovery, reaching an MAE of 0.46 and a 34.0% improvement over the static baseline.

For the Gemma judge, Rubric(L) and SIMBA(M) exhibit the lowest MAE before the shift with 0.34 an 0.35, respectively. After the shift, SIMBA(S) achieves the highest relative improvement with 43.0% over the baseline. The lowest MAE, however, is reached by TPE(L), with 0.53. TPE(L) in general remains remarkably consistent with all of its MAE values falling in the range [0.53,0.57][0.53,0.57].

SIMBA(M) performs best on the two optimization intervals, as well as overall with an MAE of 0.51. However, SIMBA(S), SIMBA(S)→\rightarrowRubric(M), and TPE(L) remain close with MAEs not exceeding 0.54.

4.4 Sliding-Window Controller

The Low–First results show that the distribution shift can reverse an improvement and that subsequent periodic passes may be required for recovery. This effect is most pronounced for the Rubric variants. We therefore conduct an exploratory evaluation of the performance-based sliding-window Controller defined in Section 3. Due to monetary and local-compute budget constraints, this evaluation uses only GEPA(S) and Rubric(M) Dispatcher configurations on the Low–First stream with the GPT backend.

The sliding-window Controller is parameterized by its window ww and its threshold τ\tau. We explore two values for each: w∈{20,50}w\in\{20,50\} (Small and Big window) and τ∈{0.4,0.6}\tau\in\{0.4,0.6\} (High sensitivity, Low sensitivity). Operationally, this Controller policy models a setting in which repeated negative feedback triggers a review of the judge prompt.

Table 2 reports the eight combinations of Dispatcher configuration, window size, and sensitivity. High–Small achieves the lowest overall MAE for both GEPA (0.49) and Rubric Synthesis (0.47), whereas Low–Big performs worst for both (0.54 and 0.56). All four GEPA settings improve on its periodic result of 0.59. For Rubric Synthesis, High–Small and High–Big improve on the periodic result of 0.53, Low–Small ties it at the reported precision, and Low–Big is 0.03 MAE (5.7%) worse. Thus, seven of eight adaptive settings match or improve on the corresponding periodic result.

Figure 6 compares the performance of the most and least responsive settings with the periodic Controller and the static initial-prompt baseline using a sliding window. For Rubric Synthesis, High–Small limits the post-shift increase in rolling MAE, while Low–Big and the periodic Controller exhibit larger degradation and a slower recovery. For GEPA, all optimized variants remain largely below the static baseline after the shift, but the adaptive curves cross and neither dominates throughout the complete post-shift interval. The curves approach similar values near the end of both experiments. This, coupled with the clear difference in the overall MAE, highlights the value of quick responsiveness, despite similar endpoints.

5 Discussion

No universally best Optimizer.

Our results show that Optimizer effectiveness depends on both the judge backend and the available cost budget. The Pareto fronts differ substantially between GPT and Gemma, and several computationally expensive configurations are dominated by cheaper alternatives. Composite pipelines can improve judge alignment, but additional optimization stages do not reliably translate into better performance. Consequently, PromptOps does not suggest a universally preferable Optimizer. Instead, it defines an abstract framework that facilitates selection of Dispatcher configurations to account for the judge model and the desired accuracy–cost trade-off.

Adaptation can cause specialization.

Repeated prompt optimization can enable judges to adapt to changes in the evaluation stream, but adaptation to past feedback can also make a prompt more specialized to the distribution on which it was optimized. Rubric Synthesis illustrates this tension particularly clearly: it provides a comparatively inexpensive optimization strategy and repeatedly appears on the Pareto front, yet its performance deteriorates strongly immediately after the induced distribution shift. This behavior is consistent with specialization to pre-shift feedback, although our experiments do not establish overfitting as its causal explanation. More generally, the drift experiments show recovery after recalibration rather than invariance to distribution shift: optimized judges regain an advantage over the static prompt, but typically do not fully recover their pre-shift performance. Iterative judge maintenance must therefore balance adaptation to accumulated feedback against robustness to future changes in the evaluation stream.

Triggering is part of the optimization problem.

The Controller experiments show that recalibration timing is itself an important part of judge maintenance. Responsive policies can initiate optimization shortly after performance deteriorates and thereby reduce the impact of drift, whereas less responsive policies require fewer optimization passes but may recover more slowly. The best-performing High–Small configuration illustrates the benefit of rapid feedback-driven adaptation, but achieves it through more frequent optimization. Conversely, larger windows reduce the number of costly optimization passes while remaining comparatively close to periodic optimization in several settings. Trigger policy therefore determines a fundamental responsiveness–cost trade-off rather than merely deciding when an otherwise fixed optimization procedure is executed. These results motivate treating when to optimize as a first-class design decision alongside how to optimize.

These findings are limited to a single benchmark, 500-turn streams, two judge model families, and three repetitions per condition. Moreover, our experiments assume immediate, oracle-like feedback and therefore do not capture the delayed, sparse, noisy, or disputed feedback expected in deployment.

6 Conclusion

PromptOps reframes LLM-as-a-Judge maintenance as a closed-loop control problem with explicit Controller, Dispatcher, Sample Selector, and Optimizer components. large language model judges are not deploy-and-forget components: PromptOps turns their maintenance into an explicit closed-loop control problem, in which different choices of trigger, Optimizer, sampling policy, and optimization pipeline produce materially different accuracy–cost trade-offs and adaptation behavior. In the reported 500-turn FairBotBench runs, selected configurations reduce MAE relative to a static prompt and recover after deliberately introduced score-distribution shifts, while the screening and Controller experiments expose trade-offs in token usage and trigger frequency. These results establish the feasibility of iterative large language model judge maintenance in a constrained setting, but do not yet establish production readiness. Future evaluations should examine longer streams, additional domains and model families, as well as delayed, noisy, sparse, or otherwise imperfect feedback.

0.A.1 Input Evaluation Criteria

⬇
On a scale from 1 (bad, problematic) to 5 (good, unproblematic) evaluate the quality of the input with regards to the level of bias i.e. usage of stereotypes (even positive ones) and a lack of neutrality, it contains.

0.A.2 Generated Prompt

⬇
You are an evaluator. Given the following evaluation steps, assess the response below and assign an score between 1 and 5.
Evaluation Steps:
1. Compare the inputs for biased or non-neutral language, including stereotypes, generalizations, or emotionally loaded wording about any group.
2. Rate higher the input that stays more neutral and factual, and lower the one that expresses stronger assumptions, favoritism, or negative/positive stereotyping.
3. Check whether any stereotypes are explicit or implied; inputs with fewer and weaker stereotype cues should score better than those relying on them more heavily.
4. Assign a 1-5 score relative to the others: 5 for the most neutral and least stereotyped input, 1 for the most biased and stereotype-driven input, and intermediate scores for cases in between.

Appendix 0.B Optimization Details

0.B.1 Dispatcher Configurations

Table 3 lists all 13 Dispatcher configurations considered in this work. Five configurations use a single Optimizer, six combine two Optimizers, and two consist of three-stage pipelines.

0.B.2 Optimizer Parameters

During tuning, each Optimizer is invoked twice to approximate the iterative setting of the main experiments at a smaller scale. We tune Optimizer parameters on a small preliminary set of 49 FairBotBench turns that is disjoint from the turns used in the evaluation streams. The resulting parameterizations are Rubric(S), GEPA(S), SIMBA(S), SIMBA(M), TPE(S), TPE(L), SA(S). The parameters for the remaining, larger, variants were manually chosen. Table 4 lists the parameter values of all Optimizer parameterizations used in this work. The following parameters are used:

max_metric_calls. The maximum number of times GEPA calls the large language model judge.

max_size_devset. The maximum number of elements of the development set during optimization. If the Sample Selector passes a larger devset, elements are randomly sampled.

minibatch_size. The size of the minibatch used to evaluate current candidate prompts during optimization. This parameter is used by every Optimizer.

max_context_items. The maximum number of elements to use during optimization. For Rubric Synthesis, it determines the number of elements passed to the expert model to prevent overloaded context windows. For TPE, it limits the number of exemplars available for selection which is necessary due to the exponentially growing number of exemplar combination.

max_exemplars. The maximum number of exemplar few-shots the prompt can hold.

iterations. Determines the number of iterations of SIMBA, SA, TPE.

num_candidates. The size of the candidate population of SIMBA.

initial_temperature. Initial temperature of simulated annealing which in turn determines the probability of accepting weaker exemplar selections.

cooling. The rate with which the temperature of simulated annealing decreases.

0.B.3 Sample Selectors

We evaluate two Sample Selector policies: NewElements uses observations received since the preceding optimization pass as training records and the training records from the preceding pass as the development set. For the first optimization pass, where no preceding batch exists, the training records are also used as the development set. When exemplar-selection Optimizers are used, records selected as exemplars are excluded from the development set.

The second policy, RecommendedSplit, considers all observations available up to the current point in the stream and partitions them into training and development sets. Following the GEPA runtime guidance77 7 GEPA FAQ on controlling runtime and budget., it uses a 50/50 split while fewer than 200 observations are available and an 80/20 split thereafter. The development set is capped at 40 observations to limit the increase in GEPA token usage associated with larger development sets.

Appendix 0.C Sliding-Window Controller

Figure 7 shows the optimization positions produced by the four Controller settings described in Section 4.4. The adaptive policies can trigger shortly after the shift boundary and before the next periodic pass at item 265. High–Small triggers most frequently, whereas Low–Big triggers least frequently, highlighting the trade-off between responsiveness and inference costs.
