In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining large language model judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps , a closed-loop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate large language model judges and recover performance after judge drift. However, effective maintenance is inherently context-dependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process. Keywords: LLM-as-a-Judge PromptOps Prompt Optimization Trustworthy AI Chatbot Evaluation 1 Introduction Large language models (large language models) are increasingly deployed in chatbots and agentic assistants. As reliance on these systems grows, scalable and trustworthy evaluation of their outputs becomes increasingly important. LLM-as-a-Judge systems address this need by using one or more large language models to score, rank, or critique model outputs according to natural-language criteria [ 15 , 8 ] . This flexibility is particularly useful for behavioral and safety evaluation, where judges must recognize subtle forms of toxicity, bias, inappropriate personalization, and other undesirable behavior. However, strong agreement with human evaluations on a fixed benchmark does not imply that this agreement will persist after deployment. A judge that is well aligned with human evaluations at one point in time may lose this agreement as the stream of evaluated interactions changes. We refer to this phenomenon as judge drift : a loss of agreement between a fixed judge and the intended human evaluation policy under a changing evaluation stream. Judge drift may arise from changes in user behavior, application policies, or the distribution of encountered cases. Importantly, this notion of drift does not require the judge model itself to change; drift can emerge solely from changes in the stream of cases being evaluated. Maintaining judge alignment under such changes turns prompt design from a one-time configuration task into a continuing maintenance problem. Human-centered and practitioner workflows already describe evaluation design as an iterative process in which people define criteria, inspect disagreements, and extend test sets [ 19 , 24 , 14 ] . At the same time, prompt revisions are not guaranteed to improve behavior globally: changes that correct known failures can introduce regressions on previously well-handled cases [ 3 ] . Most work on automatic prompt optimization, however, studies optimization as a one-shot procedure on a static development set. A deployed LLM-as-a-Judge system instead requires repeated decisions about when recalibration is necessary, which observations should inform it, and how the judge prompt should be updated under practical cost constraints. To address this problem, we introduce PromptOps , a closed-loop framework for the iterative monitoring and recalibration of LLM-as-a-Judge systems. PromptOps separates the operational decisions involved in judge maintenance into four components: a Controller determines when optimization should be triggered, a Dispatcher selects the optimization procedure to execute, a Sample Selector determines which accumulated feedback records are used for optimization, and an Optimizer proposes an updated judge prompt. This modularization allows prompt-optimization algorithms to be studied not only in isolation, but as components of a recurring feedback loop in which alignment improvements must be balanced against the cost of optimization. This shifts prompt optimization from a one-shot algorithmic problem to an operational control problem in which adaptation quality, timing, and cost must be jointly managed. Specifically, we make the following contributions: • We formulate judge drift as a deployment-time maintenance problem for LLM-as-a-Judge systems and provide a controlled experimental setting for studying adaptation under changing evaluation streams. • We introduce PromptOps , a modular closed-loop framework that makes optimization triggering, optimizer selection, feedback-record selection, and prompt updating independently configurable and evaluable. • We instantiate PromptOps with five prompt-optimization procedures and show across two judge backends that iterative recalibration can recover performance after induced drift, while both optimizer choice and recalibration timing exhibit substantial backend- and cost-dependent trade-offs. 2 Related Work 2.1 LLM-as-a-Judge The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm uses instruction-tuned large language models as flexible evaluators across a wide range of criteria [ 15 , 8 ] . Prompted general-purpose models have emerged as an alternative to learned evaluation metrics such as BARTScore and UniEval [ 33 , 37 , 29 , 6 ] . Benchmarks such as MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena established their use for model comparison [ 36 ] , while G-Eval demonstrated improved agreement with human ratings through explicitly generated evaluation steps [ 16 ] . Despite these advances, human agreement, reliability, robustness, and systematic judge biases remain central challenges [ 8 ] . Recent work therefore focuses on improving the evaluation procedure itself. CHECK-EVAL and RocketEval decompose evaluation criteria into explicit checklists [ 21 , 30 ] , RevisEval constructs response-adapted references [ 34 ] , and inversion learning has been used to derive task-specific evaluation prompts from single examples [ 10 ] . These approaches improve individual evaluation procedures, whereas we study how prompt-improvement methods can be repeatedly orchestrated within an operational feedback loop. 2.2 Human Alignment of LLM Judges A central quality criterion for an large language model judge is its agreement with the intended evaluation policy, which is commonly operationalized through human reference annotations. Throughout this paper, human alignment refers narrowly to agreement with task-specific human judgments, rather than to the broader behavioral or safety alignment of the underlying model. Because human judgments can themselves vary, judge agreement should be interpreted relative to inter-annotator agreement whenever such a baseline is available. Prior work has documented several systematic deviations from human judgments. These include position bias, where the ordering of candidate responses affects pairwise decisions [ 25 , 36 ] ; verbosity or fluency bias, where stylistic properties influence ratings independently of task quality [ 38 , 36 ] ; and self-preference, where evaluators favor outputs generated by the same model family [ 20 ] . Such vulnerabilities are not eliminated simply by selecting a more capable judge model [ 27 ] . Human-centered approaches therefore retain people in the process of specifying evaluation criteria, reviewing failures, and updating evaluation policies [ 19 , 24 ] . This perspective also treats datasets and prompts as coupled artifacts: newly validated cases inform prompt revisions, while revised prompts can in turn expose further failure cases [ 14 ] . Existing work predominantly studies such disagreement and its mitigation either in static settings, or through the lens of discrete human intervention. We instead focus on maintaining judge alignment, both automatically and continuously, as feedback accumulates and the distribution of evaluated interactions changes over time. 2.3 Automatic Prompt Optimization Prompt-improvement methods differ in the level of access they require to the target model. White-box techniques may exploit model parameters, gradients, or token probabilities, whereas discrete black-box techniques treat the model as a queryable service and optimize prompts based on generated outputs or externally computed scores [ 22 ] . We focus on the latter setting because it reflects many API-based judge deployments. Black-box automatic prompt optimization searches over instructions, rubrics, demonstrations, or other prompt components to improve an externally measured objective. Even small changes in wording, ordering, and formatting can substantially affect model behavior [ 23 ] . Evolutionary search constitutes one prominent family of black-box automatic prompt optimization methods. EvoPrompt instantiates genetic and differential-evolution strategies using large language model-generated mutations [ 9 ] , while GEPA combines reflective prompt evolution with Pareto-aware candidate selection [ 1 ] . Related work has examined mutation operators and early-stopping strategies for improving the efficiency of evolutionary prompt search [ 7 ] . HPSS specializes genetic search to large language model judges by decomposing a judge prompt into dimensions such as evaluation criteria, scoring scale, and component order [ 31 ] . A complementary line of work seeks to reduce annotation or evaluation cost. Active-sampling automatic prompt optimization selects uncertain and diverse records for human labeling [ 35 ] , while uncertainty-aware comparative optimization can reduce the number of pairwise evaluations required on human-annotated targets [ 5 ] . Prompt Duel Optimizer instead formulates label-free prompt comparison as a dueling-bandit problem, although its optimization signal remains dependent on the quality of the evaluating large language model [ 32 ] . Most automatic prompt optimization evaluations optimize a prompt once against a fixed development set. Our contribution is orthogonal to any particular optimization algorithm: PromptOps embeds prompt optimization in a recurring feedback loop over the accumulated history ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} and separates decisions about when optimization is triggered, which records are selected, and which Optimizer or sequence of Optimizers is executed. 3 PromptOps Framework Figure 1 : Overview of PromptOps as a closed-loop extension of an LLM judge. At time t t , the judge evaluates input item x t x_{t} using prompt p t p_{t} and produces evaluation y ^ t \hat{y}_{t} . When reference feedback f t f_{t} is available, the resulting error e t e_{t} and all evaluation artifacts are accumulated in history H t H_{t} . The Controller monitors this history, while the Dispatcher, Sample Selector, and Optimizer determine whether and how a new prompt p t + 1 p_{t+1} is produced. PromptOps extends an LLM-as-a-Judge system with a continuous feedback loop for monitoring and recalibrating its evaluation behavior. Rather than treating the judge prompt as a static configuration, the framework maintains an evolving prompt p t p_{t} that can be updated as new evaluations and reference feedback accumulate. At time t t , the judge applies p t p_{t} to an input item x t x_{t} and produces an evaluation, including a numerical score y ^ t \hat{y}_{t} . When reference feedback f t f_{t} becomes available, it is added to the accumulated history ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} , which provides the basis for subsequent recalibration decisions. Figure 1 summarizes this closed-loop process and its main components. Note that feedback f t f_{t} does not necessarily belong to the same domain as y ^ t \hat{y}_{t} , e.g. binary user evaluation ´´thumbs up´´ / ´´thumbs down´´, or written feedback. The accumulated history ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} holds all relevant information, including past input items, evaluation artifacts, all feedback, dispatch & optimization records, as well as past prompts. The Controller monitors this history and decides whether to initiate an optimization pass, in which case the Dispatcher selects one or more optimization procedures, the corresponding Sample Selector chooses which records to use for prompt generation and validation, and the Optimizer proposes p t + 1 p_{t+1} . The operational objective is therefore not only to minimize predictive loss, but to do so under a budget for model calls, tokens, latency, and human feedback. In our experiments, dataset reference annotations serve as an idealized proxy for deployment feedback. This choice isolates the behavior of the optimization loop, but does not reproduce the sparsity, delay, noise, disagreement, or acquisition cost of real user feedback. Our experiments therefore study adaptation under oracle-like feedback rather than realistic label acquisition. 3.1 Optimizers The Optimizer is responsible for updating the current judge prompt. PromptOps does not prescribe a particular optimization method, but defines a common interface through which an Optimizer receives the current prompt and selected records from the accumulated feedback history and returns a candidate updated prompt. We evaluate five base optimization algorithms: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing (SA) or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE): GEPA is an evolutionary automatic prompt optimization method that uses language-model reflection on execution traces to propose revisions of the current prompt p t p_{t} [ 1 ] . Within PromptOps , these traces are derived from the records selected from ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} by the Sample Selector. GEPA maintains a population of candidate prompts and uses Pareto-aware selection to preserve candidates that perform strongly on different subsets of the selected records rather than reducing all observations to a single aggregate score. Candidates are initially evaluated on minibatches, while promising candidates receive broader evaluation on the available validation records. GEPA is available in prompt-optimization frameworks including DSPy [ 12 ] 1 1 1 https://dspy.ai/learn/optimization/optimizers/ and DeepEval 2 2 2 https://deepeval.com/docs/prompt-optimization-introduction . SIMBA iteratively derives candidate rules and demonstrations from execution trajectories associated with previously observed records. Within PromptOps , SIMBA operates on the records provided by the Sample Selector and uses them to generate and evaluate candidate revisions of p t p_{t} . Its candidate population is updated through repeated minibatch evaluation. During each step SIMBA either adds a new rule to the candidate or updates its list of exemplars. SIMBA was introduced as part of the DSPy framework 3 3 3 https://dspy.ai/api/optimizers/SIMBA/ . Singhvi et al. report that SIMBA slightly outperformed GEPA on medical-imaging benchmarks [ 26 ] , motivating its inclusion as a complementary optimization strategy despite the substantial difference in evaluation domain. Rubric Synthesis is a lightweight custom optimization method that restricts revisions of the current prompt p t p_{t} to its scoring rubric, while leaving all other prompt components unchanged. This design is consistent with prior approaches that focus on generating detailed or adaptive evaluation criteria [ 17 , 4 ] . During each optimization pass, the Sample Selector provides a bounded set of feedback records from the accumulated history ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} . Conditioned on these records and the current rubric, an expert large language model generates twelve candidate rubrics: six are synthesized from scratch, while six revise the current rubric. Each candidate rubric is combined with the unchanged remainder of p t p_{t} , yielding twelve candidate prompts. Together with the unmodified prompt p t p_{t} , these thirteen candidates are evaluated on a common development minibatch. The highest-scoring candidate is retained as the updated prompt p t + 1 p_{t+1} . Bounding the number of records exposed to the expert large language model keeps its optimization context focused and the associated inference cost predictable. A complementary optimization strategy is exemplar selection, which modifies the current prompt p t p_{t} through demonstrations rather than instruction or rubric revision. Given a pool of candidate exemplars obtained from the selected records in ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} , we search the combinatorial space of possible exemplar subsets and insert the selected subset into the judge prompt to produce p t + 1 p_{t+1} . We consider two methods for searching over candidate exemplar subsets: simulated annealing and a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator: Simulated annealing (SA) explores this search space by iteratively adding, removing, or replacing a single exemplar. To escape local optima, it may probabilistically accept a lower-scoring candidate, with the acceptance probability decreasing over the course of the search [ 13 ] . The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) instead treats exemplar selection as a hyperparameter optimization problem. It models promising and less promising configurations separately and uses these models to estimate which exemplar subsets are most likely to improve the optimization objective [ 2 ] . We include exemplar-selection Optimizers because prior work suggests that exemplar optimization remains comparatively underexplored relative to instruction optimization and can provide complementary improvements [ 28 ] . Our TPE-based variant follows a similar principle to the exemplar-selection procedures employed by SIMBA and MIPROv2 [ 18 ] . 3.2 Dispatcher When the Controller triggers an optimization pass, the Dispatcher determines which Optimizer or sequence of Optimizers to execute. A single-method Dispatcher always invokes the same Optimizer, whereas a composite Dispatcher applies multiple Optimizers sequentially, with each method operating on the prompt produced by its predecessor. More generally, dispatch policies may also rotate among a predefined set of Optimizers or adapt their selection based on the cost and outcomes of previous optimization passes. In this work, we evaluate single-method dispatch and fixed composite configurations. For the latter, Optimizer order is fixed. 3.3 Controller The Controller monitors the accumulated history ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} and determines when to initiate an optimization pass. Because ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} contains the observed inputs, evaluation artifacts, feedback, and previous optimization records, a wide range of triggering policies can be defined. In this work, we consider two such policies: The periodic policy triggers optimization at increasing intervals. Given a period p p , optimization is first triggered at t 0 = p t_{0}=p . Subsequent passes follow at steps t n + 1 t_{n+1} defined by Equation 1 . t n + 1 = ⌈ t n + p ⋅ 1.5 n + 1 ⌉ , t_{n+1}=\left\lceil t_{n}+p\cdot 1.5^{n+1}\right\rceil, (1) The performance-based policy computes an error statistic E t E_{t} over a sliding window containing the most recent w w feedback records from F = { f t ^ ∈ ℋ t ∣ t ^ ≤ t } F=\{f_{\hat{t}}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}\mid\hat{t}\leq t\} and triggers an optimization pass whenever E t ≥ τ E_{t}\geq\tau for a predefined threshold τ \tau . After a trigger, the window is reset. Consequently, at least w w new feedback records must be accumulated before another optimization can be initiated, making w w also serve as a cooldown period to prevent overly frequent optimization passes. 4 Experiments We structure our evaluation around three questions. First, we examine the error–cost trade-offs of different Dispatcher configurations under stationary data streams ( Section 4.2 ). Second, we investigate whether iterative prompt optimization can recover judge performance after an induced shift in the reference-score distribution ( Section 4.3 ). Third, we study how a performance-based Controller affects the timing and effectiveness of recalibration compared with periodic triggering ( Section 4.4 ). 4.1 Experimental Setup Data and metric. We evaluate PromptOps on FairBotBench , which comprises 600 German–English e-commerce conversations with human reference annotations across three dimensions: bias, toxicity, and personalization [ 11 ] . Each run processes a stream of 500 conversation turns, and each experimental condition is repeated on three separately sampled streams to reduce sensitivity to individual stream samples. We follow the iterative procedure outlined by PromptOps . Consequently, during prompt optimization, only observations encountered so far may be accessed, never future ones. For each turn, we average the three associated human reference annotations on the 1 1 – 5 5 scale and use the resulting value as reference feedback. Our primary error measure is mean absolute error (MAE), where lower values indicate closer agreement between judge predictions and human reference scores. The initial judge prompt is generated using the DeepEval implementation of G-Eval 4 4 4 https://deepeval.com/docs/metrics-llm-evals . Following the procedure described by [ 16 ] , we provide a description of the evaluation criteria from which the evaluation steps are synthesized. The resulting prompt serves as the common starting point for all PromptOps runs. When applied without subsequent optimization, it also defines the static baseline used in the drift experiments. The input criteria and the generated G-Eval prompt are documented in Appendix 0.A . Models. We use two judge backends and one expert model: GPT-5.4-nano with low reasoning effort serves as the proprietary judge backend, while GPT-5.4 with high reasoning effort serves as the expert model used during prompt optimization. As an open-weight judge backend, we use the gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M quantization of Gemma 4 5 5 5 https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF . The OpenAI models are accessed through the OpenAI API, whereas Gemma 4 is served locally using the llama.cpp server module with default settings. For each condition, we record cumulative token usage to characterize the computational cost of the different Dispatcher configurations. Because tokenization differs across model families, token counts are compared only between configurations using the same judge backend. Dispatcher, Sample Selector, and Optimizer. We consider a total of 13 Dispatcher pipelines in this work comprising the five Optimizers described in Section 3 . Before the main evaluation, we tune Optimizer parameters on a small stream of 49 turns from FairBotBench , disjoint from those used during evaluation. Our default Sample Selector policy, NewElements , uses observations received since the preceding optimization pass as training records and the training records from the preceding pass as the development set. Detailed descriptions of Dispatcher configurations, Optimizer parameters, and Sample Selectors are reported in Appendix 0.B . Controller. Unless stated otherwise, experiments use a deterministic periodic Controller with p = 20 p=20 . This schedule places optimization passes more densely near the beginning of the stream and increasingly sparsely thereafter. For a stream of 500 500 items, optimization passes are thus scheduled, following Equation 1 , at steps t ∈ { 20 , 50 , 95 , 163 , 265 , 417 } t\in\{20,50,95,163,265,417\} . Together with the initial G-Eval prompt, these six passes yield at most seven distinct prompt versions per run. An optimization pass does not necessarily change the prompt, as an optimizer may retain the current prompt if it does not identify an improvement. 4.2 Optimizer Screening and Cost–Error Trade-offs We first screen 23 parameterized configurations spanning 13 Dispatcher pipelines. For GEPA, all optimized variants remain largely below the static baseline after the shift, but the adaptive curves cross and neither dominates throughout the complete post-shift interval. The curves approach similar values near the end of both experiments. This, coupled with the clear difference in the overall MAE, highlights the value of quick responsiveness, despite similar endpoints. (a) Rubric Synthesis. (b) GEPA. Figure 6 : Median rolling MAE (lower values are better) computed over a sliding evaluation window of 50 observations, for High–Small, Low–Big, the periodic Controller, and the static initial-prompt baseline. The dotted vertical line marks the distribution boundary, item 214. 5 Discussion No universally best Optimizer. Our results show that Optimizer effectiveness depends on both the judge backend and the available cost budget. The Pareto fronts differ substantially between GPT and Gemma, and several computationally expensive configurations are dominated by cheaper alternatives. Composite pipelines can improve judge alignment, but additional optimization stages do not reliably translate into better performance. Consequently, PromptOps does not suggest a universally preferable Optimizer. Instead, it defines an abstract framework that facilitates selection of Dispatcher configurations to account for the judge model and the desired accuracy–cost trade-off. Adaptation can cause specialization. Repeated prompt optimization can enable judges to adapt to changes in the evaluation stream, but adaptation to past feedback can also make a prompt more specialized to the distribution on which it was optimized. Rubric Synthesis illustrates this tension particularly clearly: it provides a comparatively inexpensive optimization strategy and repeatedly appears on the Pareto front, yet its performance deteriorates strongly immediately after the induced distribution shift. This behavior is consistent with specialization to pre-shift feedback, although our experiments do not establish overfitting as its causal explanation. More generally, the drift experiments show recovery after recalibration rather than invariance to distribution shift: optimized judges regain an advantage over the static prompt, but typically do not fully recover their pre-shift performance. Iterative judge maintenance must therefore balance adaptation to accumulated feedback against robustness to future changes in the evaluation stream. Triggering is part of the optimization problem. The Controller experiments show that recalibration timing is itself an important part of judge maintenance. Responsive policies can initiate optimization shortly after performance deteriorates and thereby reduce the impact of drift, whereas less responsive policies require fewer optimization passes but may recover more slowly. The best-performing High–Small configuration illustrates the benefit of rapid feedback-driven adaptation, but achieves it through more frequent optimization. Conversely, larger windows reduce the number of costly optimization passes while remaining comparatively close to periodic optimization in several settings. Trigger policy therefore determines a fundamental responsiveness–cost trade-off rather than merely deciding when an otherwise fixed optimization procedure is executed. These results motivate treating when to optimize as a first-class design decision alongside how to optimize . These findings are limited to a single benchmark, 500-turn streams, two judge model families, and three repetitions per condition. Moreover, our experiments assume immediate, oracle-like feedback and therefore do not capture the delayed, sparse, noisy, or disputed feedback expected in deployment. 6 Conclusion PromptOps reframes LLM-as-a-Judge maintenance as a closed-loop control problem with explicit Controller, Dispatcher, Sample Selector, and Optimizer components. large language model judges are not deploy-and-forget components: PromptOps turns their maintenance into an explicit closed-loop control problem, in which different choices of trigger, Optimizer, sampling policy, and optimization pipeline produce materially different accuracy–cost trade-offs and adaptation behavior. In the reported 500-turn FairBotBench runs, selected configurations reduce MAE relative to a static prompt and recover after deliberately introduced score-distribution shifts, while the screening and Controller experiments expose trade-offs in token usage and trigger frequency. These results establish the feasibility of iterative large language model judge maintenance in a constrained setting, but do not yet establish production readiness. Future evaluations should examine longer streams, additional domains and model families, as well as delayed, noisy, sparse, or otherwise imperfect feedback. References [1] L. A. Agrawal, S. Tan, D. ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance

Hangyu Qin Affiliation: National University of Singapore    Junbin Xiao11 1 Corresponding author: junbinxiao@ustc.edu.cn Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Angela Yao Affiliation: National University of Singapore
Abstract

Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, “Where did I leave it?” may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. ReferClaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.

1 Introduction

Egocentric cameras paired with multimodal AI assistants are becoming natural interfaces to the physical world, enabling continuous visual memory, navigation, and daily assistance. Recent benchmarks have advanced episodic memory (Bärmann and Waibel, 2022; Yang et al., 2025b), long-range understanding (Mangalam et al., 2023), and situated assistance (Xiao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2026). Their standard QA protocols, however, evaluate answers against fixed questions and observation histories, rather than how an assistant acquires missing intent information. In practice, user requests are brief and ego-deictic, and the available context may support several interpretations. For “Did she put it back?” (Fig. 1), different persons may perform the same action at different times. Even when both encounters are visible, the intended one may remain unclear. An answer can therefore be compatible with the video yet irrelevant to what the user meant.

Despite this progress, the challenge remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches (Peng et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026) exploit eye gaze and hand gesture as visual or textual prompts for disambiguating user intent. While effective, the gains remain limited for the complexity of real-world interactions. Recent VLMs instead explore proactive request for clarification  (Jian et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), showing that models can ask rather than guess based on the utterance and a single observation. This may suffice for a static image, but may not for dynamic video stream, where different encounters can support different interpretations of the same question (Fig. 1). We therefore study how explicit spatio-temporal interpretations can guide what to ask, how to interpret the response, and which evidence to use for answering.

We formulate intent disambiguation as bounded information acquisition over grounded candidate interpretations. We propose ReferClaw which coordinates three agents around these candidates. The Intention Grounding Agent (IGA) constructs the candidate intents by grounding the question against the observed video, pairing each candidate with its supporting visual evidence, and scores the candidates by evidential support; the Cost-Aware Clarification Agent (CCA) generates and chooses the best clarification question by balancing expected information gain against respondent effort; and the Evidence-Fused Answering Agent (EFA) answers the original question from the resolved intent and its evidence. Their shared state allows clarification responses to refine the candidates or trigger re-grounding. A deterministic controller bounds clarification turns and question complexity, and decides when to ask or answer. ReferClaw also learns from past interactions to reduce recurring disambiguation errors. Following MetaClaw’s two-timescale design (Xia et al., 2026), verified feedback produces intent-specific skills that take effect immediately and process rewards that guide updates to the responsible agent. The skills encode which contrasts distinguish competing interpretations, while agent-level updates target failures in grounding, clarification, or answering. In our evaluation protocol, the annotated target intent, supporting evidence, and answer correctness become available only after each prediction, so updates affect subsequent interactions.

To facilitate the study, we augment two recent egocentric streaming QA benchmarks BuddyVQA  (Qin et al., 2026) and EgoBlind (Xiao et al., 2025) with ambiguity labels, target intents, and spatio-temporal visual evidence. Experiments separate the benefits of clarification from learning, test ambiguity across repeated encounters, and assess transfer to independent image-based clarification benchmarks ClearVQA (Jian et al., 2025) and ContextClarify (Cao et al., 2026). We additionally evaluate well-specified questions and human respondents to examine unnecessary interruptions and the applicability of simulated interactions. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We formulate intent disambiguation in egocentric QA assistance as bounded information acquisition over spatio-temporally grounded interpretations.

  • •

    We develop ReferClaw, which coordinates grounding, clarification, and answering agents through shared candidates, and learns from feedback through intent-specific skills and agent-level updates.

  • •

    We augment two ego-streaming QA benchmarks with intent and grounding annotations, and evaluate clarification, continual adaptation, and transfer under controlled interaction protocols.

2 Related Work

Clarification and User Intent Disambiguation. Clarification establishes common ground by acquiring missing information and resolving alternative interpretations (Clark and Brennan, 1991; Saeidi et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019; Rao and Daumé III, 2018; Min et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Cooperative visual dialog agents (Das et al., 2017) and GuessWhat (de Vries et al., 2017) extend goal-directed question asking to images, and later methods select questions through uncertainty (Abbasnejad et al., 2019) or expected information gain (White et al., 2021). Recent work localizes plausible image regions for ambiguous questions (Chen et al., 2025a), teaches VLMs to request clarification on ClearVQA (Jian et al., 2025), and learns ask-or-answer policies on ContextClarify (Cao et al., 2026). Plug-and-Play Clarifier (Yang et al., 2026) addresses linguistic ambiguity, capture quality, and pointing gestures in egocentric interaction. Existing clarification benchmarks are largely image-based, motivating our augmentation of BuddyVQA and EgoBlind with intent annotations for video-based disambiguation (Sec. 4.1). Methodologically, prior works clarify from the utterance and a single observation; ReferClaw instead focuses on competing interpretations grounded across video history, using shared candidates to connect clarification with evidence selection under bounded respondent effort.

Egocentric and Grounded Video QA. Ego4D (Grauman et al., 2022) evaluates episodic memory, while EgoSchema (Mangalam et al., 2023) tests long-range egocentric video understanding. EgoBlind (Xiao et al., 2025) emphasizes situated assistance, and BuddyVQA (Qin et al., 2026) evaluates ego-deictic and history-dependent questions over a causal stream. GroundVQA (Di and Xie, 2024) and NExT-GQA (Xiao et al., 2024) couple answering with temporal localization, GeLM (Chen et al., 2025b) develops grounded multi-hop reasoning, D2VLM (Zeng et al., 2025) factorizes grounding and answering, and recent systems expose explicit temporal or spatio-temporal evidence for verifiable answers (Meng et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Related systems support interactive video questioning (Wang et al., 2025a), pixel-level conversational grounding (Munasinghe et al., 2025), and streaming evidence retrieval (Di et al., 2025). These methods localize evidence under a single interpretation of the query, so stronger retrieval may confidently ground the wrong referent when several intentions remain plausible. ReferClaw represents the alternatives explicitly and acquires clarifications on which interpretation to guide evidence selection and answering.

Multi-Agent Collaboration. Multi-agent systems coordinate specialized roles through structured communication (Hong et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2026; Dang et al., 2025). Interaction-based adaptation uses self-feedback, verbal reflection, and reusable skills or routines (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025c; Tu et al., 2026). MetaClaw combines fast skill adaptation with slow policy optimization (Xia et al., 2026), while process supervision rewards intermediate steps (Lightman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). ReferClaw adapts these mechanisms to intent disambiguation: skills encode ambiguity triggers and decisive contrasts, while process rewards guide updates to the grounding, clarification, and answering agents.

3 Method

Clarifying an ambiguous question requires three decisions that ordinary VideoQA does not: whether the question admits more than one visually supported interpretation, what to ask so that the user can resolve it at little effort, and how to answer from the interpretation the user selects. ReferClaw assigns each decision to a dedicated agent operating on shared grounded candidate interpretations, coordinated by a fixed controller that bounds the user’s burden (Fig. 2), and learns from verified interaction feedback so that disambiguation mistakes are not repeated.

3.3 Learning From Interaction

Following MetaClaw (Xia et al., 2026), our learning maintains a versioned skill library 𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g} and agent adapters θg\theta_{g} indexed by skill generation gg. Under our prequential protocol (Sec. 4.1), z⋆z^{\star}, e⋆e^{\star}, and the judge’s verdict are revealed only after a prediction is logged. A trajectory whose answer is wrong, whose evidence misses e⋆e^{\star}, or that asked unnecessarily is a verified failure. Verified failures are attributed by type: coverage and grounding failures to IGA, non-separating or unnecessary questions to CCA, and inconsistent answers to EFA. A process-review prompt handles residual cases (91%91\% agreement with manual labels; Appendix B.5). Verified trajectories feed two loops, scheduled by whether the assistant is currently serving requests (Fig. 2, top).

Fast Loop: Intent-specific Skills. Each agent-specific skill records an ambiguity trigger, candidate topology (e.g., one object encountered twice), decisive contrast, corrected action, anti-pattern, and two regression tests against unnecessary asking. Up to three skills, retrieved by trigger–topology embedding similarity, immediately enter the responsible agent’s prompt. For example, a CCA skill contrasts repeated encounters through the user’s visible action rather than their order; Appendix B.6 provides the worked example.

4 Experiments

Our experiments answer four questions. Q1: Does targeted clarification improve intent-aligned and grounded answering over direct and interactive baselines (Sec. 4.2)? Q2: Does grounding the alternatives across time help most when the competing referents are separated in time (same object seen twice / similar objects seen at different moments) rather than visible at once (Sec. 4.4)? Q3: Are the gains obtained with limited user effort (Sec. 4.4)? Q4: Does learning from interaction reduce future errors beyond simpler adaptation (Secs. 4.2 and 4.4)?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

To facilitate our study, we augment two closest-aim egocentric QA datasets with intent-ambiguity labels, minimal supporting temporal intervals and spatial boxes. BuddyVQA (Qin et al., 2026), our primary benchmark, with its causal streaming protocol, ego-deictic expressions, and history-dependent question chains; and EgoBlind-Intent (Xiao et al., 2025), with timestamped assistance questions from blind and visually impaired users, used for zero-shot transfer. We also test transfer on two independent image-based clarification benchmarks, ClearVQA (Jian et al., 2025) and ContextClarify (Cao et al., 2026), treating the image as a one-frame prefix with their official metrics and respondents. More benchmark augmentation details are in Appendix C.

Protocol and Metrics. A model may access only frames observed before the question timestamp and the preceding dialogue; gold labels, resolved questions, intervals, and boxes are never inputs at prediction time; only the latter three and the judge verdict are revealed to learning methods, after a prediction is logged. Answer accuracy uses each benchmark’s multi-reference LLM-as-a-judge protocol over all test inputs, with Conditional and Abstain counted as incorrect; temporal metrics are computed on grounding-eligible questions, spatial metrics and Acc@GQA (Xiao et al., 2024) (we further require correct answer with both T-IoU and S-IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5) on the box-annotated subset. Interactive evaluation additionally reports ambiguity-detection F1, ask precision/recall, clarification accuracy, unnecessary-ask and abstention rates, turns, question tokens, response time, latency, respondent cost, and the utility of Eq. 1. All numbers are means over three fixed stream orders, and all subset values of a row come from the same runs and checkpoint; the full protocol, the population of every metric, and confidence intervals are in Appendices C.4 and E.3.

Baselines and Implementation. We compare against direct MLLMs (Qwen Team, 2026), grounded and streaming VideoQA systems (Meng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Di et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Qin et al., 2026), and interactive clarification methods (Jian et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026). Framework-level baselines and all ReferClaw variants use Qwen3.5-9B, under the same input protocol. To avoid conflating clarification, extra information, and online learning, we evaluate in two regimes. Frozen inference compares fixed systems, including ReferClaw (Base) and its asking-disabled control, which retains grounding, rewriting, and verification. Learning from interaction follows MetaClaw’s online evaluation (Xia et al., 2026): feedback follows each logged prediction and updates affect only later inputs. We compare ReferClaw (Skills) (fast skill adaptation), ReferClaw (Full) (adding agent-attributed GRPO, Eq. 6), Reflexion-style memory (Shinn et al., 2023), and MetaClaw-style adaptation (generic skills, all-adapter updates, final-answer reward). All share the initial system, feedback, stream, and update budget. Details are in Appendix D.

4.2 Main Results

Frozen Inference (Q1): Tab. 1 compares answer accuracy under the streaming protocol. Frozen ReferClaw reaches 66.2%, versus 58.5% for Clarify-or-Answer. Disabling asking while retaining grounding and verification lowers accuracy to 60.5%, giving a 5.7-point matched clarification gain. Improvements also appear on deictic and history-dependent questions: Base reaches 69.0% and 66.8%, respectively, versus 58.3% and 55.2% for Clarify-or-Answer. The category breakdown and published reference results appear in Tab. 1. Learning From Interaction (Q4): Starting from Base, intent-specific skills raise accuracy to 70.1%, and Full reaches 74.3%, versus 67.4% for Reflexion-style memory and 69.5% for MetaClaw-style adaptation. These comparisons measure adaptation under the same feedback and update budget. Sec. 4.4 further tests whether improvements also hold on an unchanged probe set.

Generalization: Fig. 3 addresses two concerns: whether clarification helps beyond our own annotations, and whether it disrupts questions whose intent is already clear. F1 measures ambiguity detection on ClearVQA and the ask/answer decision on ContextClarify; Turns counts questions per input, U-Ask is the unnecessary-ask rate, and latency excludes respondent time. Without training skills or adapters on either image benchmark (protocols and populations in Appendix C.3), enabling clarification raises ClearVQA score from 41.5% to 48.1% and ContextClarify accuracy from 42.9% to 54.8%. These image-based tests assess clarification transfer, not temporal disambiguation. On well-specified BuddyVQA questions, accuracy changes by +0.4+0.4 points and the assistant asks on 4.1% of inputs. Confidence intervals are in Appendix E.3. Joint Grounding and Cross-domain Transfer: Correct answers may not be supported by the intended visual evidence. We therefore also evaluate Acc@GQA on our augmented benchmarks (Tab. 7, Appendix E.1). Frozen Base reaches 36.2% on BuddyVQA versus 35.0% for EG-Reasoner (Huang et al., 2026), while Full reaches 41.8%. Under zero-shot transfer to EgoBlind-Intent (Tab. 2, all thresholds, skills, and adapters frozen; full results for both benchmarks in Tab. 7), Full keeps a 4.0-point Acc@GQA and 5.9-point answer-accuracy advantage over EG-Reasoner, while both metrics drop by 10–12 points relative to BuddyVQA; the drop concentrates on blurred or off-center instances, whereas clarification quality transfers almost fully (Appendix E.2), so the gap lies in perception rather than in the clarification policy.

4.3 Ablation Study

Agents and Shared Candidates:

Tab. 3 evaluates ReferClaw (Full) under matched stream order, backbone, interaction limit, and training budget. Grounded candidates support both intent resolution and clarification: replacing IGA’s candidate evidence with global video lowers Acc@GQA by 11.3 points, while withholding its candidates from CCA reduces clarification success by 16.2 points. The EFA ablations show that selected evidence, the resolved-intent rewrite and history, and verification each contribute to answer quality. Posterior-based stopping also improves accuracy while reducing respondent cost. Together, these results support sharing grounded alternatives across question selection and answering. Appendix E.4 (Fig. 8) maps the four core designs to case types: grounded candidates and contrastive clarification account for the gains on referents separated in time and for staying silent when history resolves the reference, evidence-fused answering for questions that require reasoning after the referent is resolved, and learning from interaction for failure types that recur along the stream, so the designs are complementary rather than redundant. Isolating Clarification: Disabling asking while holding the entering model state and history fixed lowers Full accuracy from 74.3% to 66.9%, measuring the immediate benefit of clarification. A separate online run that never asks reaches 64.8%, reflecting the combined effects on answering and subsequent learning. A top-two clarification heuristic reaches 71.0% at higher respondent cost, supporting selective question choice. Removing the ambiguity gate or cost penalty increases asking frequency, while generic questions reduce clarification success from 81.4% to 64.9%. Full controls and further ablations are in Appendices E.5 and E.6.

4.4 Further Analysis

1. Direct Test of Temporal Ambiguity (Q2). Fig. 7 tests whether the benefit is concentrated in temporal ambiguity by partitioning the referentially underspecified questions into five groups (sizes and assignment rules in Appendix C.2). Frozen Base exceeds Clarify-or-Answer by 19.1 points for repeated encounters with the same object (G2) and 16.1 for similar objects at different times (G3), versus 7.8 for objects visible simultaneously (G1); the Full-minus-Clarify-or-Answer margins annotated in the figure follow the same pattern. When history already resolves the ambiguity (G4), the baselines still ask on about a quarter of the inputs (27.9% for Plug-and-Play Clarifier, 24.4% for Clarify-or-Answer), whereas Base asks on 7.0% and Full on 6.5%; all methods degrade when the target is absent from the proposals (G5). The result visualization (Fig. 9, Appendix E.8) shows both effects on one episode: ReferClaw names two temporally separated encounters in one question and answers the history-resolved follow-up without asking. A separate paired-intent test presents identical video and questions with two mutually exclusive target answers, changing only the respondent’s clarification. Full answers both presentations correctly on 71.3% of pairs (Base: 64.2%), versus 38.8% for Clarify-or-Answer and 33.3% for Plug-and-Play Clarifier; deterministic direct answering scores zero because it receives identical inputs. This tests whether answers follow the clarified intent rather than a fixed interpretation; clarification-quality metrics on the ambiguous set and example traces are in Appendices E.7 and E.8.

2. Efficiency and Respondent Effort (Q3). Fig. 7 averages respondent cost over all inputs; the Full curve sweeps λC\lambda_{C} from 00 (right) to asking disabled (left). Filled markers denote frozen systems and hollow markers Full-based policy controls. Base outperforms frozen clarification baselines at lower cost. Full asks on 18.6% of inputs, averaging 0.22 questions per input. Its questions average 20.6 tokens and take humans 5.1 s to answer, against 24.0 tokens and 6.9 s for Clarify-or-Answer. Removing the cost penalty more than doubles cost without improving accuracy; a fixed two-turn policy also costs more and performs worse. Gains over the matched asking-disabled replay are larger for high-entropy candidates (Fig. 7; Appendix E.9). Timing and cost components are in Appendix E.10. Human-respondent results are reported in Appendix E.11.

3. Learning Dynamics (Q4). On an unchanged held-out probe, Skills improves over Base by 4.2 points and Full by 9.4, compared with 0.9 for Reflexion-style memory and 2.8 for MetaClaw-style adaptation (Fig. 7). Full also cuts failure recurrence from 34.2% to 10.7% with positive backward transfer (++4.1), versus 21.3% and ++1.1 for MetaClaw-style adaptation. Targeted ablations further show that a generic skill schema reduces answer accuracy by 1.8 points and updating all adapters rather than the attributed agent reduces it by 2.0 (Appendix E.6). Since the MetaClaw-style variant alters the skill schema, the adapter-update scope, and the reward jointly, its gap to Full confounds the three factors; the single-factor ablations above disentangle them and attribute a gain to each. Learning curves, recurrence rates, and backward-transfer results are reported in Appendix E.12, and a manual audit of residual errors is provided in Appendix E.9.

5 Conclusion

We studied intent ambiguity in egocentric assistance, where video and dialogue evidence supports multiple possible referents. ReferClaw explicitly represents competing interpretations with spatio-temporal evidence, allowing the same grounded candidates to determine whether to clarify, what to ask, and which evidence to use. Three cooperating agents make these decisions under a fixed interaction budget, while verified feedback is distilled into intent-specific skills and agent-attributed process rewards to reduce recurring errors. On augmented ego-streaming assistance benchmarks, ReferClaw asks more useful clarification questions than strong interactive baselines, improves intent-aligned and jointly grounded answers with lower user effort, and provides the largest gains when competing referents are temporally separated. The learned skills and parameters further improve fixed probes and reduce repeated failures, while the frozen system transfers to two independent image-based clarification benchmarks without degrading well-specified questions.

Ethics Statement

This work adheres to the ICLR Code of Ethics. All video and image data come from publicly released benchmarks (BuddyVQA, EgoBlind, ClearVQA, and ContextClarify) and are used under their licenses. The user study (Appendix B.3) involved adult volunteers who gave informed consent, answered clarification questions about public clips, and were compensated; only anonymized responses and response times were recorded. Because ReferClaw targets assistive use, including questions from blind and visually impaired users, an answer to the wrong interpretation could mislead a user who cannot verify the evidence, and clarification imposes effort. The system therefore grounds answers in verifiable evidence, abstains or gives conditional answers when the intent cannot be resolved, and bounds the number, length, and cost of questions; it remains a research prototype and should not be deployed for safety-critical assistance without validation.

We have taken care to avoid any possible biases or discriminatory outcomes in our research process. No personally identifiable information was used, and no experiments were conducted that could raise privacy or security concerns. We are committed to maintaining transparency and integrity throughout the research process.

Reproducibility Statement

We have made every effort to ensure that the results presented in this paper are reproducible. All code, prompts, trained LoRA adapters, the skill library, and our augmented annotations (intent-ambiguity labels, target intents, supporting intervals, evidence-frame boxes, diagnostic groups, and the paired-intent set) will be provided upon acceptance. The method is specified in Sec. 3 and Appendix B (controller transition table, response likelihood and cost, process reward, promotion rule); all hyperparameters are listed in Tab. 6 and the hardware and optimization setup in Appendix D. The evaluation protocol, including what the assistant and the simulated user receive, when feedback is revealed, and the population of every metric, is documented in Appendix C.4, and all prompts are given verbatim in Appendix F. All benchmarks and backbone or tool models are publicly available. Human-respondent results depend on the recruited participants and are reported separately. We believe these measures will enable other researchers to reproduce our work and further advance the field.

Appendix B Method Details

B.1 Module Instantiation and Candidate Grounding

IGA, CCA, and EFA share a Qwen3.5-9B backbone but use separate LoRA adapters, which keeps the visual representation fixed while allowing agent-specific updates. IGA uses the released GroundVQA checkpoint for coarse temporal proposals, Grounding DINO 1.5 Pro (Ren et al., 2024) for open-vocabulary boxes, and SAM 2 Hiera-Large (Ravi et al., 2025) to propagate the selected box through the retrieved interval. CCA and EFA operate on the resulting evidence cards and Qwen3.5-9B video tokens. BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024a) encodes skills and trajectories for cosine retrieval. The process reward model initializes from Qwen3.5-9B, adds a scalar value head, and is trained to regress the computed reward of Eq. 6 on query trajectories with feedback (held-out Spearman 0.830.83, MAE 0.090.09 on a [0,1][0,1]-scaled reward). The predictive respondent model used by CCA to estimate response likelihoods is the Qwen3.5-9B backbone under the predictive-respondent prompt of Appendix F; it never receives the annotated target intent. The evaluation simulator that generates the actual responses during testing and learning rollouts is Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025a); it receives the hidden target intent and its evidence but never the system posterior, candidate scores, or reference answer. Eight samples per (c,zi)(c,z_{i}) pair estimate each response-class distribution.

B.2 Response Likelihood and Respondent Cost

Response Classes and Likelihood.

Free-text responses are assigned to the nearest response class (a partition cell, “other/none”, uncertain, or invalid/missing) by BGE-M3 embedding similarity. B.4 Interaction Control Algorithm

The interaction controller of Sec. 3.2 is a deterministic state machine over the state (t,𝒵t,pt,ht,ℬt,nrg)(t,\mathcal{Z}_{t},p_{t},h_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t},n_{\mathrm{rg}}), where ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} is the set of banned partitions and nrg∈{0,1}n_{\mathrm{rg}}\in\{0,1\} counts re-grounding passes. Tab. 4 lists its transitions; at every turn the first row whose condition holds is executed, and the implementation, the pseudocode, and the main text share this table. All limits (TmaxT_{\max}, LmaxL_{\max}, MmaxM_{\max}, no repeated partitions) are enforced before generation, so every trajectory terminates within TmaxT_{\max} turns. Two procedures are shared by all rows. AnswerPath(i⋆)(i^{\star}) runs the EFA on candidate i⋆i^{\star} and then the verifier: pass returns the answer; revise regenerates once and returns the answer if the second verdict is pass, otherwise Abstain; abstain returns Abstain. Reground(⋅)(\cdot) runs the IGA once more, with relaxed detector thresholds (initial state) or restricted to the constraint stated in the response (after “other/none”); it may be invoked at most once per question (nrg≤1n_{\mathrm{rg}}\leq 1), new candidates absorb the mass of z∅z_{\varnothing} in proportion to their grounding scores, and an empty result triggers row T1 on the next evaluation.

Three consequences of the table are used in the analysis. First, every formal answer, including each branch of a Conditional output, is produced by the same EFA-then-verifier path, so verifier statistics are comparable across output types. Second, a question is asked only through T3, so the number of questions per input is Nask≤TmaxN_{\mathrm{ask}}\leq T_{\max} and a question can be asked only if n0≥2n_{0}\geq 2 (with n0=1n_{0}=1 the gate is closed). Third, uncertain and invalid responses never change the belief, which matches the candidate-independent failure-class likelihood used when scoring questions (Appendix B.2), so the expected information gain computed before asking and the update executed after asking are consistent.

B.5 Failure Attribution Rules and Their Validation

A verified failure is attributed to one agent by deterministic rules on the logged trajectory wherever possible: z⋆z^{\star} absent from 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, or present but grounded with IoU<0.5\mathrm{IoU}<0.5 against e⋆e^{\star}, attributes to IGA (coverage or grounding failure); z⋆z^{\star} present but placed in the same partition cell as the top competitor of the asked question, or a question asked when all plausible provisional answers already agreed, attributes to CCA (non-separating or unnecessary question); z⋆z^{\star} selected with correct evidence but a wrong or unsupported answer attributes to EFA (inconsistent answer). Only trajectories that match none of these rules are attributed by the process-review prompt of Appendix F. Two authors independently attributed 200 randomly sampled verified failures using the trajectory and feedback (inter-annotator agreement κ=0.86\kappa=0.86; disagreements adjudicated). The deterministic rules cover 84% of the failures and agree with the adjudicated label in 94% of covered cases; the process-review prompt handles the remaining 16% with 78% agreement, for a combined agreement of 91%. Most residual disagreements concern trajectories in which the target intent was covered with borderline IoU (0.40.4–0.50.5) and the question also failed to separate it, i.e., cases with two plausible responsible agents.

B.6 Skill Schema and a Worked Example

Each skill stores an ambiguity trigger, a candidate topology, the decisive visual contrast, the corrected action, an anti-pattern, a retrieval key, and two regression tests (Appendix F gives the evolver prompt and schema). Retrieval uses BGE-M3 cosine similarity between the current trigger–topology description and stored keys with threshold 0.450.45; at most three skills are injected into the responsible agent’s prompt. The following trace illustrates what is learned beyond the initial prompt, which already instructs CCA to contrast occurrences rather than repeat a noun. Failure: for a mug picked up twice in the same kitchen within 40 seconds, CCA asked “the first or the second time?”; the user answered uncertain and the final answer was wrong. Feedback: z⋆z^{\star} was the second encounter, during which the user was pouring. Stored skill (CCA): trigger “same object, repeated encounters, same location, gap <60<60 s”; corrected action “contrast by the user’s action visible in each track (holding vs. pouring), not by order or location”; anti-pattern “ordinal or location contrast for repeated encounters at one place”. Later behavior: on a subsequent kettle question with the same topology, CCA asked “when you were filling it or when you were pouring?”, the response resolved the intent, and the answer was correct. Such action-contrast skills account for 23%23\% of the CCA skills learned on Augmented BuddyVQA.
